translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the jiaxu year, the second year of the Wanli reign (1574), it was time to examine the scholars of the realm in the Metropolitan Examination, and the scholars awaiting examination at the Ministry of Rites numbered nearly four thousand five hundred men. At that time, Minister of Rites Wan Shihe 萬士和 had newly received his appointment and was on the road hastening to answer the summons, so Vice Ministers [Wang] Tang 汪鏜 and [Wang] Shimei 王士美 petitioned for the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty, mindful that the selection of talent is a weighty state institution, commanded your servant [Lü] Tiaoyang 呂調陽 to suspend his duty in attendance at His Majesty's side and, together with Academician [Wang] Xilie 王希烈, take charge of the affair. Your servant is shallow and meager in conduct and ability. Recently, while awaiting punishment in the Ministry of Rites, at the very beginning of Your Imperial Majesty's ascension to the throne, I was the first to be granted promotion and placed in the ranks of the Grand Secretaries. 謬領是役又竊自念力惡其
不出於身也不必爲己臣誠
無可效得藉手是事蒐拔才
俊以備驅使異日者幸不至
顛仆即力不出臣無論已既
陛辭入院誓諸同事者竭晝夜
===

translation_en: … grace so lofty and profound, I fear I have no means to repay even one part in ten thousand; and now I have again unworthily been entrusted with this duty. Yet I privately reflected to myself: "One hates for strength not to exert itself from one's own person, yet it need not be for oneself." Truly, your servant has nothing else to offer, but if I may make use of this task to seek out and select men of talent and distinction to be ready for imperial employment, and if in the future they fortunately do not stumble and fall, then even though the strength does not come from your servant himself, it makes no difference. After taking leave of the throne and entering the examination compound, I swore an oath with all my colleagues to exhaust our strength day and night in carefully grading and evaluating the essays. In compliance with the imperial decision, we selected three hundred men, and have printed their names and those of their essays that can serve as models to form a record, which we present to the throne. According to precedent, whenever there is an examination there is a record, which fully records the admonitory words of the examiners at the beginning and end. In the past, your servant once took the Records of the Metropolitan Examinations (Huishi lu) of successive examination years of our dynasty, perused them, and sighed, saying: "Alas! title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
懼也夫然亦可覘士習矣大
抵創造之初士尚質樸相信
以心告誡之意不煩詞說逮
及百年人文漸盛所爲規誨
亦稍詳密至近歲人文稱極
盛矣然其禁厲防閑之意書
於冊者亦無所不用其至言
===
之詳法之密士習之漓也豈
得已哉雖然高岡鳴鳳梧桐
朝陽氣類相感固有然者況
於人乎是故勳華御世元凱
彙升宰衡登選不仁遠去
聖人一舉錯之間而轉移人心之
機至速矣我

得已哉雖然髙岡鳴鳳梧桐
朝陽氣類相感固有然者况
於人乎是故勳華御世元凱
彚升宰衡登選不仁遠去
聖人一舉錯之閒而轉移人心之
機至速矣我
punctuated: 懼也夫！然亦可覘士習矣。大抵創造之初，士尚質樸，相信以心，告誡之意，不煩詞說。逮及百年，人文漸盛，所爲規誨，亦稍詳密。至近歲人文稱極盛矣，然其禁厲防閑之意，書於冊者，亦無所不用其至。言之詳，法之密，士習之漓也，豈得已哉！雖然，高岡鳴鳳，梧桐朝陽，氣類相感，固有然者，況於人乎？是故勳、華御世，元、凱彙升；宰、衡登選，不仁遠去。聖人一舉錯之間，而轉移人心之機至速矣。我
translation_en: … feared! Yet from this one may also observe the customs of the literati. Generally speaking, at the beginning of the dynasty's founding, scholars esteemed plain simplicity and trusted one another in their hearts; the intent of admonitions did not require elaborate words. When a hundred years had passed, literary culture gradually flourished, and the regulations and instructions provided also became somewhat more detailed and precise. Down to recent years, literary culture has been acclaimed as at its utmost flourishing, yet the intent of strict prohibitions and preventive restraints written into the records has also gone to every possible length. That the words are so detailed and the regulations so dense reflects the thinning of literati customs—how could this have been done by choice! Even so, when the phoenix sings on the high ridge and the wutong tree faces the morning sun, things of the same qi and kind naturally respond to one another; how much more so with human beings? Therefore, when Fangxun [Yao] and Chonghua [Shun] ruled the world, the Eight Worthies (Ba Yuan) and Eight Talents (Ba Kai) advanced together; when the Counselor-in-Chief [Gao Yao] and Yiheng [Yi Yin] were raised and selected, the unbenevolent went far away. translation_en: … Emperor ascended the throne in the prime of his youth. Looking far ahead and pondering deeply, and seeing that people's minds were growing daily more indolent and lax, he thereupon handed down bright edicts and promulgated his benevolent voice, hoping to make a fresh start with the realm through the way of broad impartiality and uprightness. Thereafter, he restored what had fallen into neglect, revitalized regulations and statutes, reiterated the canons for evaluating performance, and enforced strict orders demanding actual results. This year, when the officials from throughout the realm came up for the triennial evaluation, he issued a special edict to the competent authorities to investigate and cite the most conspicuous cases of the worthy and the unworthy, so as to clearly display encouragement and warning. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
慮易聴改觀風行草偃一日
而達乎天下矣諸士委質之
初遘際
昌期語云新浴者振衣新沐者
彈冠誠不可不自愛也往辛
未之試臣嘗以誠之一言爲
告茲豈復有他論無亦再申
===
前說耳夫誠者真實不二即
蕩平正直之理也人臣能以
真實不二之心事
主則忠矣孔子曰臣事君以忠忠
以中心爲義發於由中之實
心即所謂誠也忠與誠同理
而異名者是故大臣格心之

punctuated: 慮，易聴改觀，風行草偃，一日而達乎天下矣。諸士委質之初，遘際昌期。語云：「新浴者振衣，新沐者彈冠。」誠不可不自愛也。往辛未之試，臣嘗以「誠」之一言爲告，茲豈復有他論？無亦再申前說耳。夫誠者，真實不二，即蕩平正直之理也。人臣能以真實不二之心事主，則忠矣。孔子曰：「臣事君以忠。」忠以中心爲義，發於由中之實心，即所謂誠也。忠與誠同理而異名者。是故大臣格心之
translation_en: …and purify their thoughts, transforming what they hear and changing how they view things; like grass bending before the wind, in a single day this reaches throughout the realm. At the very beginning of pledging your allegiance to enter official service, you scholars have encountered a flourishing era. As the saying goes, "He who has just bathed shakes out his robes; he who has just washed his hair dusts off his cap"—truly, one cannot fail to cherish one's own integrity. In the past examination of the xinwei year (1571), I once offered the single word "sincerity" (cheng) as my counsel; how could I now have any other discourse? I would simply reiterate what I said before. Now, sincerity means being genuine, true, and undivided—it is none other than the principle of being broad, level, upright, and straight. When a subject is able to serve his ruler with a genuine, true, and undivided heart, that is loyalty (zhong). Confucius said, "A minister serves his prince with loyalty." Loyalty takes "centering the heart" (zhongxin) as its meaning; issuing forth from a genuine heart within, it is precisely what is called sincerity. Loyalty and sincerity share the same principle under different names. Therefore, a grand minister's benefit in rectifying the ruler's heart…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
益非誠不孚小臣服采之勞
非誠不效疑危難定之勢非
誠不濟艱難重大之託非誠
不勝人臣垂大名建大功於
天下未有不本之實心者非
其心則非其事矣何也爲利
祿而效忠其事似忠其心在
===
利祿也爲名譽而爲善其事
似善其心在名譽也故曰不
誠無物農人之自力其田者
有兼人之力以力他人之田
必不然矣此非其心之說也
夫誠偽之分始於一念在定
其志而已奕者舉棋不定不

===

punctuated: 益，非誠不孚；小臣服采之勞，非誠不效；疑危難定之勢，非誠不濟；艱難重大之託，非誠不勝。人臣垂大名、建大功於天下，未有不本之實心者。非其心，則非其事矣。何也？爲利祿而效忠，其事似忠，其心在利祿也；爲名譽而爲善，其事似善，其心在名譽也。故曰：「不誠無物。」農人之自力其田者，有兼人之力；以力他人之田，必不然矣。此非其心之說也。夫誠偽之分，始於一念，在定其志而已。奕者舉棋不定，不
translation_en: … benefit [of great ministers rectifying the ruler's mind] cannot inspire trust without sincerity; the toil of minor officials performing their duties cannot be effective without sincerity; situations of doubt, peril, and instability cannot be resolved without sincerity; and arduous, momentous charges cannot be borne without sincerity. Among subjects who have handed down great names and established great achievements in the empire, there has never been one who did not base them on a genuine heart. If it is not truly in one's heart, then the deed is not truly one's own. Why is this? If one renders loyalty for the sake of profit and emolument, the deed resembles loyalty, yet the heart is set on profit and emolument; if one does good for the sake of fame and reputation, the deed resembles goodness, yet the heart is set on fame and reputation. Therefore it is said: "Without sincerity there is nothing." A farmer who works his own field exerts twice the strength of others; if he works another man's field, it is certainly not so. This illustrates what is meant by "not being truly in one's heart." Now, the divergence between sincerity and falsity begins with a single thought, and lies simply in fixing one's resolve. text:
勝其耦况有治人之責者乎
臣所云總之不出前人然其
所受之者不過如此諸士若
以爲故說習聞而漫不加省
則前轍未遠

translation_en:
… defeat his opponent; how much more so for one who bears the responsibility of governing others! What your servant has said altogether goes no further than what predecessors have stated, yet what I myself have received and understood is nothing more than this. If the scholars regard these as old sayings and familiar talk and carelessly fail to reflect upon them, then the tracks of previous overturned carts are not far off, and the imperial edicts and decrees are strictly explicit—why should your servant need to multiply empty words!

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰學如不及猶恐失之
唯天下至聖焉能聰明睿知足以有臨也
寬裕溫柔足以有容也發強剛毅足以
有執也齊莊中正足以有敬也文理密
察足以有別也溥博淵泉而時出之
用下敬上謂之貴貴用上敬下謂之尊賢
貴貴尊賢其義一也
===
===
易
大觀在上順而巽中正以觀天下觀盥而
不薦有孚顒若下觀而化也
象曰山上有澤咸君子以虛受人
是故易有太極是生兩儀
夫易彰往而察來而微顯闡幽開而當名
辨物正言斷辭則備矣其稱名也小其
取類也大其旨遠其辭文其言曲而中
其事肆而隱因貳以濟民行以明失得

punctuated:
第壹場
《四書》
子曰：「學如不及，猶恐失之。」
「唯天下至聖，焉能聰明睿知，足以有臨也；寬裕溫柔，足以有容也；發強剛毅，足以有執也；齊莊中正，足以有敬也；文理密察，足以有別也。溥博淵泉，而時出之。」
「用下敬上，謂之貴貴；用上敬下，謂之尊賢。貴貴、尊賢，其義一也。」
《易》
「大觀在上，順而巽，中正以觀天下。觀，盥而不薦，有孚顒若，下觀而化也。」
「《象》曰：山上有澤，咸；君子以虛受人。」
「是故《易》有太極，是生兩儀。」
「夫《易》，彰往而察來，而微顯闡幽，開而當名，辨物正言，斷辭則備矣。其稱名也小，其取類也大。其旨遠，其辭文，其言曲而中，其事肆而隱。因貳以濟民行，以明失得
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books (Sishu)

The Master said: "Learn as though you cannot catch up, and still fear losing what you have gained."

"Only the most sagely in the world have the quickness of apprehension, clearness of discernment, far-reaching intelligence, and all-embracing knowledge sufficient to exercise rule; the magnanimity, generosity, benignity, and gentleness sufficient to embrace others; the impulsiveness, strength, firmness, and resolution sufficient to maintain a firm hold; the self-adjustment, gravity, centrality, and correctness sufficient to command reverence; and the accomplished order, distinction, concentration, and searching penetration sufficient to exercise discrimination. All-embracing and vast, deep and unceasingly springing forth, these qualities come forth in due season." [Note: 焉能 in the transcription stands for 為能 in the received Doctrine of the Mean.]

"For a subordinate to show respect to a superior is called honoring the noble; for a superior to show respect to a subordinate is called venerating the worthy. Honoring the noble and venerating the worthy are one and the same in principle."

Book of Changes (Yi)

"The great spectacle is on high; docile and penetrating, central and correct, so as to be viewed by all under heaven. 'Viewing: the laving of hands, but not yet the offering; there is sincerity and an aspect of solemn dignity'—those below look up toward it and are transformed."

"The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: Above the mountain there is a marsh: Mutual Influence (Xian). Thus the noble man receives others with an open mind."

"Therefore in the Changes there is the Supreme Ultimate; this generates the Two Modes."

"Now the Changes makes clear the past and discerns the future; it makes manifest the minute and elucidates the obscure; opening things up, it assigns fitting names to them, distinguishes myriad things, makes speech correct, and with decisive judgments is complete. The names it cites are small, yet the categories it draws upon are broad. Its purport is far-reaching, its expressions are refined, its words are indirect yet hit the mark, and the matters it treats are set forth plainly yet hold hidden meaning. On account of doubts, it aids the conduct of the people, so as to clarify [the recompense of] loss and gain…"

…and the recompense thereof.

Classic of Documents (Shu):
1. Yi 益 said, "Oh! Be cautious! Maintain vigilance when there is no cause for anxiety, and do not fail to uphold the laws and regulations. Do not wander in idleness; do not indulge to excess in pleasure. In employing the worthy, do not be double-minded; in putting away the wicked, do not hesitate. Do not carry out doubtful plans, and all your purposes will be illustrious. Do not go against the Way to court the praise of the hundred surnames; do not oppose the hundred surnames to follow your own desires. Without slackness and without neglect, the four Yi peoples will come and acknowledge your sovereignty."
2. "As in making a well-seasoned soup, you are the salt and the plum."
3. "I have heard it said: the men of antiquity still admonished and informed one another, protected and cherished one another, and taught and instructed one another."

1. "Before the sky is dark with rain, I strip that mulberry root-bark and bind tight the window and door."
2. "They yoke those four steeds, the four steeds so grand. With red knee-covers and gold-adorned slippers, they assemble at court in orderly array."
3. "Bright, bright is the Son of Heaven, his good renown never ending."
4. "From the beginning of the sacrifice, up to now it has had success; this is the auspicious sign of Zhou."

What he lavished forth as moral bounty and established as laws and institutions directly rivaled and surpassed those of Tang, Yu, and flourishing Zhou. Today, what is recorded in the Record of Sacred Governance (Shengzheng ji) and other books shines as brightly as the sun and stars; can you set forth and elaborate upon their splendour? The Sacred Ancestor also once composed the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun) in one compilation, raising up both virtue and law to clearly instruct future descendants; can we hear an account of its main thrust? Successive sacred emperors inherited the throne one after another, flourishingly expanding upon and continuing their predecessors' work. Coming down to Emperor Jing, Temple Name Xiaozong (r. 1487–1505), he nurtured all with tolerance and generosity so that moral bounty grew ever deeper; Emperor Su, Temple Name Shizong (r. 1521–1567), ruled with heroic decisiveness so that laws and institutions were ever more invigorated. punctuated:
前烈有光矣。而今談者猶以為德澤未盡洽，法度未盡舉，則固憂盛危明之意也。茲欲培養修飭，益宣昭令緒，永登太平，何道而可？夫古之人臣，言則稱烈祖之訓；今諸士述本朝德法以對，又何讓焉？

問：三王之教，所祖不同，故漢人述忠、敬、質、文之尚，至纖悉矣。然四者之不相沿也，果自名而自尚之耶？抑人以其政窺之乎？夫質文代變之端，與天地之運故相流通者也。乃儒者稱皇降而帝，帝降而王，若不可返者；而又有三正循環、五德終始之論，其說果孰為當與？三代而上，歷年長者莫如周；三代而下，長者莫如漢。二季之世，天下何其文盛也！然勢極致至，而天下卒返於質，則循環終始之說，無亦可徵與？我國家熙平二百餘年，其初上下之所漸濡，
translation_en:
… shines brightly upon the achievements of former reigns. Yet present-day commentators still consider that benevolent grace has not yet fully permeated the realm and institutional regulations have not yet been fully put into effect—this is, to be sure, in the spirit of worrying in times of flourishing and being vigilant in an age of enlightenment. If we now wish to nurture and put things in order, further manifest the illustrious heritage, and ascend forever to grand peace, by what way can this be achieved? In antiquity, when ministers spoke, they cited the instructions of their meritorious ancestors; today, when you gentlemen recount the virtue and laws of our dynasty in your replies, why should you hold back?

Question: The teachings of the Three Kings differed in what they took as their foundation; hence Han scholars gave a most detailed account of the respective emphases on loyalty (zhong), reverence (jing), substance (zhi), and cultural refinement (wen). Yet in not following one another in these four respects, did the rulers themselves name and esteem them? Or did later observers discern them from their governance? Now, the beginnings of the alternating succession of substance and cultural refinement naturally flow in correspondence with the operations of Heaven and Earth. Yet Confucian scholars claim that the age of August Sovereigns declined into that of Emperors, and that of Emperors declined into that of Kings, as if this could never be reversed; while at the same time there are the theories of the cycle of the Three Commencements (sanzheng) and the succession of the Five Virtues (wude). Which of these doctrines is in fact valid? From the Three Dynasties upward, none endured longer in years than the Zhou; from the Three Dynasties downward, none endured longer than the Han. In the final periods of those two dynasties, how exuberant was the cultural refinement of the world! Yet when a trend reaches its utmost extreme, the world ultimately returns to substance—does this not also serve to verify the theory of cyclical succession? Our dynasty has enjoyed bright peace for over two hundred years. In the beginning, that with which superiors and inferiors were imbued …

也然與否與聖人能通其變於未窮救

之道必有要焉可指而陳與夫世道汙

擁之

===

之而已無乃薄道待士而適以驅之歟

問：士之生也，則願析圭儋爵而垂鴻名于世矣。故爵祿、名譽，人主御士之轡銜也。至有謂「祿肥則士不死」，與「三代而下，士惟恐不好名」者。信其言也，士直用術羈之而已，無乃薄道待士而適以驅之歟？嘗觀兩漢：高祖求賢之詔，謂吾能尊顯士，故時奮尊顯，或起自刀筆，或自羊豕之間，或與時變化，或與人主俱上下；至於貢、薛、韋、匡頹其波，而苟祿者相望，爵祿安可得士也？世祖敦尚名教，而士勵…
translation_en:
…was very simple and unadorned. Coming down to the present day, renown, institutions, and cultural refinement have flourished richly. Yet men of discernment are quite worried at heart about this, holding that moral instruction and customs have grown gradually thinner, popular tastes gradually more extravagant, discussions and debates gradually more tedious, and literary writings gradually more eccentric—that these are the abuses of an excess of cultural refinement. Is this so, or is it not? The sage is able to carry through transformations before things reach exhaustion; the fundamental way to remedy exhaustion cannot be accomplished entirely through legal prohibitions and restrictions. In the way of carrying through transformation so as to suit the people, there must be some essential point—can you point it out and set it forth? The juncture between the decline and flourishing of the Way of the world is something to which scholars ought to devote their minds; I wish to deliberate and discuss it together with you [?].

Question: When a scholar is born into this world, he desires to receive a jade tablet of investiture, bear noble rank, and hand down a great name to the world. Therefore, noble rank and emolument, together with reputation and praise, are the reins and bit by which a ruler controls scholars. Yet there have even been those who said that "when emoluments are rich, scholars will not die for duty," and that "from the Three Dynasties downward, the only fear concerning scholars is that they might not love reputation." If one believes these words, then scholars are merely to be haltered by statecraft and manipulation—is this not treating scholars according to a meager Way and thereby actually driving them away? Let us examine the Two Han dynasties: Emperor Gaozu's edict seeking worthy men declared, "I am able to honor and make illustrious the scholars." Thus at the time those who rose to honor and eminence either started out as minor clerks of knife and brush, or came from among sheep and swine; some changed and adapted with the times, while others rose and fell in step with the ruler. By the time Gong Yu 貢禹, Xue Guangde 薛廣德, Wei Xuancheng 韋玄成, and Kuang Heng 匡衡 let that wave degenerate, those who unscrupulously clung to emolument could be seen everywhere in succession—how then could rank and emolument succeed in winning true scholars? Emperor Shizu [Guangwu] earnestly esteemed moral teaching and reputation, and yet among the scholars who strove after…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
於名者或令東海致譏或使壺山蒙耻
或規盛名難副或誚讓封非義至於俊
厨顧及靡其風而名實大壞名譽又安
可得士也周語曰先王之治為班爵貴
賤以列之為令聞嘉譽以享之於兩者
豈輕哉賚予善人有頌官民材有制大
常有銘大烝有祭勳功庸勞力多異其
名何殊於漢而得士獨盛也豈先王所
以用此有異抑不恃此而他有所恃歟
===
由斯而談恃爵祿名譽以籠士非義也
而士有逃之者於義何似荀卿之譏楚
子發趙充國之辭浩星賜也非篤論歟
此可明君臣事使之義也試言其槩
問自古國必有史昔人有謂觀百國春秋
者則知作者盖多家也然不可睹矣至
今傳者如國語左傳此一人作也而迥
然異者何歟漢良史莫如馬遷班固並
纂漢事宜無不同矣顧後世有作班馬

punctuated:
於名者，或令東海致譏，或使壺山蒙耻，或規盛名難副，或誚讓封非義，至於俊、厨、顧、及靡其風，而名實大壞，名譽又安可得士也？《周語》曰：「先王之治，為班爵貴賤以列之，為令聞嘉譽以享之。」於兩者豈輕哉？賚予善人有《頌》，官民材有制，大常有銘，大烝有祭，勳、功、庸、勞、力、多異其名，何殊於漢，而得士獨盛也？豈先王所以用此有異，抑不恃此而他有所恃歟？由斯而談，恃爵祿名譽以籠士，非義也；而士有逃之者，於義何似？荀卿之譏楚子發、趙充國之辭浩星賜也，非篤論歟？此可明君臣事使之義也，試言其槩。

問：自古國必有史。昔人有謂觀《百國春秋》者，則知作者盖多家也，然不可睹矣。至今傳者，如《國語》、《左傳》，此一人作也，而迥然異者何歟？漢良史莫如馬遷、班固，並纂漢事，宜無不同矣；顧後世有作《班馬
translation_en:
…by reputation: some caused the Eastern Sea to incur ridicule, some brought shame upon Mount Hu, some admonished that a grand reputation is hard to live up to, and some rebuked the yielding of a fief as unrighteous. Eventually, when the "heroes" (jun), "kitchens" (chu), "guides" (gu), and "associates" (ji) swept the trend along, name and reality were severely corrupted—how then could reputation possibly win true scholars? The Discourses of Zhou (Zhouyu) says: "In the governance of the former kings, they established graded ranks of noble and base to array them, and created fine renown and admirable praise to reward them." Did they take either of these two lightly? For bestowing gifts on good men there were the Sacrificial Odes (Song); for appointing men of talent among the people there were regulations; on the Grand Standard (tai chang) there were inscriptions; at the Great Winter Sacrifice (da zheng) there were offerings; and kingly merit (xun), state merit (gong), civil merit (yong), toil (lao), force (li), and battle achievement (duo) each had their distinct names. How did this differ from the Han, and yet the former kings alone flourished in winning scholars? Was there a difference in how the former kings used these, or did they not rely on these alone, having something else on which they relied? Speaking from this perspective, relying on rank, emolument, and reputation to ensnare scholars is unrighteous; yet when scholars flee from them, how does that stand in relation to righteousness? Xun Qing's criticism of Zifa of Chu and Zhao Chongguo's refusal of Haoxing Ci—are these not sound arguments? Through this one may clarify the principles of how ruler and minister employ and serve one another; try to state the general outline.

Question: Since antiquity, every state has necessarily had its history. Someone in the past spoke of having read the Spring and Autumn Annals of a Hundred States (Baiguo Chunqiu), from which we know there were indeed many authors, though they can no longer be seen. Among those transmitted to the present, such as the Discourses of the States (Guoyu) and the Zuo Commentary (Zuozhuan), both were written by a single man—why then are they so vastly different? Among the fine historians of the Han, none surpassed Sima Qian and Ban Gu. Both compiled Han affairs, so there ought to be no differences between them; yet in later ages someone wrote the Similarities and Differences Between Ban and Ma (Ban Ma…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
異同者果何所指歟今觀其所讎校特
紀傳世家耳二史之同異果盡於是歟
他如十表八表之殊八書十志之別豈
固各有見歟夫二史具在也諸凡且異
而不異宜同而不同者亦可縷指而數
歟繼遷固而述漢事者亡慮數十家乃
其最著者有撰漢紀而史稱辭約事詳論
辨多美者有撰後漢書而自謂體大思
精不減過秦論者有撰後漢紀而時號
===
精密者有撰漢晉春秋而世稱公論者
皆所謂齊足而並馳者也其述作大較
與二子同歟異歟王通氏曰史之失自
遷固始也夫仲尼絕筆世無全史以遷
固之勤猶然見譏於後世然則著作之
義安所折衷而後可歟諸士博綜羣籍
二史固所詳覽也願畢言之以觀考古
之學
問書曰任官惟賢才易曰何以聚人曰財

與二子同歟異歟王通氏曰史之失自

義安所折衷而後可歟諸士博綜奉籍
二史固所詳覽也願畢言之以觀考古
之學
問書曰任官惟賢才易曰何以聚人曰財
punctuated:
《異同》者，果何所指歟？今觀其所讎校，特紀、傳、世家耳，二史之同異果盡於是歟？他如十表、八表之殊，八書、十志之別，豈固各有見歟？夫二史具在也，諸凡且異而不異、宜同而不同者，亦可縷指而數歟？繼遷、固而述漢事者，亡慮數十家，乃其最著者：有撰《漢紀》而史稱辭約事詳、論辨多美者；有撰《後漢書》而自謂體大思精，不減《過秦論》者；有撰《後漢紀》而時號精密者；有撰《漢晉春秋》而世稱公論者，皆所謂齊足而並馳者也。其述作大較，與二子同歟、異歟？王通氏曰：「史之失，自遷、固始也。」夫仲尼絕筆，世無全史，以遷、固之勤，猶然見譏於後世，然則著作之義，安所折衷而後可歟？諸士博綜羣籍，二史固所詳覽也，願畢言之，以觀考古之學。
問：《書》曰：「任官惟賢才。」《易》曰：「何以聚人曰財。」
translation_en:
…Similarities and Differences Between Ban and Ma (Ban Ma yitong)—what, in truth, did it point to? When we examine what it collates today, it covers merely the basic annals, biographies, and hereditary houses; are the similarities and differences between the two histories really exhausted by these? As for other matters, such as the divergence between the ten chronological tables and the eight tables, or the distinction between the eight treatises and the ten monographs, did each historian indeed have his own particular insight? Now, both histories are extant in their entirety; regarding all the instances where they ought to differ[?] yet do not differ, or ought to agree yet do not agree, can these also be enumerated one by one? Those who succeeded Sima Qian and Ban Gu in recounting the affairs of the Han dynasty number roughly several dozen schools, and among the most illustrious of them: there was one who compiled the Annals of the Han (Hanji), whom the histories praised for concise wording, detailed events, and disquisitions of great beauty [Xun Yue 荀悅]; there was one who compiled the Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu), who himself claimed that his work was grand in scope and refined in thought, no less than the "Disquisition Finding Fault with Qin" (Guo Qin lun) [Fan Ye 范曄]; there was one who compiled the Annals of the Later Han (Hou Hanji), which in its time was acclaimed as meticulous and exact [Yuan Hong 袁宏]; and there was one who compiled the Spring and Autumn of the Han and Jin (Han Jin chunqiu), which the world praised as impartial judgment [Xi Zuochi 習鑿齒]. All of these are what may be called steeds running neck and neck. In the general outlines of their historical writing, do they agree with or differ from the two masters? Wang Tong 王通 said: "The failings of historiography began with Sima Qian and Ban Gu." Now, after Confucius ceased writing, the world had no complete history; yet despite the diligence of Sima Qian and Ban Gu, they were still criticized by later generations. Where, then, must the principles of historical authorship find their balanced standard so as to be acceptable? You gentlemen have broadly synthesized the myriad texts, and the two histories are certainly works you have perused in detail; I wish you to speak of this in full, so that I may observe your learning in the examination of antiquity.

Question: The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "In appointing to office, employ only the worthy and talented." The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "Whereby to gather the people is called wealth." …

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
才與財經國者所急也或謂天下無乏
才時又謂天之生才不數者或謂地利
無窮人有遺力又謂財貨止有此數者
其言有餘不足孰爲近攷之漢唐宋創
業時官職歳入甚簡也而用未嘗乏迨
其季年不啻數倍于初且有乏人之財
之憂何若是相反歟我
國家設官經費載在職掌賦有常額官有常
員固至足也二百年来品流日衆財計
===
日廣廼一遇緩急並稱缺乏夫豈不足
而然歟今
明主在上留神於人才國計頒
訓諭廷臣之勅裁
內廷光祿之供頃又甄敘肆覲之吏嚴稽存
積之逋
德意甚盛也持銓主計之臣思所以仰承萬一
長策安在夫士競于進而財糜于侈殆
非獨病不足也茲欲求用人理財之要

punctuated: 才與財，經國者所急也。或謂天下無乏才時，又謂天之生才不數者；或謂地利無窮、人有遺力，又謂財貨止有此數者。其言有餘、不足，孰爲近？攷之漢、唐、宋創業時，官職、歳入甚簡也，而用未嘗乏；迨其季年，不啻數倍于初，且有乏人之財之憂。何若是相反歟？我國家設官、經費載在職掌，賦有常額，官有常員，固至足也。二百年来，品流日衆，財計日廣，廼一遇緩急，並稱缺乏。夫豈不足而然歟？今明主在上，留神於人才、國計，頒訓諭廷臣之勅，裁內廷光祿之供，頃又甄敘肆覲之吏，嚴稽存積之逋，德意甚盛也。持銓、主計之臣，思所以仰承萬一，長策安在？夫士競于進而財糜于侈，殆非獨病不足也。茲欲求用人、理財之要，
translation_en:
… Talent and fiscal resources are the urgent concerns of those who govern the state. Some say that the realm never experiences a time when it lacks talent, while others say that Heaven does not bring forth talent frequently; some say that the wealth of the earth is inexhaustible and people still have untapped strength, while others say that wealth and goods exist only in a fixed amount. In speaking of surplus and insufficiency, which view comes closer to the truth? When we examine the founding eras of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, official posts and annual revenues were quite simple and modest, yet they never suffered from a shortage for their needs; by their closing years, however, though these were several times greater than at the beginning, there were nonetheless worries over a lack of men and fiscal resources [?]. Why was there such a contradiction?

In our dynasty, the establishment of offices and regular expenditures are recorded in the statutory duties of the ministries; taxes have fixed quotas and officials have fixed complements, which are truly most sufficient. Over the past two hundred years, those in the official ranks and streams of entry have grown daily more numerous, and fiscal revenues and accounting have grown daily more expansive; yet the moment an urgent crisis arises, a scarcity of both is proclaimed. Can it really be because of actual insufficiency that things are so?

Today our enlightened ruler is on the throne, devoting his attention to human talent and state finances: he has promulgated an imperial command instructing and admonishing the court officials, curtailed the supplies furnished to the Inner Court by the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and recently evaluated and ranked the officials attending the triennial court audience while strictly auditing accumulated tax arrears. His virtuous intentions are magnificent indeed. As the ministers in charge of personnel selection and fiscal administration ponder how to reverently fulfill even one ten-thousandth of his wishes, where does the long-term strategy lie? Now, when scholars compete for advancement and wealth is squandered on extravagance, the malady is surely not merely one of insufficiency. Here, if we wish to seek the essentials of employing men and managing finances, …

text:
第壹塲
四書
子曰學如不及猶恐失之
孫鑛
同考試官員外郎陳批體聖人講心學語莊潔而
理明徹
同考試官檢討習批莊重典雅文之復古者
同考試官檢討沈批發揮爲學勤篤之意深切
著明盖嘗實用其力者
===
同考試官編修徐批抒思冲融屬詞嚴密
考試官侍讀學士王批說理精確
考試官大學士呂批典實
聖人勉人爲學期於必得而已盖學以致其道
者也力求其得而心慮其失斯其庶幾乎且夫
道不可以易求學莫貴于有得人之于學其惕
勵者存乎心而力實副之是學之須于力者甚
急也其進爲者存乎力而心實主之是力之須
于心者尤急也君子于此而知所從事矣是故

「子曰：學如不及，猶恐失之。」
孫鑛
同考試官員外郎陳批：體聖人講心學，語莊潔而理明徹。
同考試官檢討習批：莊重典雅，文之復古者。
同考試官檢討沈批：發揮爲學勤篤之意，深切著明，盖嘗實用其力者。
同考試官編修徐批：抒思冲融，屬詞嚴密。
考試官侍讀學士王批：說理精確。
考試官大學士呂批：典實。
聖人勉人爲學，期於必得而已。盖學以致其道者也，力求其得，而心慮其失，斯其庶幾乎！且夫道不可以易求，學莫貴于有得。人之于學，其惕勵者存乎心，而力實副之，是學之須于力者甚急也；其進爲者存乎力，而心實主之，是力之須于心者尤急也。君子于此，而知所從事矣。是故
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
"The Master said: 'Learn as if you could not reach your goal, and still fear losing what you have gained.'" [Analects 8.17]
Sun Kuang 孫鑛
Comment by Associate Examiner Vice Director Chen 陳: He embodies the sage in discussing the learning of the mind; the language is dignified and pure, and the reasoning is clear and penetrating.
Comment by Associate Examiner Examining Editor Xi 習: Dignified and classically elegant, an essay that restores antiquity.
Comment by Associate Examiner Examining Editor Shen 沈: It brings out the meaning of diligence and earnestness in learning, deeply relevant and manifestly clear; surely one who has actually applied his own strength to it.
Comment by Associate Examiner Junior Compiler Xu 徐: The expression of thought is harmonious and blended; the composition of words is rigorous and tight.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Wang 王: The explanation of principles is precise and exact.
Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Lü 呂: Classical and substantive.
When the sage encourages people to engage in learning, he aims simply at their assuredly attaining it. For learning is that by which one reaches the Way; if one strives with all one's strength to attain it, while in one's mind one worries about losing it, is one not close to the mark! Moreover, the Way cannot be easily sought, and in learning nothing is more valuable than genuine attainment. In a person's relation to learning, what keeps him vigilant and spurred on abides in the mind, while his strength actually matches it—thus learning's need for strength is most urgent; what makes him advance and act abides in his strength, while the mind actually directs it—thus strength's need for the mind is even more urgent. Understanding this, the gentleman knows what to devote himself to. Therefore…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
窮理格物以致其知孜孜然殫吾精以事之而
惟日不足若有不及知者焉反躬力行以踐其
實亹亹然竭吾才以從之而日不暇給若有不
及行者焉夫知如此其勤則知固無失矣而警
省之心猶日廑于中意者道之微妙難窮而終
莫我知也所以求其知者爲益勤行如此其篤
則行固無失矣而悚惕之念猶日切于懷意者
吾之學力有限而終莫能行也所以求其行者
爲益篤方度其始卽慮其終憂勤並切無敢一
===
息之暫寧蓋必如是而後所謂不及者可與及
矣方求其得遽恐其失志氣相須無敢須臾之
少懈蓋必如是而後所謂恐失者可弗失矣嗚
呼學之道何以加于是哉抑此未易言也蓋雖下
學有天道存焉乾天德也易曰天行健君子以
自強不息惟夫子足以當之其曰發憤忘食樂
以忘憂不知老之將至噫純亦不已聖人之合
德于天者此夫子之自道也此所謂弟子不能

德于天者此夫子之自道也此所謂弟子不能
學也
punctuated: 窮理格物以致其知，孜孜然殫吾精以事之，而惟日不足，若有不及知者焉；反躬力行以踐其實，亹亹然竭吾才以從之，而日不暇給，若有不及行者焉。夫知如此其勤，則知固無失矣，而警省之心猶日廑于中，意者道之微妙難窮，而終莫我知也，所以求其知者爲益勤；行如此其篤，則行固無失矣，而悚惕之念猶日切于懷，意者吾之學力有限，而終莫能行也，所以求其行者爲益篤。方度其始，卽慮其終，憂勤並切，無敢一息之暫寧，蓋必如是，而後所謂不及者可與及矣；方求其得，遽恐其失，志氣相須，無敢須臾之少懈，蓋必如是，而後所謂恐失者可弗失矣。嗚呼！學之道何以加于是哉？抑此未易言也。蓋雖下學，有天道存焉。乾，天德也，《易》曰：「天行健，君子以自強不息。」惟夫子足以當之。其曰：「發憤忘食，樂以忘憂，不知老之將至。」噫！「純亦不已」，聖人之合德于天者，此夫子之自道也，此所謂弟子不能學也。
translation_en: …exhausting principle and investigating things to extend one's knowledge, tirelessly expending all my mental energy in pursuing it, finding the day too short, as though I could never reach such knowledge; and reflecting on oneself and practicing vigorously to fulfill its reality, unwearyingly exhausting all my talent in following it, having no leisure the whole day through, as though I could never reach such practice. Now when seeking knowledge is this diligent, surely nothing is lost in knowing; yet an alert and self-examining mind remains daily anxious within, suspecting that the subtlety of the Way is hard to exhaust and that in the end I might never know it—and so the effort to seek that knowledge becomes all the more diligent. When practice is this earnest, surely nothing is lost in acting; yet a fearful and apprehensive thought remains daily urgent in the heart, suspecting that my strength in learning is limited and that in the end I might never be able to carry it out—and so the effort to seek that practice becomes all the more earnest. Just as one contemplates the beginning, one immediately worries about the end; anxiety and diligence are equally acute, not daring to take even a single breath's momentary rest. For only when it is like this can what was considered unattainable finally be attained. Just as one seeks to obtain it, one suddenly fears losing it; will and vital energy mutually sustain each other, not daring to slacken even for an instant. For only when it is like this can what one feared losing not be lost. Alas! What more could be added to the Way of learning than this? Yet this is not easy to speak of. For even in lower-level learning, the Way of Heaven is present therein. Qian is the virtue of Heaven. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "The movement of Heaven is full of power; thus the superior man makes himself strong and untiring." Only the Master is worthy of matching this. As he said: "In eager pursuit of knowledge he forgets his food, in the joy of its attainment he forgets his sorrows, and he does not perceive that old age is coming on." Ah! "Unceasing in his purity"—the sage matching his virtue with Heaven—this is what the Master said of himself, and this is what is meant by "what we disciples cannot learn."

The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) discusses how the most sagely possesses the entirety of heavenly virtue, uniting substance and function into one. Now, heavenly virtue has its natural substance and function; to possess it in its entirety is thus to unite them into one. Who other than the most sagely could be capable of this? The Doctrine of the Mean adduces this to illuminate the Way of Heaven. It means that Heaven endows human beings with their nature and substance, and complete virtue is contained therein; combined, there is only a single root, yet analyzed, there are ten thousand differentiations. That which is achieved through practice is not of Heaven—is this not found only in the most sagely in the world! Uniting [the complete dynamic and static aspects of the Supreme Ultimate]…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
極動靜之全氣禀其完而不累得天地中和之
至理極其備而無遺其具乎質之美也則聰明
睿知縱于天而居上臨下之體備焉貞明未運
之先而吾已知其無遺照矣其具乎性之全也
則仁義禮智根于心而容執敬别之用裕焉大
業未徵之際而吾已知其有全能矣純乎天不
間以人足乎己無待于外至聖之德天德也有
不積中而發外者哉方夫物之未感而德與心
而相涵則溥博不可禦淵泉不可窮渾然積於
===
中而天下之大本立矣及夫時之既至而德與
化而並運則隨事以順應因物以曲成沛然見
於外而天下之達道行焉由其積之大而時出
之所以覆冒天下者此也由其積之深而時出
之所以澤潤生民者此也體用相須内外合一
至哉聖人之德即天道之敦化而川流者也聖
同天不既深乎抑至聖之所以合德于天者性
之也有本焉一誠而已矣誠則無貳無貳則無
息盛德大業所由出也由教而入者明善以復

punctuated: 極動靜之全，氣禀其完而不累；得天地中和之至，理極其備而無遺。其具乎質之美也，則聰明睿知縱于天，而居上臨下之體備焉；貞明未運之先，而吾已知其無遺照矣。其具乎性之全也，則仁義禮智根于心，而容執敬别之用裕焉；大業未徵之際，而吾已知其有全能矣。純乎天，不間以人；足乎己，無待于外。至聖之德，天德也。有不積中而發外者哉？方夫物之未感，而德與心而相涵，則溥博不可禦，淵泉不可窮，渾然積於中，而天下之大本立矣。及夫時之既至，而德與化而並運，則隨事以順應，因物以曲成，沛然見於外，而天下之達道行焉。由其積之大而時出之，所以覆冒天下者此也；由其積之深而時出之，所以澤潤生民者此也。體用相須，内外合一。至哉聖人之德，即天道之敦化而川流者也！聖同天，不既深乎？抑至聖之所以合德于天者，性之也，有本焉，一誠而已矣。誠則無貳，無貳則無息，盛德大業所由出也。由教而入者，明善以復
translation_en:
… [unites] the completeness of the Supreme Ultimate's activity and tranquility, receiving its vital force in full perfection without encumbrance; and attains the utmost of the equilibrium and harmony of Heaven and Earth, with moral principle wholly complete and nothing left out.

In possessing the beauty of innate substance, his quickness of apprehension, intelligence, insight, and wisdom are lavished upon him by Heaven, and the substance requisite for occupying the high position and overseeing those below is complete within him; even before his pure brightness is set in motion, we already know that nothing escapes its illumination. In possessing the fullness of human nature, humanity, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom are rooted in his heart, and the functions of being magnanimous, resolute, reverent, and discerning are abundant within him; even before great enterprises are manifested, we already know that he possesses complete capability. Purely of Heaven, unmixed with human artifice; self-sufficient, depending on nothing external—the virtue of the supreme sage is the virtue of Heaven. How could it fail to accumulate within and issue forth without?

When external things have not yet stirred him, and virtue and mind mutually nourish one another, it is all-embracing and irresistible, deep and inexhaustible; it accumulates seamlessly within, and the great foundation of the world is established. When the proper time arrives, and his virtue moves in concert with cosmic transformation, he responds smoothly according to affairs and brings all things to intricate completion according to their nature; it manifests copiously without, and the universal道 (way) of the world is put into practice. Because what he accumulates is vast and he puts it forth at the proper time, by this he overspreads and covers the world; because what he accumulates is deep and he puts it forth at the proper time, by this he moistens and enriches the living people. Substance and function depend on each other; inner and outer unite as one. Supreme indeed is the virtue of the sage—it is none other than the Way of Heaven, which makes transformations abound and flows like river currents! Is not the sage's identity with Heaven profound?

Moreover, that whereby the supreme sage matches his virtue with Heaven is that he possesses it by nature; and it has a root—namely, a single sincerity and nothing more. Being sincere, there is noduality; having no duality, there is no ceasing—this is whence glorious virtue and great enterprise arise. As for those who enter through instruction, they clarify the good so as to restore…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
貴者在是則舉國而臣事之君道也父道也敢
弗敬與故其名曰貴貴自夫上之人忘南面之
尊以禮士而有用上敬下者焉此盖論德而交
以爲賢者在是則舉國而倚重之賓道也師道
也敢弗敬與故其名曰尊賢夫上下異位也敬
人與見敬於人異施也何以同歸于義哉盖事
得其宜之謂義而下宜于急君上宜于好士其
當理一也能行吾敬之謂義而尊有爵則敬尚
有德則敬其稱情一也勢分與性分相表裏以
===
並立而一偏重則抗盖自有天地以来而交泰
之義如此矣天爵與人爵相低昂以兼濟而一
偏輕則陵盖自有國家以来而一體之義如此
矣故觀貴貴尊賢均之爲義則知挟貴挟賢均
之爲非義而君人者自處於可敬之地毋亦慎
所以敬人哉噫甚矣交之不可挟也挟則相勝
之迹形而相成之道乖相成則賢者亦尊貴者
亦賢而明良之道合相勝則位與德各有所負
上下卒至于不交嗚呼道德之隆污治化之

人與見敬於人異施也何以同歸于義哉蓋事
得其宜之謂義而下宜于急君上宜于好士其
當理一也能行吾敬之謂義而尊有爵則敬尚
有德則敬其稱情一也勢分與性分相表裏以
===
並立而一偏重則抗蓋自有天地以來而交泰
之義如此矣天爵與人爵相低昂以兼濟而一
偏輕則凌蓋自有國家以來而一體之義如此
矣故觀貴貴尊賢均之爲義則知挾貴挾賢均
之爲非義而君人者自處於可敬之地毋亦慎
所以敬人哉噫甚矣交之不可挾也挾則相勝
之迹形而相成之道乖相成則賢者亦尊貴者
亦賢而明良之道合相勝則位與德各有所負
□上下卒至于不交嗚呼道德之隆汙治化之
punctuated: 貴者在是，則舉國而臣事之，君道也，父道也，敢弗敬與？故其名曰「貴貴」。自夫上之人忘南面之尊以禮士，而有用上敬下者焉，此盖論德而交，以爲賢者在是，則舉國而倚重之，賓道也，師道也，敢弗敬與？故其名曰「尊賢」。夫上下異位也，敬人與見敬於人異施也，何以同歸于義哉？盖事得其宜之謂義，而下宜于急君，上宜于好士，其當理一也；能行吾敬之謂義，而尊有爵則敬，尚有德則敬，其稱情一也。勢分與性分相表裏以並立，而一偏重則抗，盖自有天地以来，而交泰之義如此矣；天爵與人爵相低昂以兼濟，而一偏輕則陵，盖自有國家以来，而一體之義如此矣。故觀貴貴、尊賢均之爲義，則知挟貴、挟賢均之爲非義，而君人者自處於可敬之地，毋亦慎所以敬人哉！噫！甚矣，交之不可挟也。挟則相勝之迹形，而相成之道乖。相成則賢者亦尊，貴者亦賢，而明良之道合；相勝則位與德各有所負，上下卒至于不交。嗚呼！道德之隆污、治化之
translation_en:
… that where nobility resides, the entire state serves him as a subject—this is the way of the ruler and the way of the father; how could one dare not show respect? Therefore its name is called "honoring the noble" (gui gui). As for the superior forgetting the majesty of facing south as a ruler in order to treat scholars with ritual courtesy, there is thus the practice of the superior respecting the inferior. This is a relationship based on virtue, considering that where worthiness resides, the entire state relies heavily upon him—this is the way of the guest and the way of the teacher; how could one dare not show respect? Therefore its name is called "honoring the worthy" (zun xian).

Now, superior and inferior occupy different positions, and respecting others and being respected by others are different in practice; how then do they both return to righteousness (yi)? Because when affairs attain their proper measure, it is called righteousness: it is proper for the inferior to be devoted to the ruler, and proper for the superior to be fond of scholars—their conformity to principle is one and the same. Being able to carry out one's respect is called righteousness: honoring one who possesses rank with respect, and esteeming one who possesses virtue with respect—their correspondence to human sentiment is one and the same. Status allotted by position and endowment allotted by nature form the outer and inner aspects of each other so as to stand together, whereas if one side is overly weighted, they come into conflict; indeed, ever since heaven and earth have existed, the righteousness of harmonious interaction has been thus. The nobility of Heaven (tianjue) and the nobility of man (renjue) balance each other to be mutually complementary, whereas if one side is slighted, encroachment arises; indeed, ever since states and families have existed, the righteousness of forming a single body has been thus.

Therefore, by observing that "honoring the noble" and "honoring the worthy" are equally righteousness, one knows that presuming upon nobility and presuming upon worthiness are equally unrighteous. And for one who rules over others and places himself in a position worthy of respect, should he not also be cautious in how he respects others? Alas! How extreme is the principle that in intercourse one must not presume upon one's advantages! If one presumes, the traces of mutual contention appear, and the way of mutual completion is perverted. When there is mutual completion, the worthy are also honored and the noble are also worthy, so that the way of an enlightened ruler and virtuous ministers is united; when there is mutual contention, position and virtue each rely stubbornly on their own strengths, and superior and inferior ultimately fail to interact. Alas! The flourishing or decay of morality and the … of governance and transformation …

"A great view is above, compliant and penetrating, centered and correct in offering a view to all under heaven. 'Viewing (Guan): the ablution has been made, but not yet the offering; there is sincerity and an aspect of solemnity'—those below view it and are transformed."

The Commentary on the Judgments (Tuanzhuan) explains the name and the judgment words of the hexagram Viewing (Guan), showing how the Way of the ruler is established and transformation is carried out thereby. Indeed, nothing in the Way of the ruler is greater than centrality and correctness; when this Way is established above and those below are transformed by it, only then can one speak of "viewing." The meaning of the Commentary on the Judgments is that when above there is a ruler who deliberates upon the Way, below there will be a people who follow the Way. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
在上内順外巽而以中正示人則位陟元后分
至隆矣德備元良本至端矣由是以其執中者
立斯民則而下之罔中於我觀中也以其守正
者爲天下範而下之不正於我觀正也盖惟皇
建極先之也亦以示之也下觀之化基于斯矣
不然道揆未立天下何觀焉聖人之名卦以此
下之觀於上觀其所以示之者也辭曰盥而不
薦有孚顒若則篤恭不顯聖德純矣誠精自著
王度昭矣由是觀中者化於中順帝之則而偏
===
黨不形也觀正者化於正遵王之路而反側自
消也盖惟民歸極化之也而非强之也中正之
觀驗於斯矣不然民志未應君道猶歉焉聖人
之係辭以此吁此夫子於爲觀者示之法也甞
觀堯舜恭已於上所謂顒若之孚而詢岳咨牧
克艱乂政又曰孜孜求之不少置何歟盖聖心
無一日不流通於天下而未甞以天下擾其心
雖時幾是勅而無思無爲者自若也此中正也
故曰神道設教又曰省方觀民考唐虞之業其

…is in the upper position, compliant within and penetrating without, and displays centrality and correctness to others. Thus, ascending to the position of Supreme Sovereign, his status is most exalted; possessing the virtue of supreme goodness, his foundation is most upright. Thereby, through his holding fast to centrality, he establishes a standard for the people, so that those below who lack centrality look up to him for centrality; through his maintaining correctness, he serves as a model for the world, so that those below who are not correct look up to him for correctness. Indeed, when the august sovereign establishes the supreme standard, he leads them with it and also displays it to them; the transformation of those below who look up is founded upon this. Otherwise, if the principles of the Way are not yet established, what would the world have to look up to? It is for this reason that the sage named the hexagram.

When those below look up to the one above, they observe that which he displays to them. The judgment text says, "The ablution has been made, but not yet the offering; there is sincerity and an aspect of solemn dignity." Thus, in his steadfast reverence without ostentation, his sagely virtue is pure; in the natural manifestation of his sincere essence, his kingly bearing is illustrious. Thereby, those who observe centrality are transformed into centrality, following the pattern of the sovereign so that partiality and factionalism do not take shape; those who observe correctness are transformed into correctness, following the royal road so that perversity and instability naturally vanish. Indeed, when the people return to the supreme standard, it is because they are transformed by it, not coerced into it; the manifestation of centrality and correctness is verified in this. Otherwise, if the minds of the people have not yet responded, the way of the ruler is still deficient. It is for this reason that the sage appended the judgment text.

Ah! In this the Master has shown the model for those who serve as the object of observation. I have observed how Yao and Shun maintained reverent self-composure above—which is what is meant by the sincerity of solemn dignity—and yet they inquired of the Four Peaks, consulted the Twelve Pastors, and attended to the difficulties of governing, day after day tirelessly seeking after it without the slightest pause; why was this? It is because the mind of the sage never for a single day fails to circulate throughout the world, and yet he never allows the world to disturb his mind; although he cautiously attends to the timely imperatives of affairs, his state of being without deliberate thought and without purposeful action remains unchanged. This is centrality and correctness. Therefore it is said, "He establishes teaching by the spirit-like Way," and again it is said, "He inspects the regions and observes the people." Because of this it generates yin and generates yang—and can the subtlety of the sages' drawing of the hexagrams not be known from this? The Great Commentary touches upon this in discussing divination. This means that when the sages created the Changes, its function was manifested in divination, while its substance was embodied in the drawing of the hexagrams. text:

大極者涵易之精者也象數因至理而始具故
惟有大極乃有易易者洩大極之秘者也是以
大極動而為陽聖人畫一竒于左以象之而陽
儀生焉竒雖畫于聖人而其所以為竒者實因
其自有之形容而擬議之耳大極靜而為隂聖
人畫一偶于右以象之而隂儀生焉偶雖畫于
聖人而其所以為偶者實因其自有之物宜而
想象之耳由是而四象而八卦孰非太極之生
===
生不窮者而豈聖人以智力為之哉抑觀自古

translation_en:
…[root?]? The ultimate principle transcends images and numbers and exists independently; therefore, before the Classic of Changes (Yi) existed, there was already the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji). The Supreme Ultimate is that which encompasses the essence of the Changes. Images and numbers only come into full being on the basis of the ultimate principle; therefore, only because there is the Supreme Ultimate is there the Changes. The Changes is that which reveals the mysteries of the Supreme Ultimate. Thus, when the Supreme Ultimate moves and becomes yang, the sage draws a single unbroken line on the left to symbolize it, and the yang mode is generated therein. Although the unbroken line is drawn by the sage, that by which it is unbroken is actually nothing more than modeling and deliberating upon its own inherent form. When the Supreme Ultimate is tranquil and becomes yin, the sage draws a divided line on the right to symbolize it, and the yin mode is generated therein. Although the divided line is drawn by the sage, that by which it is divided is actually nothing more than visualizing its own inherent suitability to things. From this come the Four Images and the Eight Trigrams—which of them is not the inexhaustible generation and regeneration of the Supreme Ultimate, and how could the sage have fabricated them through his own intellect and strength? Moreover, looking since antiquity, none of the sages spoke of the Supreme Ultimate, yet the Master [Confucius] alone expounded it in the Commentaries on the Changes (Yizhuan), truly because the Changes is the source of the Five Classics. By observing the Changes, the secret transmitted by the learning of the sages for ten thousand generations can be known. Afterward, Master Zhou [Zhou Dunyi] composed the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu), seeming to have grasped the Master's intention in transmitting the Changes; yet scholars cannot help having doubts about it—why is this alone so?

punctuated: 樂者，必約其戒于身心可焉。功成則賢邪易混，或有疎君子而昵小人者，必嚴其戒于用舍可焉。因循疑似之見，多乘于豫泰之時，吾戒之而闕其疑，以廣吾志也。要名縱慾之心，每起于豐亨之日，吾戒之而守其道，不咈乎民也。此皆儆戒之所有事，而一或不慎，鮮不生心而害政者。誠能省察于一念而無時豫怠，兢業于萬幾而不敢荒寧，則治起于精明而文命之敷益廣，不特黎民敏德，而四夷且爲之嚮化也；功崇于明作而廣運之化益弘，不特萬邦咸寧，而遠人相率以咸賓也。至是，則惠迪之吉捷于影響，克艱之效達乎華夷，而治之無虞可永保矣。否則，怠荒一作，亂之階也，可不戒哉！吁！益之責難于帝也至矣。嘗攷虞帝之朝，寅恭懋勉，方内乂寧，治之極也。而益之戒舜，以四夷來王者期之，蓋化以無外爲盛，道以克艱爲端，率服分北，何莫非君臣交警之致邪？以此爲訓，而後世猶有頌聖功、圖王會以侈其君者。
translation_en:
…pleasures; one must bind one's vigilance to body and mind. When achievements are completed, the worthy and the wicked are easily confounded, and there may be those who distance themselves from gentlemen and grow intimate with petty men; one must strictly apply one's vigilance to appointments and dismissals. Views born of laxity and dubiousness mostly take advantage of times of ease and peace; I guard against them and set aside what is doubtful in order to broaden my aims. Desires to court fame and indulge passions constantly arise in days of abundance and prosperity; I guard against them and hold fast to my Way so as not to go against the people. All these are matters in which vigilance and caution are engaged, and if in a single instance one is not careful, seldom will it fail to arise in the mind and bring harm to governance.

If one can truly examine oneself in every single thought and never relax in ease, and be cautious and diligent in the myriad affairs of state without daring to indulge in idleness and repose, then good order will arise from clear discernment and the spreading of civilizing ordinances will grow ever broader—not only will the black-haired people be quick to embrace virtue, but the Four Barbarians too will turn toward transformation because of it; meritorious achievement will be exalted through enlightened exertion and the transformation of vast, moving virtue will grow ever wider—not only will the myriad states all enjoy peace, but people from afar will lead one another to come in submission as guests. When this point is reached, the good fortune of following the right path will be swifter than shadow or echo, the efficacy of overcoming difficulties will extend to both Chinese and barbarian, and a governance free from anxiety can be preserved forever. Otherwise, once idleness and neglect arise, they are the stepping-stones to disorder—how can one not be on guard!

Ah! Boyi's urging of difficult duties upon the Emperor was exhaustive indeed. If we examine the court of the Emperor of Yu [Shun], with reverent respect and strenuous effort the realm within the four quarters was well-governed and peaceful—the pinnacle of good order. Yet when Boyi admonished Shun, he set the coming of the Four Barbarians to acknowledge his kingship as the expectation. For transforming influence takes having nothing left outside it as its perfection, and the Way takes overcoming difficulties as its starting point. Whether bringing all to submission or dividing and scattering the顽 [Northern tribes, the Sanmiao], what was not the result of ruler and minister mutually admonishing one another? Even with this as an instruction, in later ages there were still those who praised sacred achievements and painted illustrations of royal assemblies to flatter their rulers into extravagance.

"I have heard it said: 'The ancients still mutually admonished and instructed one another, mutually protected and cherished one another, and mutually…'" [Book of Documents, "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi), incomplete topic line]

Comment by Associate Examiner Secretary Ren: Refined, pure, antique, and elegant; moreover, a spirit of loyalty and devotion overflows beyond the words. It should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Left Supervising Secretary Chen: The phrasing is refined and the meaning earnest; it may serve as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer Shen: Classical, substantive, refined, and pure—a fine piece of scriptural exposition.
Comment by Associate Examiner Left Companion to the Heir Apparent Fan: Concise and unadorned; worthy of selection.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Wang: It captures the loyal and devoted intent of the ancients.
Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Lü: Able to bring out the essential meaning of not indulging in luxurious ease.

Even when the rulers of antiquity were able to fulfill their role as sovereigns, their ministers still joined in exhausting their loyalty toward them. Now, when a ruler is able to avoid luxurious ease, the way of the ruler is already fulfilled; yet his ministers still exhaust their loyalty to assist him—is this not why the ancients cannot be equaled? The Duke of Zhou recounted this in order to instruct King Cheng. It is as if he said: To be cautious in one's position is the part of the ruler; to assist with uprightness is the part of the minister. Only when a ruler indulges himself in ease do ministers withhold their loyalty. I have heard that among the ancients, such as the Three Ancestors [of the Shang] and King Wen, what was exalted and allowed for unrestrained indulgence was their position, yet what dwelt in security while mindful of danger was their heart. Able to recognize the difficulties of being sovereign, even though their virtue and achievements were both lofty, they delighted in taking good from others, remaining humble and receptive in order to benefit. As for their ministers, they did not dare say that, having such a ruler, they need only respond to him with reverent compliance and nothing more. Rather, even before the ruler had acted, they joined together in admonishing and instructing him, setting forth the sources of order and disorder and examining the realities of benefit and harm; in all that sincerely [or: warns against (誠 for 誡?)]…

其怠荒而啟其明作者，不遺餘力矣。猶未也，及其方為也，而相與保惠焉。為之培養其端，為之將順其美，凡迎其欲達而擴其未充者，罔不同心矣。猶未也，及其既成也，而相與教誨焉。或論思于朝夕，或交修于左右，凡為之規正而期之大成者，罔不協恭矣。夫訓告不足而保惠之，保惠不足而教誨之，責難無已，固人臣自靖之忠；而終始相成，由古人克勤之感，此德業之所以益盛也歟！抑成王之時，康事無斁，敷教不迷，庶幾遠追三宗，近守家法矣。而周公惓惓乎《無逸》之訓，且以古人之能受盡言者相戒勉；乃召公之誥，亦曰「無遺壽耇」，而以稽古達天啟之，其即訓誥、保惠、教誨意也。周、召謀國之同心，成王迓衡之盛治，可想見哉！

translation_en:
…against indolence and negligence and inspiring his clear initiative, they spared no effort. Nor was that all: when he was in the midst of acting, they together protected and cherished him. They nurtured his nascent beginnings and furthered his good qualities; in all that met what he wished to achieve and expanded what he had not yet fulfilled, none failed to be of one mind. Nor was that all: when his work was already accomplished, they together taught and instructed him. Whether deliberating and reflecting morning and evening, or mutually cultivating him at his side, in all that corrected him and looked toward his great completion, none failed to show harmonious reverence. Now, when admonition and instruction were not enough, they protected and cherished him; when protecting and cherishing were not enough, they taught and instructed him. Making ceaseless demands for what is difficult is indeed the loyalty through which a minister fulfills his own duty; yet that they brought things to completion from beginning to end came from being moved by the ancients' capacity for diligence—is this not why their virtue and achievements grew ever more flourishing? Moreover, in the time of King Cheng, peaceful affairs were pursued without weariness and the spreading of instruction did not go astray, so that he nearly matched the Three Ancestors of old and closely upheld the family model. Yet the Duke of Zhou was earnestly devoted to the admonitions of "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi), and furthermore admonished and encouraged him with how the ancients were able to accept unreserved speech; and the announcement of the Duke of Shao likewise said, "Do not neglect the aged and elders," enlightening him by examining antiquity and reaching Heaven—this was precisely the meaning of admonition, cherishing protection, and instruction. The shared heart of the Dukes of Zhou and Shao in taking counsel for the state, and the flourishing governance of King Cheng in welcoming equilibrium, can well be imagined!

Classic of Poetry (Shi)
"Illustrious and bright is the Son of Heaven; his good renown never ceases."
Lin Zuanzhen

…the intent of the poet. It may be recorded to serve as a model.

Associate Examiner, Historiographer (Bianxiu) Yu comments: The diction and meaning are pure and profound, and the unspoken admonition is vividly apparent. He may truly be called one skilled in explaining the Odes (Shi).

Associate Examiner, Historiographer Zhang comments: It brings out the loyalty and affection in the Duke of Shao's thoughts. Could it be that the author himself has long possessed a heart of loyalty and affection? We record it not merely for its literary style.

Associate Examiner, Historiographer Han comments: As one reads it, the Duke of Shao's intent in praising and expressing his hopes is vividly present.

Associate Examiner, Historiographer Tian comments: It brings out the Duke of Shao's intent at the time in urging his ruler onward; the words are not wasted, and the main idea leaps to life.

Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting (Shidu xueshi) Wang comments: Skilled at bringing out the poet's intent of combining admonition with praise.

Examiner, Grand Secretary (Daxueshi) Lü comments: One who is skilled in explaining the Odes.

The great minister praises his ruler's illustrious reputation and urges him onward with constancy. Indeed, only when a sovereign's virtue is constant will his illustrious reputation be endless. That the Duke of Shao wished this for his ruler—was this not the ultimate in loyalty and affection! King Xuan commanded Duke Mu of Shao to pacify the Yi tribes south of the Huai River. His achievement was completed and the patent of appointment was inscribed, yet what took form in his ode of reply contained boundless loyalty. Thus he said: "Reputation is the outward manifestation of achievement. Since my ruler has established a great enterprise in the world, he must surely attain an illustrious reputation in the world; yet what I, Hu, wish for goes even further than this. Our bright, brilliant Son of Heaven inherits the enduring blessings of Kings Wen and Wu, and in manifesting their glory and exalting their achievements, his awe-inspiring merit…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
與天地而為昭也紹成康之顯德而起敝興衰
濯濯之靈與日月而並明也肆今經營成而天
下稱武義聞固宣昭矣而未已也保治于後猶
其勵精于初者焉而有以流英聲于無極疆理
明而天下頌德仁聲固洋溢矣而未已也持盈
于終猶其興治于始者焉而有以布德音于靡
窮令聞在中國則明明我后之誦彌逺彌光殆
萬年無斁也盖久于其道則亦久于其譽而豈
虞其過佚也哉令聞及蠻貊則明王有道之仰
===
彌久彌芳雖萬世猶在也盖恒于其德則亦恒
享其名而何患于終晦也哉吁美之以令聞則
其道光進之以不已則其祚長召公之忠愛至
矣哉大抵名不可以倖致而尤難於不已宥初
罔終人主之深戒也而老成之慮誠逺矣觀周
公述文王之令聞不已以戒成王而先之以亹
亹召公繼此亦曰矢其文德夫亹亹者言心之
恒也文德之不已固令聞之本也吁大臣之告
君類如此

君類如此
punctuated: 與天地而為昭也；紹成、康之顯德，而起敝興衰，濯濯之靈，與日月而並明也。肆今經營成而天下稱武，義聞固宣昭矣，而未已也。保治于後，猶其勵精于初者焉，而有以流英聲于無極；疆理明而天下頌德，仁聲固洋溢矣，而未已也。持盈于終，猶其興治于始者焉，而有以布德音于靡窮。令聞在中國，則明明我后之誦，彌逺彌光，殆萬年無斁也。盖久于其道，則亦久于其譽，而豈虞其過佚也哉？令聞及蠻貊，則明王有道之仰，彌久彌芳，雖萬世猶在也。盖恒于其德，則亦恒享其名，而何患于終晦也哉？吁！美之以令聞，則其道光；進之以不已，則其祚長。召公之忠愛至矣哉！大抵名不可以倖致，而尤難於不已。宥初罔終，人主之深戒也，而老成之慮誠逺矣。觀周公述文王之令聞不已以戒成王，而先之以亹亹；召公繼此，亦曰「矢其文德」。夫亹亹者，言心之恒也；文德之不已，固令聞之本也。吁！大臣之告君類如此。
translation_en: … shines forth alongside heaven and earth; continuing the illustrious virtue of Kings Cheng and Kang to revive what was decayed and raise up what was in decline, his resplendent majesty is as bright as the sun and moon. Now that his planning and ordering are accomplished and all under Heaven praises his martial prowess, his righteous reputation is indeed proclaimed and manifest—yet may it never cease! By preserving good governance hereafter just as he roused his spirit at the beginning, he will cause his heroic renown to flow on without limit. Now that the boundaries and divisions of the land are clearly defined and all under Heaven extols his virtue, his benevolent reputation indeed brims over—yet may it never cease! By guarding fullness until the end just as he raised up order at the start, he will spread the fame of his virtue unendingly. When his good reputation abides in the Central States, the praises of our bright sovereign grow ever more distant and ever more glorious, never to be wearied of for ten thousand years. For when one perseveres long in the Way, one will likewise endure long in praise—how could there be any worry of it being lost or forgotten? When his good reputation extends to the Man and Mo tribes, the reverence for a sage king who possesses the Way grows ever more enduring and ever more fragrant, remaining even for ten thousand generations. For when one is constant in one's virtue, one will likewise constantly enjoy one's fame—what fear could there be of it falling into obscurity in the end? Ah! To extol him for his good reputation makes his Way glorious; to urge him onward with unceasingness makes his dynastic fortune long-lasting. How supreme were the loyalty and affection of the Duke of Shao! In general, a reputation cannot be attained by mere luck, and it is especially difficult to make it unceasing. Having a beginning[?] [宥初, for 有初] but lacking an end is the deep warning for a ruler of men, and the concern of this experienced statesman was truly far-reaching. Observe how the Duke of Zhou recounted King Wen's unceasing good reputation in order to admonish King Cheng, prefacing it with "untiringly" (weiwei); following this in his ode, the Duke of Shao likewise says, "Display your civil virtue." Now, "untiringly" speaks of the constancy of the mind, and the unceasingness of civil virtue is truly the root of a good reputation. Ah! The counsels that great ministers give their sovereigns are generally of this sort.

Associate Examiner Historiographer Tian 田 comments: Able to bring out the intent of the men of Zhou in modeling themselves on their ancestor.

Examiner Grand Secretary Lü 呂 comments: Concrete and substantial.
From the fact that the sage’s statutes brought about the governance of an entire era, one sees that the sage’s statutes are the auspicious omen of an entire era. For a state takes supreme governance as its auspicious omen; when the sage’s statutes are employed and governance achieves success, to call them an auspicious omen is indeed fitting. This ode for sacrificing to King Wen means in effect: the methods by which our Zhou orders the world are complete in the statutes of King Wen, which we descendants ought indeed to keep pure, bright, and continuously radiant. Does one not see this from the efficacy of employing his statutes? Now, King Wen has passed on. From the time when the pure sacrifice was first begun in the Pure Temple, down to the present after two transmissions of the throne, all who have succeeded to the sacrifices to King Wen have employed the statutes of King Wen. We see that when they were employed to continue the royal succession, they already achieved peerless…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
功而典則之貽于今者一儀刑焉而萬邦之作
孚可觀也用之以安民既致乎永清之治而舊
章之垂於後者一率由焉而四方之日靖未艾
也世其祀者世其典世其典者世其治是典也
是周之禎也訏謨洩至治之精而佑啓所貽允
為明時之嘉瑞王猷顯太平之象而方策所布
實維昌世之貞符制作於一時而百代之文明
以啓蒼姬卜世之長此其預兆也盖不必考瑞
於河圖而美哉聖典其即周之圖矣禎孰大哉
===
經綸於一人而百王之大法以昭郊鄏定鼎之
遠此其休徵也盖不必稽祥於洛範而顯哉文
謨不啻周之範矣禎孰加哉然則繼是而清明
緝熈之固所以自保其禎也非我後人之責哉
吁周人告成之頌其知守成之道者矣抑不特
周也夏有典則商有典刑皆禎也用之則治不
用則否顧嗣守何如耳然典者法也聖心之精
蘊寓焉得其心而法舉第曰法而已矣是以前
人之陳迹為已希祥也又嗣守者所宜知

punctuated: 功，而典則之貽于今者一儀刑焉，而萬邦之作孚可觀也；用之以安民，既致乎永清之治，而舊章之垂於後者一率由焉，而四方之日靖未艾也。世其祀者世其典，世其典者世其治，是典也，是周之禎也。訏謨洩至治之精，而佑啓所貽，允為明時之嘉瑞；王猷顯太平之象，而方策所布，實維昌世之貞符。制作於一時，而百代之文明以啓，蒼姬卜世之長，此其預兆也。盖不必考瑞於河圖，而美哉聖典，其即周之圖矣，禎孰大哉！經綸於一人，而百王之大法以昭，郊鄏定鼎之遠，此其休徵也。盖不必稽祥於洛範，而顯哉文謨，不啻周之範矣，禎孰加哉！然則繼是而清明緝熈之，固所以自保其禎也，非我後人之責哉？吁！周人告成之頌，其知守成之道者矣。抑不特周也，夏有典則，商有典刑，皆禎也。用之則治，不用則否，顧嗣守何如耳。然典者，法也，聖心之精蘊寓焉。得其心而法舉；第曰法而已矣，是以前人之陳迹為已希祥也，又嗣守者所宜知。
translation_en: …achievement, and once the statutes and rules handed down to the present are taken as a model, the confidence inspired across the myriad states can be witnessed; employed to bring peace to the people, they have already brought about an era of enduring purity, and once the old canons transmitted to posterity are followed, the daily pacification of the four quarters continues without end. Those who inherit the sacrifices from generation to generation inherit the statutes from generation to generation; those who inherit the statutes from generation to generation inherit the governance from generation to generation. These statutes are indeed the auspicious portent of the Zhou! The grand counsels reveal the essence of supreme governance, and what is bequeathed to aid and enlighten us is truly a fine auspice for an enlightened age; the kingly plans manifest the image of Great Peace, and what is set forth on wooden and bamboo tablets is indeed the true tally of a flourishing era. Created in a single time, they opened up the civilization of a hundred generations; this was the advance omen of the long span of generations divined for the house of Ji. Truly, there is no need to verify auspices in the River Chart—how admirable are the sage statutes, for they are themselves the Chart of the Zhou! What auspicious portent could be greater? Ordered by a single man, they illuminated the great laws for a hundred kings; this was the felicitous sign of the enduring dynastic tripods established at Jiaoru. Truly, there is no need to examine omens in the Luo Norm—how illustrious are the counsels of King Wen, for they are nothing less than the Norm of the Zhou! What auspicious portent could surpass them? This being so, to succeed to them and keep them clear, bright, and continuously radiant is assuredly the means to preserve our own auspicious portent; is this not the responsibility of us descendants? Ah! The ode in which the people of Zhou announced the completion of their work shows that they understood the way of preserving an accomplished enterprise. Yet this is not true of the Zhou alone: the Xia had its statutes and rules, and the Shang had its statutes and models—all were auspicious portents. When employed, there was order; when not employed, there was not—it depended solely on how their successors preserved them. Nevertheless, statutes are laws, and the subtle essence of the sage's mind resides within them. When one grasps that mind, the laws are upheld; if one speaks merely of laws and nothing more, that is to take the stale traces of predecessors as though one had already attained the auspicious omen. This, too, is what successors who preserve the realm ought to know.

春秋
王人子突救衞莊公六年齊師宋師曹師
城邢僖公元年

考試官侍讀學士王批詞義嚴正錄之
考試官大學士呂批有操縱有斷制
春秋善恤患宥以正言者有以權言者夫權正
===
不偏廢也尊子突美齊桓義各有攸當矣盖聞
道之有正取諸禮之經焉而貞臣守之奉辟故
其詩曰王于出征以佐天子夫是役也天下不
以多吉甫之功而歸之君言有正耳迺春秋則
於子突之救衞發之豈不曰自四征九伐之威
替而世不知有王於是有拒命如朔者介大國
以爭衞幾無衞矣而幸突也渙汗是將黔牟救
焉受鉞于廷受脤于社天子負黼扆而遣之君
臣之分凛如也噫使其摧逆旅而迄天誅功烈

translation_en:
Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The King's man Zitu went to the rescue of Wei." (Sixth year of Duke Zhuang). "The army of Qi, the army of Song, and the army of Cao walled Xing." (First year of Duke Xi).

Chen Yujiao 陳與郊

Comment by Associate Examiner and Chief Supervising Secretary Liu: It expounds upon expediency and rectitude with very rigorous and precise intent. Record it.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Right Admonisher Wang: A refined and polished work; the concluding thought is especially fine.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Wang: The diction and meaning are strict and upright. Record it.
Comment by Examiner and Grand Secretary Lü: It possesses both deft control and decisive judgment.

In commending the relief of distress, the Spring and Autumn Annals has cases spoken of in terms of rectitude [reading 宥 as 有], and cases spoken of in terms of expediency. Now, expediency and rectitude are not to be emphasized one to the exclusion of the other; in honoring Zitu and praising Duke Huan of Qi, the moral principles each have their proper application.

I have heard that the existence of rectitude in the Way is taken from the invariable norms of the Rites (Li), and upright ministers hold fast to it in serving their sovereign. Thus the Ode says: "At the King's command we went forth on the expedition, to assist the Son of Heaven." Now, in that campaign, the world did not exalt the merit of Jifu, but attributed it to the ruler—meaning simply that there was rectitude in it. And the Spring and Autumn Annals brings this out in Zitu's rescue of Wei. Does it not say: Since the majesty of the four punitive expeditions and nine chastisements declined, the world no longer knew that there was a King. Thereupon there were those who defied royal mandates like Shuo, relying on great states to contend for Wei, until Wei almost ceased to exist. Fortunately there was Tu, who carried out the royal proclamation to rescue Qianmou. Receiving the battle-axe in the court and the sacrificial meat at the altar of the soil, he was dispatched by the Son of Heaven standing before the axe-embroidered screen; the distinction between ruler and minister was awe-inspiring. Alas! Had he crushed the rebel troops and completed Heaven's punishment, his meritorious achievements…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
可勝道哉而奈何天之未前定也吾姑論其理
可矣故曰春秋之尊子突者正也又聞道之有
權取諸易之變焉而仁人用之匡時故其詩曰
哀我人斯亦孔之將夫是役也天下不以非成
王之意而疑其臣言有權耳廼春秋則於齊桓
之城邢發之豈不曰自五侯九伯之命遠而世
不知有伯於是有亂華如狄者宿重兵以臨邢
幾無邢矣而幸桓也簡書是畏夷儀城焉斬之
蓬蒿歸之器用諸侯屬櫜鞬而從之夷夏之防
屹如也噫使其揚休命而敵王愾盛德不益光
哉而奈何勢之不兩全也吾姑錄其功可矣故
曰春秋之美齊桓者權也夫正以行權權以濟
正聖人於君臣夷夏之際若持衡然而其他曰
譏緣陵甚楚丘抑陘亭終桓之世以權受賞者
什一以正受決者什九故儒者之論曰兵諫以
為忠不如無忠焉謹父以為直不如無直焉斯
□惟深於春秋者知之
□鄭人侵陳遂侵宋宣公元年

punctuated:
可勝道哉？而奈何天之未前定也，吾姑論其理可矣。故曰：《春秋》之尊子突者，正也。又聞道之有權，取諸《易》之變焉，而仁人用之匡時。故其詩曰：「哀我人斯，亦孔之將。」夫是役也，天下不以非成王之意而疑其臣，言有權耳。廼《春秋》則於齊桓之城邢發之。豈不曰：自五侯九伯之命遠，而世不知有伯。於是有亂華如狄者，宿重兵以臨邢，幾無邢矣；而幸桓也，簡書是畏，夷儀城焉。斬之蓬蒿，歸之器用，諸侯屬櫜鞬而從之，夷夏之防屹如也。噫！使其揚休命而敵王愾，盛德不益光哉？而奈何勢之不兩全也，吾姑錄其功可矣。故曰：《春秋》之美齊桓者，權也。夫正以行權，權以濟正，聖人於君臣夷夏之際，若持衡然。而其他曰譏緣陵、甚楚丘、抑陘亭，終桓之世，以權受賞者什一，以正受決者什九。故儒者之論曰：「兵諫以為忠，不如無忠焉；謹父以為直，不如無直焉。」斯□惟深於《春秋》者知之。

□鄭人侵陳遂侵宋宣公元年
translation_en:
…be fully expressed! Yet what could be done when Heaven had not yet settled the outcome? We may simply judge it by its principle. Therefore it is said that the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) honoring Zitu represents the regular norm (zheng).

We have also heard that the Way has expediency (quan), which is taken from the transformations in the Book of Changes (Yi), and which benevolent men employ to rectify their times. Thus the Ode says: "To compassionate our people—this also is vastly great." Now in that campaign, the realm did not suspect the minister on the grounds that it was not King Cheng's intention; this means there was expediency. The Spring and Autumn Annals brings this out in Duke Huan of Qi's walling of Xing. Does it not say: Since the mandate given to the five marquises and nine regional earls receded into the distance, the world no longer knew that there were hegemons (bo). Thereupon there were those who threw the Chinese states into disorder, like the Di barbarians, stationing heavy forces to press upon Xing until Xing almost ceased to exist. Fortunately there was Huan, who revered the warning dispatches on bamboo slips and walled Yiyi for them. He cleared away its tangled weeds and restored its implements and supplies; the feudal lords strapped on their bow-cases and quivers to follow him, and the defense between barbarians and Chinese stood like a towering peak. Alas! Had he proclaimed the glorious royal mandate and fought against the enemies hated by the King, would not his abundant virtue have shone even brighter? Yet what could be done when circumstances did not allow both to be完美 achieved? We may simply record his merit. Therefore it is said that the Spring and Autumn Annals praising Duke Huan of Qi represents expediency.

Now, the regular norm is used to carry out expediency, and expediency is used to aid the regular norm; in dealing with the relations between ruler and minister and between barbarians and Chinese, the Sage was as if holding a balance scale. As for other instances—such as criticizing the walling of Yuanling, censuring still more severely the walling of Chuqiu, and Restraining the covenant at Xingting—throughout Duke Huan's lifetime, cases where he received reward by reason of expediency were one in ten, while cases where he was judged according to the regular norm were nine in ten. Hence the Confucian scholars' discussion says: "To remonstrate by force of arms and count it loyalty is not as good as having no such loyalty; to bear witness against one's father [?] and count it uprightness is not as good as having no such uprightness." This [meaning?] is understood only by those who are deeply versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals.

[…] The men of Zheng made an incursion into Chen, and thereupon made an incursion into Song (First year of Duke Xuan).

text:
陶允宜

考試官侍讀學士王批〔得春秋謹嚴之旨〕
考試官大學士吕批〔善發經意〕
貳國附夷凌夏春秋正之以義焉夫楚固夷也
况所為不義而鄭從之幾何不胥為夷也哉且
陳宋之侵鄭所以不憚征繕而從楚者大抵皆
起於罪晉也夫晉何以見罪乎子鮑之弑不能
===
討而入之賂甚矣棐之會又甚矣于時鄭穆公
有後言焉而楚因之以收鄭天下亦因之以觀
鄭然則鄭之舉動可輕也哉迺兹腹心之好一
託于蠻夷而唇齒之親遂剪為仇敵陳無罪也
附楚以侵之宋有罪也因陳以及之此無論人
言何如而鄭之情状已不能自解矣何者天子
討諸侯伐皆聲罪執言使天下共知之無詭道
焉而是役也陳直以不備見侵則鄭之情可知
也臣弑君子弑父皆洿宫瀦室與天下共棄之

言何如而鄭之情狀已不能自觧矣何者天子
討諸侯伐皆聲罪執言使天下共知之無詭道
焉而是役也陳直以不備見侵則鄭之情可知
也臣弒君子弒父皆瀦宮瀦室與天下共棄之

陶允宜

貳國附夷凌夏，《春秋》正之以義焉。夫楚固夷也，况所為不義，而鄭從之，幾何不胥為夷也哉！且陳、宋之侵，鄭所以不憚征繕而從楚者，大抵皆起於罪晉也。夫晉何以見罪乎？子鮑之弑，不能討而入之賂，甚矣；棐之會，又甚矣。于時鄭穆公有後言焉，而楚因之以收鄭，天下亦因之以觀鄭，然則鄭之舉動可輕也哉？迺兹腹心之好，一託于蠻夷，而唇齒之親，遂剪為仇敵。陳無罪也，附楚以侵之；宋有罪也，因陳以及之。此無論人言何如，而鄭之情状已不能自解矣。何者？天子討、諸侯伐，皆聲罪執言，使天下共知之，無詭道焉。而是役也，陳直以不備見侵，則鄭之情可知也。臣弑君、子弑父，皆洿宫瀦室，與天下共棄之，

Associate Examiner and Right Admonisher Wang comments: [In adjudicating the crime, he does not place the main weight on following Chu; he has grasped the meaning of the Classic.]

When a wavering state attaches itself to barbarians and encroaches upon the Chinese states, the Spring and Autumn Annals rectifies it with righteousness. Now, Chu is inherently barbarian; how much worse when what it does is unrighteous, and yet Zheng follows it—how close do they come to all becoming barbarians together! Moreover, in the invasions of Chen and Song, the reason Zheng did not shrink from levying troops and repairing weapons to follow Chu generally arose entirely from blaming Jin. Now, how did Jin incur blame? In the regicide by Prince Bao, Jin failed to punish the crime and instead accepted bribes from them—that was extreme enough; and the meeting at Fei was even more extreme. At that time, Duke Mu of Zheng made critical remarks afterward; Chu took advantage of this to win over Zheng, and the world likewise took note of this to observe Zheng. Such being the case, could Zheng's actions be taken lightly? Yet now it entrusts its most intimate friendship entirely to the southern barbarians, and consequently severs relations as close as lips and teeth, turning them into hated enemies. Chen was guiltless, yet Zheng attached itself to Chu in order to invade it; Song was guilty, yet Zheng only reached it incidentally by way of Chen. Regardless of what others might say, Zheng's actual conduct already admits of no self-justification. Why is this? When the Son of Heaven carries out a punitive expedition or the feudal lords launch adeclared attack, they always proclaim the offense and uphold a just pronouncement, making it known to the entire world, without recourse to deceitful ways. Yet in this campaign, Chen was invaded simply by being caught unprepared; from this, Zheng's true motives can be known. When a minister murders his ruler or a son murders his father, in all cases their palaces are demolished and turned into foul ponds, and they are cast out together by the whole world, …

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
無還戮焉而是役也宋不聞以無君致討則鄭
之情又可知也噫如是而猶曰晉不足與此可
謂能罪晉乎夫不見楚之能勝晉而挟楚以惡
於晉詐也不見我之能忠楚而虐人以媚於楚
私也故為鄭計者有討宋而已不能討宋有從
晉而已不然而陽以釋宋為晉罪陰以侵宋說
已罪是兩失之故春秋書曰楚子鄭人侵陳遂
侵宋稱人以見其可賤稱侵以志其無名其貶
之至矣抑觀鄭之發憤叛晉自子家執訊之書
===
則已曰無所逃命矣晉直以竅文空質縻之未

無還戮焉。而是役也，宋不聞以無君致討，則鄭之情又可知也。噫！如是而猶曰「晉不足與」，此可謂能罪晉乎？夫不見楚之能勝晉，而挟楚以惡於晉，詐也；不見我之能忠楚，而虐人以媚於楚，私也。故為鄭計者，有討宋而已；不能討宋，有從晉而已。不然，而陽以釋宋為晉罪，陰以侵宋說已罪，是兩失之。故《春秋》書曰：「楚子、鄭人侵陳，遂侵宋。」稱「人」以見其可賤，稱「侵」以志其無名，其貶之至矣。抑觀鄭之發憤叛晉，自子家執訊之書，則已曰「無所逃命」矣。晉直以竅文空質縻之，未始得堅决也。其一往而不復，豈真為釋宋故哉？要之，鄭人多詐，必無始終不叛之理；而晉欲得鄭，要使過不自我，先負鄭以不義之名而後討之。故齊、魯、宋三大賊不誅，而能成伯者，未始有也。

故聖人作樂以應天，制禮以配地。禮樂明備，天地官矣。
translation_en:
…without turning back from executing them. Yet in this campaign, Song was not heard to be subjected to punitive action for regicide; thus Zheng's true motives can again be known. Alas! Acting like this and still saying, "Jin is not worth allying with"—can this be called having grounds to blame Jin? Now, not seeing that Chu is able to defeat Jin, yet relying on Chu to turn hostile toward Jin, is deceitful; not seeing that we ourselves are able to be loyal to Chu, yet mistreating others in order to curry favor with Chu, is selfish. Therefore, in planning for Zheng, there was only punishing Song; if unable to punish Song, there was only following Jin. Doing otherwise—openly treating the release of Song as Jin's crime while secretly using the invasion of Song to excuse its own crime—was to fail on both counts. Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records: "The Viscount of Chu and a man of Zheng invaded Chen, and thereupon invaded Song." It calls him "man" to show how despicable he was, and calls it an "invasion" to record that it lacked any just cause; its condemnation is extreme indeed. Moreover, if we observe Zheng's indignant rebellion against Jin, ever since the letter carried by Zijia, it had already said, "There is nowhere to escape your command." Jin merely tethered it with empty words and hollow pledges [?], never achieving a firm resolution. When Zheng went off once and for all without returning, how could it truly have been because of the release of Song? In short, the people of Zheng were full of deceit, and there was certainly no principle by which they would remain unrebelling from beginning to end; whereas if Jin wished to secure Zheng, it needed to ensure that the fault did not lie with itself, first making Zheng bear the reputation of unrighteousness and only afterward punishing it. Yet for the three great regicides of Qi, Lu, and Song to go unpunished while one is still able to achieve hegemony—such a thing has never existed.

Record of Rites (Liji)

"Therefore the sages created music to respond to Heaven, and instituted rites to match Earth. When rites and music are illuminatingly complete, Heaven and Earth fulfill their functions."

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
李夢陽
同考試官署員外郎林批詞醇理到佳文也取之
同考試官編修陳批聖人以禮樂合造化其義甚精是作能發之
考試官侍讀學士王批清潤典雅
考試官大學士呂批切實
聖人盡制作以賛化而天地得其職也盖禮樂
與化育相通也曾謂制作善而不足以官天地
哉今夫禮樂之道其求端于天地而成能于聖
===
人者乎故聖人法周流同化之和而作之為樂
不但極音而已優柔平中之蘊與絪縕摩盪者
而交孚盖乾知太始而樂助其顯仁之機矣非
應天者耶法高下散殊之序而制之為禮不但
盡飾而已等威儀則之陳與摯察嚴凝者而相
契盖坤作成物而禮相其蔵用之能矣非配地
者耶夫禮樂足以賛化如此惟制作有未善故
天地不官耳今聖人之禮樂既皆本造化之精
微而為之則情見乎文而肅雝之全體畢著何

聖人盡制作以賛化，而天地得其職也。盖禮樂與化育相通也，曾謂制作善而不足以官天地哉？今夫禮樂之道，其求端于天地而成能于聖人者乎！故聖人法周流同化之和，而作之為樂。不但極音而已，優柔平中之蘊，與絪縕摩盪者而交孚；盖乾知太始，而樂助其顯仁之機矣，非應天者耶？法高下散殊之序，而制之為禮。不但盡飾而已，等威儀則之陳，與摯察嚴凝者而相契；盖坤作成物，而禮相其蔵用之能矣，非配地者耶？夫禮樂足以賛化如此，惟制作有未善，故天地不官耳。今聖人之禮樂，既皆本造化之精微而為之，則情見乎文，而肅雝之全體畢著，何
