Li Mengyang 李夢陽
Associate Examiner, Acting Vice Director (shu yuanwailang) Lin comments: "The diction is pure and the reasoning thorough; it is an excellent essay. Accepted."
Associate Examiner, Historiographer (bianxiu) Chen comments: "The sage unites with creative transformation through rites and music; the meaning of this is exceedingly subtle, and this composition is able to bring it out."
Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu xueshi) Wang comments: "Clear, lustrous, and classically elegant."
Examiner, Grand Secretary (daxueshi) Lü comments: "To the point and substantive."

The sage exhausts his institutions and creations in order to assist transformation, and thereby heaven and earth fulfill their functions. Indeed, rites and music communicate directly with creative nurturing; could it ever be said that when institutions and creations are perfected, they are still insufficient to govern the functions of heaven and earth? Now, as for the Way of rites and music, does it not seek its beginnings in heaven and earth, and achieve its efficacy through the sage? Therefore, the sage models himself on the harmony of all-pervading, unifying transformation, and creates music. It does not merely carry sound to its utmost; the inner richness of its gentle, even, and balanced qualities mutually corresponds with the generative forces that intertwine and palpitate against one another. For the Heavenly Principle (Qian) governs the Great Beginning, and music assists the mechanism by which it manifests benevolence—is this not responding to heaven? He models himself on the order of high and low in their dispersed distinctions, and institutes rites. They do not merely carry ornament to its utmost; the array of gradations of authority and ceremonial rules tallies with the forces that gather, discern, and sternly congeal. For the Earthly Principle (Kun) brings things to completion, and rites aid its capacity to store up function—is this not matching earth? Now, since rites and music are sufficient to assist transformation in this manner, it is only when institutions and creations are less than perfected that heaven and earth fail to fulfill their functions. Now, since the rites and music of the sage are all made on the basis of the subtle essence of creative transformation, sentiment becomes manifest in outer pattern, and the entire substance of solemnity and harmony is completely displayed—how…

也故以厚造化之和則陽一噓而煕煕乎品物

之所昭宣矣樂之功其猶天乎以辨造化之宜
則陰一吸而秩秩乎性命之各正是歛藏之得

translation_en:
…so brilliant it is! When the subtle coalesces [?] in the coarse, the coherent threads of centrality and harmony are gathered together [?]; how complete it is! Therefore, to enrich the harmony of creation, when yang breathes out once, all things flourish in joyful abundance; this is Heaven fulfilling its office of giving life and nourishment, yet none of it is not manifested and proclaimed by great music—is the achievement of music not like that of Heaven? To distinguish what is fitting in creation, when yin breathes in once, the natures and destinies of all things are each set right in orderly array; this is Earth fulfilling its office of gathering in and storing, yet none of it is not consolidated and fixed by great rites—is the achievement of rites not like that of Earth? Ah! Seeing the greatness of the completed achievements of rites and music, how flourishing is the way of their institution! Yet why must this necessarily be attributed to the sage? It is because the foundation of rites and music is cherished within the mind. Only the sage's mind penetrates the workings of creation; therefore, even before rites and music are instituted, he already possesses the complete capacity for the wondrous work of establishing the cosmic order and nurturing all things. How vast and overflowing is his admirable virtue! Encompassing and binding together the Three Ultimates, how could this be achieved by mere human strength? Master Xun Qing said: "When the sage keeps his heavenly ruler clear and nourishes his heavenly dispositions, then Heaven and Earth fulfill their offices and the myriad things serve him." Did he too not penetrate the great source of rites and music?

"When clarity and brightness are within his person, his vital energy and will are like those of a spirit. When what he desires is about to arrive, there is surely a prior opening; as when Heaven is about to send down timely rain, the mountains and streams send forth clouds."

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
簡而盡
考試官侍讀學士王批善發天人感應之理
考試官大學士呂批說無私得大意盡
論至德先幾之應因有以明之焉夫無私之德
至德也王業啓而賢佐生豈非應之必然者哉
孔子告子夏以三王之德此則舉文武言之也
若曰天地至大也而聖王能與之參者以其德
之無私耳故吾觀聖德之在躬者清通以瑩其
體而本原之澄徹湛然無所殽虛靈以廓其衷
===
而德性之昭融炯然無所蔽其諸全智之獨稟
乎由是氣之所運無事思惟而機緘燭于未露
志之所嚮不假探索而象數炳于未形其諸至
誠之如神乎夫聖王之德如此雖無心于獲福
也然而上天祚德之理則確乎不可誣焉故大
命集而至治昌所以副生民之願欲者既有將
啓之幾國家興而禎祥出所以產名世之英賢
者自有先見之兆不觀之天乎時雨之降方霈
然以澤乎物而山川之雲先油然以示其徵彼

…concise yet exhaustive.

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: This skillfully brings out the principle of resonance between Heaven and man.

Examiner Lü, Grand Secretary, comments: In explaining selflessness, it captures the main idea exhaustively.

Discussing the prescient response to supreme virtue, he thereby adduces an illustration to make it clear. Now, selfless virtue is supreme virtue; when the kingly enterprise is about to open and worthy coadjutors are born, is this not an inevitable response? Confucius instructed Zixia on the virtue of the Three Kings, and here he speaks by citing King Wen and King Wu as examples. It is as if to say: Heaven and Earth are supremely great, and the reason the sage-king can form a triad with them is simply because his virtue is selfless. Thus, when I observe how sacred virtue resides in his person, it is pure and penetrative in polishing his substance, so that the limpid clarity of his fundamental source is deep and unmixed; it is empty and numinous in broadening his inner mind, so that the bright harmony of his moral nature is radiant and unobscured. Is this not the unique endowment of complete wisdom! Consequently, wherever his vital energy moves, without need of deliberation, the subtle mechanisms are illuminated before they are disclosed; wherever his will is directed, without relying on inquiry, the images and numbers are manifest before they take form. Is this not supreme sincerity that is like a spirit! Now, when the virtue of the sage-king is such as this, although he has no intention of obtaining blessings, the principle by which High Heaven blesses virtue is nonetheless firm and undeniable. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
天之佑聖將寵之以興王之業而必豫畀之以
佐王之臣者亦猶夫此爾然非其無私之德足
以格天而能然哉此聖王之所以與天地參也
微文武其孰能當之抑非獨文武焉然也自古
有明哲之君天必生賢以輔之故帝賚商弼嶽
降周楨此雖氣數使然而感召之機實原于君
德故洪範以俊民用章為休徵所應乃其要尤
在皇建有極修五事于身焉此即孔子無私之
訓也君天下者尚知純心以為得賢之地哉

translation_en:
…that Heaven aids the sage, being about to favor him with the enterprise of a rising king and therefore necessarily bestowing upon him beforehand ministers to assist a king, is also just like this. Yet if not for his selfless virtue being sufficient to move Heaven, how could it be so? This is how the sage-king forms a triad with Heaven and Earth. Were it not for Kings Wen and Wu, who could match this? Yet it was not so for Kings Wen and Wu alone. Since antiquity, whenever there has been a wise and discerning ruler, Heaven has unfailingly brought forth worthy men to assist him; thus the Supreme Lord bestowed a helper upon Shang, and the sacred peaks sent down pillars of state for Zhou. Although this was brought about by the cycles of destiny, the mechanism that moved and summoned them truly originated in the ruler's virtue. Therefore, the Great Plan (Hongfan) takes "men of outstanding talent being made illustrious" as the response to auspicious verifications, while its essential point lies above all in the sovereign establishing the Supreme Ultimate and cultivating the Five Conducts in his own person. This is none other than Confucius's teaching on selflessness. May he who rules all under Heaven know to purify his mind as the foundation for obtaining worthy men!

Second Session
Discourse
"The Ruler Preserves the Established Enterprise and Achieves Flourishing Governance"
Sun Kuang 孫鑛
Comment by Associate Examiner Vice Director Chen 陳: The spirit of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers finding each other in a flourishing age is vividly before one's eyes.
Comment by Associate Examiner Examining Editor Xi 習: In arguing that the means by which the Zhou house achieved a harmonious, radiant, and enduringly flourishing governance was rooted in the continuous radiance of King Cheng's rulerly virtue and in the Duke of Zhou's foresight in assisting and nurturing him, this truly shows insight. Moreover, its diction is vigorous, substantial, and classically elegant; it should be recorded as a model.

The sage king takes his single mind as the foundation for preserving good governance; what he guards is very concise, yet the Way he pursues is very far-reaching. Because what he guards is concise, day by day he cautiously abides by the established patrimony and dares not take it lightly; because the Way he pursues is far-reaching, he does not rest content with merely succeeding to the line and following inherited routine, but diligently ponders what lies beyond the established patrimony, and thus governance grows ever more exalted. Now, order in the realm has never been achieved by doing nothing. Even in an age of preserving the established patrimony, when the transformative influence of grand peace is already pervasive, there must still be things in what the former kings planned and expanded, and in what all within the seas long and hope for, that remain unsatisfied and unfulfilled. This cannot be accomplished merely by preserving the patrimony and busying oneself with nothing. Therefore, because the sage kings of antiquity knew that the Way they pursued was far-reaching, what they expected of themselves was ever boundless, and their minds never dared to grow self-indulgent or lax. Thus the method is very concise and easy to grasp, and loyal ministers and discerning counselors, apart from this, have nothing to offer to their ruler. Thereupon they begin with warnings to guard against subtle incipient faults and methods for assisting and nourishing the ruler's virtue, and only afterward proceed to plans for organizing and administering the state. By this means they are able to preserve the dynasty and make it prosper and grow, cause the established patrimony to shine ever more brightly, and bring the flourishing governance of the realm to ever greater heights. translation_en: … Master Cheng’s words say: “Among rulers who preserved an established patrimony and achieved flourishing governance, none equaled King Cheng of Zhou, which was rooted in the assisting merits of the Duke of Zhou.” Now, how could an established patrimony be easy to preserve, and how could flourishing governance be easy to achieve? In the dynamics of the realm, what is full is easily diminished, and what is exalted easily falls. Therefore, when an inheriting ruler is amid songs of praise and eulogy, exaltation and fullness are hard to maintain, while indulgence and pleasure are easily stirred. With respect to the patrimony of his predecessors, in advancing it he cannot gain even an inch, yet in retreating he readily falls back by yards and fathoms. For this reason, while it is certainly difficult for sage emperors and enlightened kings to found a dynasty and give rise to supreme governance, to preserve what is established and be able to achieve flourishing governance is harder still. Now, to preserve what is established and be able to achieve flourishing governance, one’s plans and deliberations must be far-reaching, and one’s arrangements and measures must go beyond the old patrimony. Yet could one instead stop up one’s hearing and cast aside wisdom, sitting idly while governing? Or could one weigh documents by the stone-weight and check routine precedents, humbling the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots to keep the watch of petty clerks who are ordered about by the hundred? Therefore the saying “the ruler’s art is concise and easy to wield” must be carefully examined. Moreover, what sort of time was the age of King Cheng? Eight hundred feudal lords holding jade tablets came to court, and the Duke stood before theembroidered screen to receive them. The virtue of Kings Wen and Wu had not yet been brought to completion above, while the rebellion of the Three Overseers had only just been pacified below. What was called “bequeathing a great task and casting difficulties upon Our person” was indeed King Cheng’s responsibility, yet how was it not also the responsibility of the Duke of Zhou? With a single extravagant thought, one might destroy one’s virtue through ease and pleasure; with a single narrow thought, one would have no means to expand the unfinished achievements of one’s predecessors. Then even the established patrimony could not be preserved, let alone the achievement of flourishing governance! When King Wu instructed Kangshu, he said: “If it is like tilling a field, you must lay out its boundaries and furrows; if it is like building a house, you must plaster and thatch it; if it is like making [timberwork, you]…”…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
其丹雘蓋聖人以成業貽之後欲其覲揚光大
期之甚遠如此而繼之曰無康好逸豫則其一
念寅恭祗懼以為致治保業之本者固歷先後
戒勉無異詞而萬世守成之法可謂一言以蔽
之矣於乎此周公所以輔相成王之心也夫成
王以前夏商稱守成之主若啓若太甲後先相
望奕葉相輝非所謂繼世賢君耶夷攷其時自
敬承先德而外禹之典則湯之典刑不少益焉

Thus, when the sages bequeathed their established patrimony to their descendants, wishing them to manifest and glorify it, their expectations were as far-reaching as this. And continuing with the words, "Do not idly love ease and pleasure," this single mind of reverent respect and cautious awe, taken as the foundation for bringing about good governance and preserving the patrimony, truly remained identical in its admonitions and encouragements from first to last; the method of maintaining an established order for ten thousand generations may be said to be summed up in a single phrase. Alas! Such was the heart with which the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng.

Now, prior to King Cheng, the rulers of Xia and Shang praised as sovereigns who maintained the established order—such as Qi and Tai Jia—succeeded one another across time and shone across generations; were they not what we call worthy hereditary rulers? Yet if we examine their eras, apart from reverently continuing the virtue of their ancestors, they added nothing at all to the canons and rules of Yu or the statutes and laws of Tang. Therefore, to call them maintainers of the established order is more than fitting, but to speak of them as having brought about flourishing governance is not yet warranted. Why is this? Because they all merely conformed to their times and followed their allotted roles; thinking that doing thus was sufficient to peacefully enjoy their rule, they simply left it at that.

In the Zhou, however, from Kings Wen and Wu down to King Cheng, cultural horizons opened up day by day, so human institutions and refinements had to be made complete; deceit and artifice multiplied day by day, so the considerations for detailed precautions when affairs arose had to be made thorough; the grand designs were already laid out, so the multitude of specific articles and ritual gradations had to be deliberated unhurriedly and implemented in turn. Had the Duke merely rested in peace and inherited blessings, aiming only to continue the old ways, saying, "It is enough for us to maintain the established order like this," then Kings Wen and Wu would have had uncompleted virtue, and the young king would have been as though he had never occupied the throne—what would the world and ten thousand generations have said of this?

Therefore, in his guidance of King Cheng, the Duke wished him to know that an established patrimony is not easy to maintain, and furthermore wished him to know that what his predecessors hoped of us goes beyond mere maintenance. Thus, day and night, with anxious care, he personally took upon himself the task of instituting rites and creating music…

Therefore, just when the state of the realm possessed the stability of Mount Tai, he regarded it as if it were a stack of eggs, precarious beyond calculation; before the desires in the sovereign's heart had even broken out as a tiny spark or a trickling stream, he regarded them as if they were a prairie fire or a flood cresting the hills, impossible to control. For this reason, he spoke to him of the hardships of sowing and reaping and the toil of farming and sericulture, so as to make him know labor; he spoke to him of not giving himself over to steeped pleasures and not indulging excessively in excursions and sightseeing, so as to make him know self-restraint; he spoke to him of how Heaven is hard to rely upon, so as to make him know awe; he spoke to him of the curses and resentments of the people, so as to make him know compassion; and he spoke to him of not disrupting the regular punishments of the former kings, so as to make him know the law. Indeed, since antiquity, among great ministers who devoted themselves to their rulers, baring their hearts and livers to exhort andhone them, none was ever as earnest and untiring as this! Furthermore, in selecting and appointing the worthy and good to assist where he himself could not reach, there were also those of篤 steadfast benevolence and fondness for learning, those of sincere principle and firm resolve, those of pure integrity and incisive candor, and those of broad learning and retentive memory, standing before, behind, to the left, and to the right of the king, so that the measures of ritual and propriety were never absent from his eyes. If the king was not broadly versed in the canons, or if the Junior Tutor was not skilled in dignified demeanor [?], the Grand Mentor would instruct him; if he was not generous to the common multitude, or did not hit the mark in punishments and litigation, the Grand Tutor would instruct him—so that the discourse of sages and wise men never ceased in his ears. For the Warders of the Robes and the Rapid-as-Tigers Guards, he invariably selected men of constant virtue and auspiciousness; for the Palace Elder and the Administrator of the Interior, he invariably employed aides promoted for their worthiness—so that the principles of self-examination and restraint were never lacking in his person. Ah! How tight were his precautions, and how thorough his cultivation! punctuated: 於踐阼，豔誘之色不闚，陵亂之聲不理，遐異之珍不奉，操斷擊搏之書不習。觀於《閔予》、《訪落》、《敬之》、《小毖》諸詩，則知周公所以斧藻王質而彌縫其闕者，可謂至而無遺憾矣。譬之决水自源，測景以表，惟其大本先定，而末從之。然後風之禮樂，散之詩書，齊之衡量，制之徽纆，藩飾之以文章，拊循之以恩厚。天子穆然深思於上，而三公、九卿、百執事、庶民競勸於下。故《周禮》一書，至於厮輿冗猥、米鹽曲析，有文、武之所未及措意者，事有宜適，物有節文，周道因以大備。而其效至於刑錯囹空，九州清晏，方外之國，無不重譯獻琛贄於廷；而後嗣得遵洪業，不下簟席而治者，且七百餘年，則以其臣主一心，而精神日流於天下故也。視之夏啟、太甲守文師故，僅無墜前人之統，功實百之。蓋明保勖迪之際，淵蛸蠖濩之中，而公所以為周家命脉計者，固已連四海萬世而覆盂之矣。故其守之約也，天下之大本也；其推之遠也，天下之大業也。大本端，故成業
translation_en: …to ascending the throne, he did not peer at alluring sights, did not attend to disorderly sounds, was not presented with exotic treasures from afar, and did not study writings on harsh manipulation and ruthless striking. Looking at such odes as "Pity Me" (Minyu), "Counsel at the Beginning" (Fangluo), "Reverence" (Jingzhi), and "Cautious against Future Trouble" (Xiaobi), one knows that the means by which the Duke of Zhou refined the king's character and mended his deficiencies can truly be called supreme and without anything left to regret. It is like channeling water from its source or measuring a shadow with a gnomon: only when the great foundation is first established do the branches follow. Thereafter, he influenced them with rites and music, diffused among them the Odes and Documents, standardized them with weights and measures, restrained them with binding cords of law, adorned them with cultural patterns, and comforted them with generous kindness. The Son of Heaven pondered in solemn depth above, while the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, hundred functionaries, and common people vied to encourage one another below. Thus, in the single work Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), down to menial servants and trivial affairs, as well as the minute details of grain and salt, there were matters to which Kings Wen and Wu had not yet had time to turn their attention; yet every affair was given its proper suitability and every thing its regulated refinement, whereby the Way of Zhou became fully complete. Its efficacy reached the point where punishments were set aside and prisons stood empty, the Nine Provinces were tranquil and clear, and countries beyond the realm all came through multiple interpreters to present precious gifts at court; and later heirs were able to follow this grand enterprise, governing without stepping down from their mats for over seven hundred years—all because sovereign and minister were of one mind, and their vital spirit flowed daily throughout the realm. Compared to Qi of Xia and Tai Jia, who merely preserved existing institutions and imitated precedent so as barely to avoid losing the succession of their predecessors, his achievement was truly a hundredfold greater. Indeed, amidst his enlightened protection and encouraging guidance, within the quiet depths of retirement and deliberation, what the Duke planned for the lifeblood of the House of Zhou had already linked the Four Seas and ten thousand generations and placed them as securely as an overturned bowl. Therefore, what he guarded with simplicity was the great foundation of the realm; what he extended afar was the great enterprise of the realm. Because the great foundation was upright, the accomplished enterprise…

translation_en:
… is preserved without decline; when the great enterprise is complete, flourishing governance is handed down to perpetuity. Admirable indeed was the Duke of Zhou's service to the Zhou! Rectifying the ruler's heart was the means by which he brought tranquility to All under Heaven; assisting the sovereign's virtue was the means by which he enriched the common people. Therefore it is said: the Duke of Zhou's conduct toward King Cheng may be called the greatest loyalty. Even so, how could the Duke take pride in himself and claim it as his own achievement? The Duke's heart was simply what is called pure loyalty and pure filiality, speaking only of boundless solicitude. Thus he did not because of favor and advantage neglect warnings of peril and ruin; he did not because of rumors alter his composed bearing; he did not because of his status as royal uncle and his many talents abandon his diligence in spitting out his food and grasping his hair to receive worthies. In bringing about order, he said only that it was "consolidating the accomplished achievements of predecessors"; in preserving what was established, he said only that the sovereign "himself reverently cultivated virtue," and the Duke claimed no part in it. Why was this? Because the duty and righteousness of a subject are as boundless as heaven; and a sage is one in whom duty and righteousness are especially innate. Thus even though as a subject he acted as regent for his ruler, combined preservation of the dynasty with foundational creation, and gathered merits unprecedented across ten thousand generations to offer up to his ruler, none of this added anything beyond his normal duty. Therefore, what All under Heaven and ten thousand generations deem to be achievements are all the achievements of the great sovereign, and merely the duty of a subject. Of the great sovereign one speaks of achievement; of the subject one speaks of duty. Therefore it is said: in serving one's ruler, to be like the Duke of Zhou is what is proper.

translation_en:
…Giving free rein to the brush in writing is merely a secondary pursuit of one whose attainment enters the realm of sages and spirits; yet observing cultural patterns to bring about transformation is the complete capacity of one who orders heaven and earth. Thus, when we examine the admonitions inscribed on the armrest of Xuan [the Yellow Emperor], and further behold the teachings engraved on the washbasin of Tang; when King Wu received the instructions of the Cinnabar Book (Danshu), the Way was arrayed upon his doors and pillars; and when the Sovereign Cheng composed his songs in the purple court, righteousness was preserved in the ancestral hall and edifice. Alas, once words of pristine simplicity declined, the purport of exhortation and admonition gradually grew faint. "The wind rises and clouds fly" indulged an ambitious heart while passing through Pei; "chrysanthemums are fragrant and orchids fair" heightened a pleasure-seeking mood while crossing the Fen River. He who imitated the Stone Classics patched together discourses like mending sable with a dog's tail; he who compiled the Golden Sea (Jinhai) exhausted his spirit only to measure the ocean with a gourd. Stringing pearls and threading jade—what need has the Great Plan for ritual jades? Elaborate colors and carved flourishes—such petty skills merely labor over ceremonial sashes and kerchiefs. Truly, only he who creates is called a sage; how else could his work be so brilliantly patterned?

Now, we humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], who responds to the prophetic register to rule Heaven, and grasps the tally to receive the Mandate. With three thousand horses returned to pasture, Chinese and non-Chinese alike join the court of those holding jade tablets in homage; as the flying dragon at the nine-five position, the universe is steeped in the transformation of governing with robes垂 hanging down. Meritorious achievement having been completed through the ordering of military affairs, the Way is further expounded through the expansion of literary culture. Recently, during moments of leisure from the pivotal affairs of state, You have broadly gathered the fragrant essence of the forest of books. translation_en: … the imperial crown tassels and earplugs. Thus You specially unfolded Your precious thoughts and personally poured forth gem-like compositions. Summarizing the essentials and compiling the profound, You molded and refined the very essence of emperors and kings; examining cultural ornament and weighing substance, Your furnace and hammer reached the utmost workmanship of nature's creation. Having completed this grand enterprise in light-blue silk book-bags, You thereupon held aloft the auspicious title of the Golden Mirror (Jinjing). First, by employing the loyal and worthy and dismissing the unworthy, You clarified the source of misfortune and blessing; next, by extending civil virtue and broadening martial awe, You set forth the strategy of relaxing and tightening. In selecting for office, You put ridgepole beams first and rafters after; in ordering the state, You treated branches and leaves as secondary and roots and trunks as urgent. By the carving of jade into patterned form, You illustrated the sage's dedication to learning; by drought-stricken sprouts longing for rain, You likened the wise ruler's quest for the worthy. In governing subordinates, You were cautious with the authority of preserving merit and appointing generals; in occupying the supreme position, You valued the filial piety that rectifies the state and brings peace to the family. Near at hand You examined Qin and Han; far back You investigated Xuan [the Yellow Emperor] and Yu [Shun]. All the appearances of rise and decline from antiquity to the present are not off by the slightest fraction; and the circumstances of success and failure between ruler and minister are tempered without omission. Observing allegiance and estrangement in the people's hearts is no different from looking at one's own eyebrows and eyelashes; distinguishing loyalty and treachery in human character is like seeing into the lungs and liver. Unfolding the words, the myriad transformations are complete at the tip of the brush; opening the scroll, the Four Seas revolve upon the palm of the hand. Fine counsels and admirable deeds are comprehensively arrayed within eighteen hundred characters; ornate thought and vigorous prose stand preeminent at the head of the seventy-two rulers. On those four walls where paintings were arrayed, the forms of the highest sages were once mounted; and where the five colors were jointly applied, the likenesses of the ancients were likewise taken. translation_en:
… [a pearl that illuminates twelve] chariots, measuring barely an inch across yet lighting up all that was forgotten; or fashioning a carriage that matches the tracks of the world, traversing every perilous pass without stepping out the door. Truly, it is a book that exhausts the miraculous and perfects sagehood, the essential guide for continuing the imperial enterprise and inheriting the dynastic foundation. Held forth to govern, it naturally enables one to unite the virtues of the Five Emperors and ascend to the level of the Three Kings; inscribed into a classic, it is worthy of succeeding the Six Classics to become the Seventh. Indeed, it is a work that heroic and righteous sovereigns cannot go a single day without reading, and that sacred sons and divine grandsons ought to treasure for ten thousand generations.

Your servants lack the literary thought of "carving dragons," and are ashamed of an understanding as narrow as "glimpsing a leopard through a tube." Attending on duty at the Phoenix Side-Apartments and the Simurgh Slope [of the Secretariat and Hanlin Academy], we are unworthy of dipping our brushes; gazing from afar at the repository of Jade Books and Golden Tablets, how could we be fit to draft imperial proclamations? Yet we have undeservedly received the resplendent bestowal of this Imperial Composition, and are fortunate to fathom the profound purity of Heaven's intent. When the Precious Robe is first conferred, it shines with the brilliance of vermilion and azure paintings; when the felicitous casket is suddenly opened, it carries the weight of tripods and pitch-pipes arrayed in court. This favor surpasses a hundred sets of cowries, and this grace exceeds the Three Bestowals. Gazing up at the five-colored auspicious clouds in the sky, how could any painting depict them? Listening to the nine movements of the Shao music, how could any praise exhaust them? How dare we not treasure and revere these jade tablets, and widely broadcast these silken cords of imperial words? Thus may the Tortoise Plan and Dragon Chart together perpetuate auspicious tallies from the Yellow and Luo Rivers, and the Heavenly Globe and Great Jade-Disk jointly hand down the Great Instructions to distant descendants. We humbly pray that…

This essay sets forth the narrative without omission; moreover, its structure is stately and its diction ornate and polished, truly capturing the style of exalted discourse. When you present your response at the Great Court, I shall have high hopes for you.

Associate Examiner and Historiographer of the Hanlin Academy Chen comments: Our Imperial Ancestors, sage and divine, succeeded one another in excellence, establishing the foundation for ten thousand myriad years of grand peace through both benevolent grace and institutional law. You are able to extol their magnificence, and furthermore bring forth nurturing and rectification as your theme; loyalty and affection overflow in your words. It is fitting to record this for presentation to the throne.

Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Wang comments: Our Imperial Ancestors followed a single Way in founding and preserving, giving equal eminence to virtue and law, while Our Majesty inherits their blessings and matches their excellence, thereby nurturing and rectifying so that transformative governance is renewed. That you are able to set forth their magnificence point by point—is it not because you are steeped in the sage's transformation and long to exert yourself in service? A fine scholar, a fine scholar!

Examiner and Grand Secretary Lü comments: The benevolent grace and institutional law of Our Imperial Ancestors are profound, illustrious, and complete, far surpassing those of high antiquity. Our Majesty gloriously continues the achievements of His predecessors, further nurturing, extending, and rousingly rectifying them; the means to prolong boundless blessings for ten thousand myriad years [麻, a woodblock print variant for 休] lies precisely in this. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
盛末復以衆和不偏為言足覘靖獻之志矣
帝王之建鴻業也以綏和天下有德焉以
整齊天下有法焉然德植于深常卒乎匱
法成于肅常卒乎弛又在乎後之人培養
而修飭之培養厚則國家之命脉愈繇絡
布濩而不可解修飭勤則國家之精神愈
奮揚融朗而不可凲此所以豐基强榦延
祚靈長之道也執事首發策以
祖
===
宗德澤法度及我
皇上纘紹之治為詢甚忠志也敢不敬效欵欵
之愚甞考孔子之言政曰以德以法皆御
民之具兩者之不偏廢尚矣唐虞之德光
海隅暢庶類至鴻茂也然而府事修和萬
世永賴觀伯益儆戒之辭則法度又未甞
失焉成周之法如八統八柄五典九職之
類至纖密也然周自后稷以來世積仁厚
暨于成康天下和同重譯來賀觀雅頌所

祖
===
宗德澤法度及我
皇上纘紹之治爲詢甚忠志也敢不敬效欵欵
之愚嘗考孔子之言政曰以德以法皆御
民之具兩者之不偏廢尚矣唐虞之德光
海隅暢庶類至鴻茂也然而府事修和□
世永賴觀伯益儆戒之辭則法度又未嘗
失焉成周之法如八統八柄五典九職之
類至纖悉也然周自后稷以來世積仁厚
暨于成康天下和同重譯來賀觀雅頌所
punctuated:
盛，末復以衆和不偏為言，足覘靖獻之志矣。
帝王之建鴻業也，以綏和天下，有德焉；以整齊天下，有法焉。然德植于深，常卒乎匱；法成于肅，常卒乎弛。又在乎後之人培養而修飭之。培養厚，則國家之命脉愈繇絡布濩而不可解；修飭勤，則國家之精神愈奮揚融朗而不可凲。此所以豐基强榦、延祚靈長之道也。執事首發策，以祖宗德澤法度及我皇上纘紹之治為詢，甚忠志也，敢不敬效欵欵之愚？
甞考孔子之言政，曰以德、以法，皆御民之具，兩者之不偏廢尚矣。唐、虞之德，光海隅，暢庶類，至鴻茂也；然而府事修和，萬世永賴，觀伯益儆戒之辭，則法度又未甞失焉。成周之法，如八統、八柄、五典、九職之類，至纖密也；然周自后稷以來，世積仁厚，暨于成、康，天下和同，重譯來賀，觀《雅》《頌》所
translation_en:
…grandeur, and at the end you further speak of universal harmony without partiality—this is enough to reveal your aspiration to offer loyal counsel to the throne.

When emperors and kings establish a great enterprise, to pacify and harmonize the realm they rely on virtue; to order and regulate the realm they rely on law. Yet virtue, though planted deep, often ends in depletion; and law, though established in strictness, often ends in laxity. It therefore depends on their successors to nurture the one and refurbish the other. When nurturing is generous, the lifeblood of the state becomes ever more interconnected and pervasive, so that it cannot be undone; when refurbishment is diligent, the vital spirit of the state becomes ever more roused, radiant, and clear, so that it cannot be worn away. This is the way to enrich the foundation, strengthen the trunk, and prolong the dynasty's blessed fortune. That Your Excellency, in posing the first policy question, has inquired into the virtuous beneficence and institutional laws of our imperial ancestors as well as the governance by which His Majesty continues their legacy shows a most loyal intent. How could I dare not respectfully offer my earnest, humble thoughts?

I have examined Confucius's words on governance, in which he spoke of governing by virtue and by law. Both are instruments for ruling the people, and the principle that neither should be neglected in favor of the other is of long standing. The virtue of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun] shone to the corners of the seas and gave free expression to all living things—it was supremely vast and flourishing. Yet the Six Treasuries and Three Affairs were well-ordered and harmonized, providing an eternal reliance for ten thousand generations; looking at the admonitory words of Boyi, one sees that institutional laws were never lacking either. The laws of成周 (Cheng Zhou, the accomplished Zhou dynasty), such as the Eight Unifying Principles, the Eight Prerogatives, the Five Moral Teachings, and the Nine Occupations, were supremely detailed and comprehensive. Yet the Zhou, from Houji onward, accumulated benevolence and generosity from generation to generation, until by the reigns of Kings Cheng and Kang the world was in harmonious unity and foreign peoples came through multiple interpreters to offer congratulations; looking at what the Odes (Ya) and Hymns (Song)…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
被則德澤之流又若是其遠焉宋儒羅從
彥謂自古德澤最厚莫若唐虞法度最明
莫若成周者蓋以唐虞之時方垂衣畫象
而理而成周則經制大備故各因其時言
之耳豈謂唐虞之法度有闕遺而成周之
德澤未豐廣乎至於人君以德法兩者垂
諸子孫均為萬世所憑藉者也然必後之
人益務博恩廣施以宣其豈弟遵制揚功
以振其綱維則德與法乃可歷久而彌新
===
故從彥又謂祖宗德澤不可恃法度不可
廢夫恃德澤是不庇其本根而尋斧斤也
廢法度是更師曠之律而變公輸之矩矱
也從彥之意要以培養修飭責繼體之君
耳豈輕德澤而重法度乎由此以觀則德
也法也肇剏者非斯無以維一統紹述者
非斯無以規萬代誠保大持盈之令圖百
王未有以易也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝神武天挺躬提三尺而復帝王自

太祖高皇帝神武天挺躬提三尺而復帝王自
punctuated: 被，則德澤之流，又若是其遠焉。宋儒羅從彥謂：「自古德澤最厚，莫若唐虞；法度最明，莫若成周」者，蓋以唐虞之時，方垂衣畫象而理，而成周則經制大備，故各因其時言之耳。豈謂唐虞之法度有闕遺，而成周之德澤未豐廣乎？至於人君以德、法兩者垂諸子孫，均為萬世所憑藉者也。然必後之人益務博恩廣施，以宣其豈弟；遵制揚功，以振其綱維，則德與法乃可歷久而彌新。故從彥又謂：「祖宗德澤不可恃，法度不可廢。」夫恃德澤，是不庇其本根而尋斧斤也；廢法度，是更師曠之律而變公輸之矩矱也。從彥之意，要以培養修飭責繼體之君耳，豈輕德澤而重法度乎？由此以觀，則德也、法也，肇剏者非斯無以維一統，紹述者非斯無以規萬代，誠保大持盈之令圖，百王未有以易也。洪惟我太祖高皇帝，神武天挺，躬提三尺，而復帝王自
translation_en:
…reached, the flow of virtuous beneficence was once again so far-reaching. When the Song-dynasty scholar Luo Congyan (羅從彥) said, "Since antiquity, none has matched Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun] in the depth of virtuous beneficence, and none has matched the flourishing Zhou in the clarity of laws and institutions," it was because in the time of Tang and Yu they governed simply by letting their robes hang down and delineating symbolic punishments, whereas in the flourishing Zhou administrative institutions were fully developed; thus he spoke according to the circumstances of each era. How could he have meant that the laws and institutions of Tang and Yu were defective or incomplete, or that the virtuous beneficence of the flourishing Zhou was not abundant and broad?

As for a ruler handing down both virtue and law to his descendants, both alike serve as what ten thousand generations rely upon. Yet successors must strive ever more to broaden grace and extend generosity so as to manifest their benignity, and to observe the institutions and exalt past achievements so as to invigorate the guiding principles; only then can virtue and law endure through time and grow ever more renewed. Therefore Congyan also said, "The virtuous beneficence of ancestors cannot be presumed upon, and their laws and institutions cannot be abandoned." Now, to presume upon virtuous beneficence is to fail to shelter the root and instead take up the axe; to abandon laws and institutions is to alter the pitch-pipes of Music Master Kuang (師曠) and change the carpenter's square and rule of Gongshu [Ban] (公輸). Congyan's intent was simply to charge succeeding rulers with the responsibility of nurturing [virtue] and maintaining [the laws]; how could he have slighted virtuous beneficence while emphasizing laws and institutions? Viewed in this light, as for virtue and law: without them, founders of dynasties have no means to hold together a unified realm, and successors have no means to plan for ten thousand generations. Truly, this is an admirable design for preserving greatness and maintaining fullness, one that a hundred kings have never been able to change.

Humbly reflecting upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao [the Hongwu Emperor], endowed by Heaven with divine martial prowess, he personally wielded a three-foot sword to restore the Central Realm founded by the emperors and kings of old…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
立之中國有乾坤再闢之功焉天下之人
得易羓羯爲冠裳化戈鋌爲衽席其摶心
揖志而奉戴者有泰山四維之固焉而
聖祖不忘厚其德澤以燠休之明其法度以綰
結之皇皇哉今載在
聖政記諸書者信如日星之布巳試舉其閎鉅
則中原一檄弘祝網之慈
大誥三編廣錫福之惠
殿廷露禱秉桑林之虔
===
宮室樸素循采椽之訓器斥雕鏤遵土鉶之
意衣存澣濯崇卑服之風他如給農器免
田租之類又不可殫書焉盖
聖祖之德澤發涌翔洽如元氣之在渾濛如江
河之演迤而不窮也劉三吾嘗謂
聖心拳拳恩德之及民者深非以此歟乃其長
念却顧垂之爲畫一之章則飭
宮闈而言無踰閾故帷帘之譽宣馭近習而
奸無憑社故綴衣之職毖戚畹優以祿入

punctuated: 立之中國，有乾坤再闢之功焉。天下之人得易羓羯爲冠裳，化戈鋌爲衽席，其摶心揖志而奉戴者，有泰山四維之固焉。而聖祖不忘厚其德澤以燠休之，明其法度以綰結之，皇皇哉！今載在《聖政記》諸書者，信如日星之布巳。試舉其閎鉅：則中原一檄，弘祝網之慈；《大誥》三編，廣錫福之惠；殿廷露禱，秉桑林之虔；宮室樸素，循采椽之訓；器斥雕鏤，遵土鉶之意；衣存澣濯，崇卑服之風。他如給農器、免田租之類，又不可殫書焉。盖聖祖之德澤發涌翔洽，如元氣之在渾濛，如江河之演迤而不窮也。劉三吾嘗謂「聖心拳拳，恩德之及民者深」，非以此歟？乃其長念却顧，垂之爲畫一之章：則飭宮闈而言無踰閾，故帷帘之譽宣；馭近習而奸無憑社，故綴衣之職毖；戚畹優以祿入…
translation_en: …the Central Realm of independent sovereigns, accomplishing the merit of opening heaven and earth anew. The people of the realm were able to exchange sheepskins and felt for caps and robes, and transform spears and halberds into mats and bedding; their uniting in heart and joining in purpose to revere and support him had the firmness of Mount Tai and the four cords of heaven. Yet the Sacred Ancestor did not forget to thicken his virtuous beneficence to comfort and soothe them, and to clarify his laws and institutions to bind and knit them together—how magnificent indeed! What is now recorded in the Record of Sacred Governance (Shengzheng ji) and other books is truly arrayed like the sun and stars. If we try to cite their grandest aspects: the single proclamation to the Central Plain expanded the compassion of Tang praying over the three-sided net; the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) broadened the grace of bestowing blessings; praying in the open air in the palace courtyard upheld the piety of the Mulberry Forest; keeping palace buildings plain and simple followed the precept of uncarved oak rafters; rejecting carved and engraved vessels observed the intent of earthenware soup-pots; keeping garments that had been washed and rinsed exalted the custom of humble dress. Other measures, such as supplying farming tools and remitting land taxes, cannot be fully written down. Indeed, the virtuous beneficence of the Sacred Ancestor welled forth and pervaded everywhere, like the primordial breath within the undifferentiated cosmos, and like the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers flowing on endlessly. Liu Sanwu 劉三吾 once said, "The Sacred Mind is earnestly devoted, and the grace and virtue reaching the people are profound"—was it not because of this? And as for his far-reaching thoughts and circumspect reflections, handed down as uniform statutes: he regulated the palace women's quarters so that words did not cross the threshold, and thus the reputation of the curtains and screens was proclaimed; he controlled close attendants so that the wicked had no altar of the soil to lean upon, and thus the duties of the royal wardrobe were kept cautious; imperial relatives by marriage were generously provided with emoluments…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
而
國典不干故内降之恩節
藩封胙以茅土而民事不預故維城之勢安
肅軍政而威柄專故居重之形壯定官制
而倖位絕故表著之地清他如决壅蔽覈
實效之類又不可縷指焉蓋
聖祖之法度震疊彪炳如風霆之鼓動如日月
之行天而燭極六合也宋濂嘗謂
睿思所斷動契典則度越千古者非以此歟當
===
===
斯時也薄海内外含甘飲醇既斟酌之不
竭謳歌之不倦其範圍于紀律者又皆帖
然循守而罔敢越軼天下之勢無鉤繩而
不可携也無關鍵而不可開也萬億年不
拔之業實始基之矣然
聖祖猶兢兢焉計深慮長則親製
祖訓一編以詒燕來裔愚莊誦而得其槩焉如

君常存敬畏以祖宗憂天下爲心則能永受

translation_en:
…while not allowing them to interfere with the statutes of the state, so favors granted by inner-court directives were curbed; he enfeoffed the princely fiefs with ceremonial soil and thatch while not allowing them to meddle in civil affairs, so their position as protective ramparts remained secure; he brought rigor to military administration and concentrated the authority of command, so the posture of central strength was formidable; he fixed the system of officialdom and cut off undeserved appointments, so the places of court rank were pure. Other measures—such as clearing away obstruction and concealment, and verifying actual results—are too numerous to recount in detail. Indeed, the Sacred Progenitor's laws and regulations were awe-inspiring and resplendent, like the stirring of wind and thunder, or like the sun and moon coursing through the heavens and illuminating the six directions to their farthest reaches. When Song Lian 宋濂 once said that "what His sagely thought decided unfailingly matched the classic norms and surpassed all antiquity," was it not on account of this?

At that time, within and beyond the seas, people savored the sweetness and drank the pure wine [of his grace], drawing from it inexhaustibly and singing its praises tirelessly; and those encompassed within his discipline and laws all docilely abided by them without daring to transgress. The configuration of the realm could not be pulled apart even without grappling hooks and cords, nor could it be pried open even without bolts and locks; the unshakeable enterprise of ten thousand myriad years truly had its foundation laid in this. Yet the Sacred Progenitorremained ever cautious, planning deeply and taking long-range thought, and thus personally composed the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun 祖訓) in one compilation to bequeath tranquility and guidance to future descendants. I have reverently recited it and grasped its main import. For instance, it says: "When emperors and kings first win the state, Heaven necessarily bestows it upon one who possesses virtue; if a sovereign who preserves the accomplishment constantly maintains reverence and awe, taking the ancestors' concern for the realm as his own mind, then he will be able forever to receive…"

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
天之眷顧是欲
後聖之樹德以保世者何懇切也又
曰凡我子孫無作聰明亂我已成之法是欲
後聖之守法以繼序者何嚴毅也猗歟休哉
明明有訓與關石俱垂琬琰並列矣其疇能易
之自是
列聖循業益光前軌鴻化昭登太平如一日至
孝宗敬皇帝以寬厚煦育而
聖祖之德澤益浸灌于人之肌骨焉觀夫斥遊
===
畋損玉食却四裔之貢獻裁百司之冗冒
讞遼東之獄而刑清罷延壽之塔而財省
以故十八年間黎甿殷阜海宇懽康可謂
與民休息者乎然而四輔晝接庶政躬裁
凛焉泰阿之謹持法何嘗不行也至
世宗肅皇帝以英斷馭臨而
聖祖之法度益炳耀于人之耳目焉觀夫葺棼
綱興曠禮恩威運于立决名實歸于綜練
罷鎮藩之使而法自近行杜貴里之謁而

translation_en:
… the favor of Heaven." How earnestly did he desire later sage rulers to establish virtue in order to preserve the realm for generations! And again it says: "None of my descendants shall play at being clever and disrupt the laws I have already established." How sternly did he desire later sage rulers to abide by the laws in order to carry on the succession! Oh, how magnificent! These luminous injunctions have been handed down alongside the standard weights and measures, and arrayed alongside the finest jades; who could ever alter them? From that time onward, the successive sage emperors followed in their enterprise, further glorifying the path of their predecessors; grand transformation shone forth and ascended, and great peace endured as if a single day.

When it came to Emperor Xiaozong (r. 1487–1505), he nurtured all with magnanimity and kindness, so that the virtuous beneficence of the Sacred Ancestor soaked ever more deeply into people's flesh and bones. Observe how he spurned pleasure excursions and hunting, curtailed imperial delicacies, rejected tribute from the four borderlands, pruned superfluous and fraudulent personnel across the hundred offices, reviewed the judicial cases of Liaodong so that punishments were cleared up, and halted construction of the Yanshou Pagoda so that expenditures were saved. For this reason, throughout the eighteen years of his reign, the common folk were prosperous and the whole empire was joyful and at peace—may this not be called giving rest and recuperation to the people? And yet, he received his chief ministers in daytime audiences, personally decided the multitude of state affairs, and awe-inspiringly guarded the hilt of the Tai'e sword of sovereign authority—when did the law ever fail to be enforced?

When it came to Emperor Shizong (r. 1521–1567), he ruled with heroic decisiveness, so that the laws and regulations of the Sacred Ancestor shone ever more brilliantly before people's eyes and ears. Observe how he mended tangled guiding threads of governance, revived long-neglected rites, wielded favor and awe through immediate decisions, aligned title and reality through comprehensive mastery, abolished the eunuch-commissioners sent to supervise the provinces and princely estates so that the law took effect starting from those close at hand, and blocked the private audiences of powerful maternal relatives so that …

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
政無旁落以故四十五年間羣僚肅乂百
度修明可謂體乾剛健者乎然而農桑必
軫膜溢有祈曠馬帡幪之廣覆德何嘗不
溥也夫
聖祖紹天闡繹則長育與震曜並行
二宗奕世承休則敦大與明作交懋故積善累
功益篤也赫聲濯靈益奮也而
皇基其丕奠已恭惟
皇上躬至聖之資撫綦隆之運
===

令飭百司毅若秋霜之肅繼治之善視
前烈有光焉而執事猶欲求所以宣昭

…and authority over governance was never usurped by others. For this reason, over the course of forty-five years, the body of officials was reverent and well-governed, and all institutional measures were kept in bright order—may this not be called embodying the firm vigor of Heaven (Qian)? Yet he always showed solicitous concern for agriculture and sericulture, and offered prayers whenever there was drought [?] or flooding; vast indeed [?] was his broad sheltering canopy—when was his virtue ever not extensive? Now, when the Sacred Ancestor (Taizu) succeeded to Heaven's mandate and unfolded his enterprise, nurturing growth and awe-inspiring brilliance proceeded side by side; when the Two Ancestors (Xiaozong and Shizong) inherited the blessings across successive generations, magnanimous breadth and clear, active governance reinforced one another. Recently, moreover, You have constantly consulted with the assembled officials, itemizing precedents and putting them into practice. Your grace extends throughout the Four Seas, mild as the moistening of spring rain; Your commands admonish the hundred offices, resolute as the severity of autumn frost. In the excellence of Your continuation of good governance, You add luster to the achievements of those who went before. Yet Your Excellency the Examiner still seeks the means to proclaim and make bright this fine heritage and ascend forever to Great Peace—is this not perhaps emulating the earnest intention of the worthies of old to remain mindful of anxiety and peril? title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
明興餘二百年于茲矣今方宇寧謐有三登
九稔之樂無賦車籍馬之煩有櫜弓卧鼓
之安無揭竿持籌之警是
國家德澤之鴻龐所淪被也而談者曰未盡
洽毋乃以時遵熙豫供億滋豐而民生之
彫抏莫能堪乎今政令嚴明有運臂使指
之便無腓大股維之憂有車閑策勁之美
無覂駕摧輈之慮是
國家法度之精詳所約束也而談者曰未盡
===
舉毋乃以世襲泰寧瑕纇潜長而俗尚之
惰窳莫能整乎愚嘗熟計今之治體惟在

孝宗之寬厚以培養

密之網則囹圄清禁末利而重本業則服

punctuated: 明興餘二百年于茲矣。今方宇寧謐，有三登九稔之樂，無賦車籍馬之煩；有櫜弓卧鼓之安，無揭竿持籌之警。是國家德澤之鴻龐所淪被也。而談者曰未盡洽，毋乃以時遵熙豫，供億滋豐，而民生之彫抏莫能堪乎？今政令嚴明，有運臂使指之便，無腓大股維之憂；有車閑策勁之美，無覂駕摧輈之慮。是國家法度之精詳所約束也。而談者曰未盡舉，毋乃以世襲泰寧，瑕纇潜長，而俗尚之惰窳莫能整乎？愚嘗熟計今之治體，惟在皇上法孝宗之寬厚，以培養聖祖之德澤；法世宗之英斷，以修飭聖祖之法度。是故蠲浮濫之征，則閭閻實；削煩密之網，則囹圄清；禁末利而重本業，則服疇者多；退貪墨而進廉平，則侵漁者息。以
translation_en: … More than two hundred years have passed since the rise of the Ming. Today, the realm is tranquil and peaceful: there is the joy of repeated bumper harvests, without the trouble of requisitioning war chariots and registering horses; there is the security of cased bows and resting war drums, without the alarm of rebels raising bamboo poles or officials clutching tally sticks for emergency exactions. This is what the vast and generous virtue and beneficence of the State have permeated and covered. Yet commentators say that this beneficence is not yet completely diffused. Could it not be that because the times abide in peace and comfort, requisitions and supplies have grown ever more lavish, so that the exhausted and worn-down livelihood of the people can no longer bear it? Today, government ordinances are strict and clear: there is the ease of the arm moving the fingers, without the worry of calves swollen larger than the thighs or limbs bound fast; there is the excellence of well-trained teams and a firm whip, without the anxiety of overturning the carriage or snapping the shaft. This is what the precise and detailed laws and institutions of the State have bound and regulated. Yet commentators say that these laws are not yet completely enforced. Could it not be that because the age inherits prolonged peace, flaws and blemishes secretly grow, so that the indolent and decadent customs cannot be rectified? I have carefully considered the essentials of governance today: they lie solely in Your Majesty emulating the magnanimity and generosity of Xiaozong (the Hongzhi Emperor) to nurture the virtue and beneficence of the Sacred Ancestor (the Hongwu Emperor), and emulating the heroic decisiveness of Shizong (the Jiajing Emperor) to refurbish and tighten the laws and institutions of the Sacred Ancestor. Therefore, if excessive and arbitrary levies are remitted, the common folk in their villages will be prosperous; if vexatious and overly dense legal nets are pared away, the prisons will be cleared; if secondary commercial profits are prohibited and fundamental agricultural pursuits are emphasized, those who till the fields will be numerous; if greedy and corrupt officials are dismissed and upright and fair ones are promoted, those who encroach upon and prey on the people will cease. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
此撫循于上而海内之氣未有不清和咸
理者也堅渙汗之令則廢格者不容清攀
援之塗則荒飽者不售殿虚談而崇實政
則吏事修湔浮文而考成績則治效著以
此提挈于上而朝廷之衆未有不競勸營
職者也然寛厚可也至于湛靜而後時柔
茹而寡執則骫法英斷可也至于苛峭以
為察嚴重以為威則妨德夫惟
聖天子含靈體睿執中履衡自能弛張百為舒
===
卷萬化澤普而不氾威震而不激包涵而
無牽制不决之患總攬而無刻覈已甚之
嫌惠加于窮民而不以養姦回嚴施于私
謁而不以塞忠諫如此則剛柔正直參和
不偏爾
本朝德法廓如天地固如金石太平之業將
濟萬世無窮極也夫普覆併包保民長世
非至仁弗運也弘馭遠撫恢網廓紘非至
勇弗舉也鏡覽燭照使德法之施無不投

punctuated: 此撫循于上，而海内之氣，未有不清和咸理者也。堅渙汗之令，則廢格者不容；清攀援之塗，則荒飽者不售；殿虚談而崇實政，則吏事修；湔浮文而考成績，則治效著。以此提挈于上，而朝廷之衆，未有不競勸營職者也。然寛厚可也，至于湛靜而後時，柔茹而寡執，則骫法；英斷可也，至于苛峭以為察，嚴重以為威，則妨德。夫惟聖天子含靈體睿，執中履衡，自能弛張百為，舒卷萬化。澤普而不氾，威震而不激；包涵而無牽制不决之患，總攬而無刻覈已甚之嫌。惠加于窮民，而不以養姦回；嚴施于私謁，而不以塞忠諫。如此，則剛柔正直，參和不偏，爾本朝德法，廓如天地，固如金石，太平之業，將濟萬世無窮極也。夫普覆併包，保民長世，非至仁弗運也；弘馭遠撫，恢網廓紘，非至勇弗舉也；鏡覽燭照，使德法之施無不投
translation_en:
… these means one comforts and nurtures from above, there will never be a case where the ethos within the Four Seas is not pure, harmonious, and universally well-ordered. If one holds firm to the edicts issued like sweat that cannot be recalled, then those who obstruct or neglect them will not be tolerated; if one clears away the paths of factional social climbing, then the idle and gluttonous will find no market; if one ranks empty talk last and exalts substantive governance, then administrative affairs will be cultivated; if one washes away superficial formalities and examines actual achievements, then the efficacy of rule will become manifest. If by these means one leads and directs from above, there will never be a case where the multitude at court do not compete in encouraging one another to attend to their duties.

Yet while magnanimity and generosity are good, if they go so far as sunken quiescence that misses the opportune moment, or pliant accommodation that lacks firm resolve, then they bend the law. And while heroic decisiveness is good, if it goes so far as harshness and severity taken for perceptiveness, or sternness and gravity taken for majesty, then it harms virtue. Only when the sagely Son of Heaven embodies numinous spirituality and profound wisdom, holds fast to the Mean and treads the balance, will he naturally be able to alternate tension and relaxation in the hundred undertakings, and unfurl or roll up the myriad transformations. His beneficence is universal without overflowing; his majesty is awe-inspiring without being extreme. He is all-encompassing without the ill of being bogged down in indecision; he holds comprehensive control without the suspicion of excessive and harsh scrutiny. Kindness is bestowed upon the destitute people, yet not so as to nourish the wicked and perverse; strictness is applied to private Audience-seeking and favor-currying, yet not so as to block loyal remonstrance. When it is thus, firmness, suppleness, and rectitude are blended in harmony without bias; the virtue and law of our reigning dynasty will be as vast as Heaven and Earth and as solid as metal and stone, and the enterprise of Great Peace will reach across ten thousand generations without end.

Now, universally sheltering and encompassing all, protecting the people and perpetuating the ages—without supreme benevolence, this cannot be set in motion. Broadly reining in and pacifying afar, expanding the net and widening the cord—without supreme courage, this cannot be raised up. Reflecting like a mirror and illuminating like a torch, ensuring that in the application of virtue and law nothing fails to hit…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
機挈會應變適節非至明弗能也三者孔
子之告其君而司馬光所為罄其生平之
學者也敢拜手為
當宁獻
第二問
沈璟
同考試官主事任批〔格正詞醇文之有裨世道者錄之〕
同考試官左給事中陳批〔氣格融渾議論雅正印于〕
===
〔言可以起敝維風矣〕
同考試官編修沈批〔發明質文循環之意甚辨是關係世教之作也〕
同考試官左中允范批〔湛深之思發以辨博之詞是有關于世教者宜錄以式〕
考試官侍讀學士王批〔本聖人賛天地化育之義而發之以古雅之詞佳作佳作〕
考試官大學士吕批〔世運循環之故聖人救世之權子能根極論之不獨見其考古亦可知其通今已〕

translation_en:
…seizing the right moment and grasping the opportunity, responding to changes and fitting the proper measure—without supreme perspicacity, this cannot be achieved. These three things are what Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) told his lord, and that for which Sima Guang 司馬光 exhausted his lifelong learning. I venture to bow with hands clasped and present this to His Majesty on the throne.

Second Policy Question
Shen Jing 沈璟
Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary (zhushi) Ren 任: [Its structure is upright and its diction pure; as a piece of writing that benefits the way of the world, record it.]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Left Supervising Secretary (zuo jishizhong) Chen 陳: [Its spirit and structure are harmonious and浑成 (well-rounded), and its arguments are elegant and orthodox; verified in [?] its words, it is sufficient to remedy decay and uphold moral customs.]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer (bianxiu) Shen 沈: [It elucidates the meaning of the cycle of substance and refinement with great discernment; this is a work of consequence for public moral instruction.]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Left Companion (zuo zhongyun) Fan 范: [Profound thought expressed in discerning and erudite language; this is something of consequence for public moral instruction and ought to be recorded as a model.]
Comment by Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu xueshi) Wang 王: [Grounded in the principle of the sages assisting the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth, and expressed in antique and elegant diction. A fine work, a fine work!]
Comment by Examiner and Grand Secretary (daxueshi) Lü 呂: [The causes of the cyclical course of worldly fortune and the expedients by which the sages save the world—you are able to discuss them thoroughly to their roots. Not only does this show your investigation of antiquity, one can also know from it your comprehension of the present.]

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
天地有不可已之運聖人之所順而不□
也聖人有不可見之權天下之所用而不
知也何也聖人教天下以樸固知其後之
必巧也教天下以簡固知其後之必繁也
然而不能使之不巧且繁者非聖人之狥
天下而天地之運為之也不能使之不巧
而能使之樸不能使之不繁而能使之簡
則聖人之微權所以移易天下而不可使
知之者也運有所必至則聖人不能違天
===
天也亦人也權有所必設則天亦不能違
聖人人也亦天也然則世道質文之變可
述已夫文質之用吾未之前聞也其義起
於三統漢儒所謂夏尚忠殷尚敬周尚文
者是也而又以殷為尚質夫質之與敬一
也而吾以為皆非聖人之教也世徒見其
道之不同而以為聖人之治天下若有所
尚而已矣非其自為之名也何也蓋上古
聖人脩無為之理而天下熈熈不施忠於

punctuated:
天地有不可已之運，聖人之所順而不□也；聖人有不可見之權，天下之所用而不知也。何也？聖人教天下以樸，固知其後之必巧也；教天下以簡，固知其後之必繁也。然而不能使之不巧且繁者，非聖人之狥天下，而天地之運為之也。不能使之不巧而能使之樸，不能使之不繁而能使之簡，則聖人之微權所以移易天下而不可使知之者也。運有所必至，則聖人不能違天，天也，亦人也；權有所必設，則天亦不能違聖人，人也，亦天也。然則世道質文之變，可述已。
夫文質之用，吾未之前聞也。其義起於三統，漢儒所謂「夏尚忠、殷尚敬、周尚文」者是也，而又以殷為尚質。夫質之與敬，一也，而吾以為皆非聖人之教也。世徒見其道之不同，而以為聖人之治天下若有所尚而已矣，非其自為之名也。何也？蓋上古聖人脩無為之理而天下熈熈，不施忠於
translation_en:
Heaven and Earth have an unstoppable cycle of progression, which the sages follow without [opposing? □]; the sages possess an invisible discretionary power, which the world relies upon without realizing it. Why is this so? When the sages teach the world simplicity, they certainly know that afterward it will inevitably become artful; when they teach the world conciseness, they certainly know that afterward it will inevitably become elaborate. Yet their inability to prevent it from becoming artful and elaborate is not because the sages yield to the world, but because the cycle of Heaven and Earth brings it about. Though unable to keep it from becoming artful, they can return it to simplicity; though unable to keep it from becoming elaborate, they can return it to conciseness—this is the subtle discretionary power by which the sages transform the world without letting people realize it. Where the cycle must inevitably arrive, the sages cannot go against Heaven—this is Heaven, and yet also man. Where discretionary power must inevitably be established, Heaven likewise cannot go against the sages—this is man, and yet also Heaven. Thus, the alternations between unadorned substance and cultural refinement in the way of the world can be set forth.

As for the deployment of cultural refinement and unadorned substance, I have not heard of it in earliest times. The concept arose with the Three Reigns, which is what Han dynasty Confucian scholars meant by saying, "The Xia esteemed loyalty, the Yin esteemed reverence, and the Zhou esteemed cultural refinement," while also taking the Yin as esteeming unadorned substance. Now, unadorned substance and reverence are one and the same, yet I consider none of these to be what the sages themselves taught. The world merely observed that their ways differed and assumed that in governing the world the sages seemed to hold a particular esteem—these were not names that the sages created for themselves. Why? In high antiquity, the sages cultivated the principle of non-action and the world was harmonious and prosperous. They did not dispense loyalty toward…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
民烏有所謂忠不施敬於民烏有所謂敬
天下有淫比而忠之名始出天下有慆慢
而敬之名始出故夫未有忠與敬之名也
謂之質焉可也既有忠與敬之名也謂之
文焉可也豈待周而文哉然則三代之教
雖不可窺而其無所尚可知也即有所尚
而周之所尚非文又可知也雖不尚文而
世道之升降必自質而文又可知也儒者
見其然遂曰三皇之時如春五帝之時如
===
夏三王之時如秋五伯之時如冬然則五
伯而降其將流為長夜而漫漫不旦乎必
不然也則冬未嘗不可為春而伯未嘗不
可為皇矣故史遷謂三王之正如循環而
鄒衍推五德之運相終始焉見其遞降而
不返哉而子以為此天地之運而王道之
所因也蓋天地之運其未至也有所不可
已而其既至也有所不可極何也數基於
一至於百千萬億而未嘗不歸於一也聲

translation_en: … the people, how could there be what is called loyalty? Without practicing reverence toward the people, how could there be what is called reverence? Only when there is licentiousness and partisanship in the world does the name of loyalty first emerge; only when there is arrogance and negligence in the world does the name of reverence first emerge. Therefore, when the names of loyalty and reverence did not yet exist, one could call it simplicity (zhi); once the names of loyalty and reverence existed, one could call it refinement (wen)—how could it wait until the Zhou to become refinement? Thus, although the teachings of the Three Dynasties cannot be fully fathomed, it can be known that they held no single quality as their supreme ideal; even if they did hold something as an ideal, it can also be known that what the Zhou held as an ideal was not refinement; and although they did not hold refinement as an ideal, it can also be known that the rise and fall of the Way of the world must proceed from simplicity to refinement. Confucians, seeing that it is so, consequently say: "The era of the Three Sovereigns was like spring, the era of the Five Emperors was like summer, the era of the Three Kings was like autumn, and the era of the Five Hegemons was like winter." If that were so, then from the Five Hegemons downward, would the world drift into a long night, vast and endless without dawn? It is certainly not so. Then winter can never fail to become spring, and the age of Hegemons can never fail to become the age of Sovereigns. Therefore, the Grand Scribe Sima Qian (Shiqian 史遷) said that the governance of the Three Kings was like a cycle, and Zou Yan 鄒衍 deduced that the revolutions of the Five Virtues end and begin anew with one another—how could one see them as merely declining step by step without returning? And I consider this to be the revolution of Heaven and Earth, upon which the Kingly Way relies. For in the revolution of Heaven and Earth, when it has not yet reached its point, there is that which cannot be halted, and when it has already reached its point, there is that which cannot be pushed to an extreme. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
起於宮至於九成八變而未嘗不相為宮
也故質而不能不文也如春之必有冬也
不可逆而止也文而可使之質也如冬之
復為春也非有強而為也一寒一暑推而
歲月日時之序順一文一質變而元會運
世之化成是所謂循環終始之說也而談
者曰文而欲返之質猶移江河而行之山
也何其妄哉夫周之始何以明其不文也
太羹玄酒則禮之極致焉朱絃洞越則樂
===
之極音焉甚朴而非華矣及其敝也分為
十二而諸侯之才臣澴子樞衣鳴玉驚其
文巧之辭合為六七而天下之策士大俠
憑軾鼓舌信其捭闔之說道術分而白馬
雕龍之辨與六藝爭道而馳文藻流而湘
纍郢客之章與大雅分曹而奏故自周至
於秦而天下之文極矣然其後不能無漢
也不能無漢是至漢而循環也漢承秦敝
斵雕為樸內而將相大臣有椎魯少文之

punctuated: 起於宮，至於九成、八變，而未嘗不相為宮也。故質而不能不文也，如春之必有冬也，不可逆而止也；文而可使之質也，如冬之復為春也，非有強而為也。一寒一暑，推而歲、月、日、時之序順；一文一質，變而元、會、運、世之化成，是所謂循環終始之說也。而談者曰：「文而欲返之質，猶移江河而行之山也。」何其妄哉！夫周之始，何以明其不文也？太羹、玄酒，則禮之極致焉；朱絃、洞越，則樂之極音焉。甚朴而非華矣。及其敝也，分為十二，而諸侯之才臣、澴子，樞衣鳴玉，驚其文巧之辭；合為六七，而天下之策士、大俠，憑軾鼓舌，信其捭闔之說。道術分，而白馬、雕龍之辨與六藝爭道而馳；文藻流，而湘纍、郢客之章與《大雅》分曹而奏。故自周至於秦，而天下之文極矣。然其後不能無漢也。不能無漢，是至漢而循環也。漢承秦敝，斵雕為樸，內而將相大臣有椎魯少文之
translation_en: … arises from the gong tone, and even through nine completions and eight variations, the notes never cease to serve mutually as the gong tone. Therefore, that simplicity cannot help becoming refinement is like spring inevitably leading to winter—it cannot be reversed or halted; and that refinement can be made to return to simplicity is like winter returning to become spring—it is not brought about by force. As cold and heat alternate, the sequence of years, months, days, and hours proceeds in order; as refinement and simplicity transform into one another, the formative transformations of epochs (yuan), cycles (hui), revolutions (yun), and generations (shi) are accomplished. This is what is meant by the doctrine of circularity, of ending and beginning anew. Yet commentators say: "When refinement has been reached, wishing to return it to simplicity is like moving the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers to make them flow over the mountains." How absurd that is! Now, at the beginning of the Zhou, how can we show that it was not overly refined? Unseasoned broth and plain water were the ultimate expression of ritual; vermilion strings and wide-spaced sound-holes were the ultimate tones of music. It was exceedingly plain and not華 (florid). When it fell into decline, the realm split into twelve states, and the talented ministers and noble sons [?] of the feudal lords lifted their robes and tinkled their jade pendants, astonishing others with their ornate and clever rhetoric; then it consolidated into six or seven powers, and the strategists and great knights-errant of the world leaned on their carriage crossbars and wagged their tongues, giving free rein to their theories of manoeuvring and coalition-building (baihe). Philosophical methods splintered, so that the disputations of the "White Horse" and "Carving Dragons" raced alongside the Six Classics in competition for the Way; literary embellishment spread, so that the verses of the "Exile by the Xiang" (Qu Yuan) and the "Guest of Ying" (Song Yu) were performed side by side as rivals to the Greater Odes (Daya). Thus, from the Zhou down to the Qin, the refinement of the world reached its extreme. Yet afterward there could not fail to be the Han. That there could not fail to be the Han means that with the arrival of the Han, the cycle came full circle. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
風下而吏士元元有清靜寧一之化渢渢
乎古風已及其敝也一變而西京經藝之
儒各立家門抱策而爭句讀又變而東都
瑰詭之士私相標植扞罔而博名高又變
而建安之才人握管而覃竒麗之聲又變
而江左之玄談揮麈而課清虛之理故自
漢至於六朝而天下之文又極矣然其後
不能無唐也不能無唐是至唐而循環也
噫由此而唐宋之末造可推已夫此數代
===
者其始固甚質矣非久而文則何其曼衍
不已也嘗思其故一代之初天造草昧其
政化風俗皆淳然有太古之風故天下朴
也既朴矣培之數十年而公私物力必充
羨而有餘故天下盛也既盛矣聲名文物
必侈汰而不可制故天下文也既文矣根
本命脉必有所撓焉而不固故天下敝也
嗟乎此豈一朝夕之故哉董子曰已雕已
琢還反其樸物之相反復歸於本物極則

…air, while below, officials, scholars, and the common people enjoyed the transforming influence of quietude, tranquility, and unity—how grandly it resembled the ethos of antiquity! Yet when it fell into decline, it changed once into the Confucian scholars of classical learning in the Western Capital, each establishing his own school, clutching bamboo slips and disputing over phrasing and punctuation; it changed again into the eccentric and unconventional scholars of the Eastern Capital, who formed private cliques for mutual praise, defying the law to win lofty reputations; it changed yet again into the talented writers of the Jian'an era (196–220), who grasped their brushes and immersed themselves in strange and華麗 [ornate] sounds; and it changed once more into the arcane conversationalists (xuantan) of Jiangzuo [the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties], who waved their fly-whisks and expounded upon principles of pure emptiness. Thus, from the Han down to the Six Dynasties, the cultural elaborateness (wen) of the world once again reached its extreme. Yet after that, there could not fail to be the Tang; and because there could not fail to be the Tang, the cycle returned again with the arrival of the Tang. Alas! From this, the waning ages of the Tang and Song can likewise be deduced.

Now, at their inception, these several dynasties were assuredly very substantial and plain (zhi); yet before long they grew elaborate (wen)—why did this proliferation continue without end? I have reflected on the reason for this: at the beginning of a dynasty, when Heaven's creation is still in a state of rough obscurity, its governance, teaching, and customs are all pure and possess the ethos of high antiquity; therefore, the world is simple and uncarved (pu). Once it is simple and uncarved, it is nurtured for several decades, and both public and private material resources inevitably become abundant and overflowing; therefore, the world flourishes. Once it flourishes, fame, renown, and cultural institutions inevitably become extravagant and unrestrainable; therefore, the world becomes elaborate (wen). Once it becomes elaborate, its fundamental roots and lifeblood inevitably suffer impairment and lose their firmness; therefore, the world falls into decline. Alas! How could this be the result of a single morning or evening? Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu] said: "Once carved and once polished, return again to the uncarved block." When things reach their opposite, they return to their root. When things reach their extreme, they…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
反豈獨人爲盖亦天之道也然二代之末
無聖人以救之而其勢遂極極而無以制
其後聽其自返于質焉則純任乎天而已
豈不惜哉
國家當
祖宗時其簡澹無爲之理可考鏡也至故老所
道說醇美愿茂之俗又可覩也令俗化常
如是
聖主握道而理何憂天下而弘正以來六七十
===
年之間則所謂豐亨豫大之時也掊固陋
而文明擺淳質而華巧上銷日月之光下
鑠山川之精天地之氣皆已流而不韞而
人之智慧已窮故識者以爲文太盛也試
核其大者夫風教嘗淳矣今也繩之以文
法而如束濕薪察之以鉤距而能見淵魚
銅墨之長日暴其情以中大吏而民日無
聊則吏之政澆也俗化嘗儉矣今也不事
本業而務於淫伎曲巧三家之市列雕琢

…reverts; how could this be merely human doing? Indeed, it is also the Way of Heaven. Yet at the end of the Two Dynasties, there were no sages to rescue them, and so their momentum reached its extreme. Once it reached the extreme without anything to control what followed, leaving it to return to substance on its own meant relying purely on Heaven and nothing more—how could that not be a pity!

In our state, during the time of the Imperial Ancestors, the principles of simplicity, tranquility, and non-action could be examined as a mirror; and the pure, fine, honest, and flourishing customs spoken of by the elders could also be witnessed. If customs and morals had always remained like this, with a sage ruler grasping the Way to govern, what worry would there be for the empire? Yet during the sixty or seventy years since the Hongzhi (1488–1505) and Zhengde (1506–1521) eras, it has been what is called a time of abundance, prosperity, comfort, and greatness. Rejecting rustic narrowness for cultural brilliance, casting aside pure substance for flowery cleverness, above it wears away the light of the sun and moon, and below it melts away the essence of the mountains and rivers. The vital energy of Heaven and Earth has all flowed out without being stored within, and human wisdom and ingenuity have been exhausted; therefore, men of insight consider cultural refinement to be overly flourishing.

Let us examine its major aspects. Moral teaching and customs were once pure; nowadays, people are bound by written laws as tightly as bundling wet firewood, and scrutinized with entrapping inquiries capable of spotting fish in the deepest渊 (abyss). Magistrates with bronze seals and black ribbons daily harden their feelings to please higher officials, while the common people grow daily more destitute and hopeless—this is because the governance of officials has become thin and harsh. Customs and habits were once frugal; nowadays, people do not attend to fundamental occupations, but devote themselves to extravagant skills and intricate contrivances. Even a market of three households displays carved and polished…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
績畫之觀十金之費而博玄黄琦瑋之色
里兒賈子厭錦綺而不御吏卒下走蹈文
組而不爲華則民之俗侈也論議嘗簡矣
今也一令之布而筐篋紛紜老吏握刀牘
而汗沾背一議之興而上書之囊滿道郵
卒馳而不得息則議論多而成之者少也
文嘗平正矣今高者窮極玄眇而盡去其
藻質不則脩先秦西京之業詰曲亢厲而
少恬愉不則呈煙雲月露之形以爲纖麗
===
則文章詭而根本撥也夫明月之珍飾之
以銀黄百年之木破而爲犧尊見謂失其
性矣天下之文致若此也是世道之憂也
愚竊以爲返之至亟矣夫吏治澆者名法
敝也其道莫如重教化使長民之吏常有
仁厚化民之志而無嚴切操下之心則上
之所爲教者敦矣民之靡侈者本業微也
其道莫如明法民遊食則法作無益則法
賈難得之貨則法脩竒僻之服而踰冒則

translation_en: …and painted sights, spending ten pieces of gold just to acquire dark, yellow, and extraordinary colors; village youths and merchants' sons grow tired of brocade and figured silk and refuse to wear them, while petty clerks, runners, and menial servants tread upon patterned silk cords without considering them luxurious—thus the customs of the people have grown extravagant. Discussions and deliberations were once concise; nowadays, when a single order is promulgated, document boxes and baskets are thrown into a flurry, and veteran clerks grip their scraping knives and writing tablets with sweat soaking their backs; when a single proposal is raised, sacks of memorials fill the roads, and postal couriers gallop without rest—thus deliberations are numerous, yet those that achieve results are few. Literary writing was once plain and balanced; nowadays, the lofty ones push abstruse subtleties to the extreme and strip away all ornament and substance; otherwise, they cultivate the writings of the pre-Qin and Western Han, becoming convoluted, strident, and lacking in calm grace; or else they display the shapes of mist, clouds, moon, and dew to contrive delicate prettiness—thus literary composition has grown bizarre and its fundamental roots are uprooted. Now, if a bright-moon pearl is embellished with silver and gold, or a hundred-year-old tree is hacked apart to make a sacrificial goblet, it is said to have lost its innate nature. That the cultural elaboration of the empire has reached such a state is a sorrow for the way of the world. I humbly believe that reversing this trend is of the utmost urgency. That official governance has grown thin and perfunctory is because the system of names and laws has deteriorated; the way to remedy it is nothing better than emphasizing moral instruction and transformation. If the officials who govern the people always possess the aspiration to transform the people through benevolence and generosity, and lack the mindset of harshly controlling their subordinates, then the instruction practiced by superiors will become sincere and solid. title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
法則下之俗偷而天下有窕財矣論議之
煩者政不信也其道在斷而畫一一言有
當何煩乎累牘之陳單辭可成不必于盈
庭之論則議簡而政省壹矣文之以華竒
為工者學不明也其道在尊經而復古學
術正而蜚摇之辭遠淳雅復而鈎棘之調
息則文正而不詖矣雖然此非法禁之所
能止也孔子曰移風易俗豈家至之哉以
身先之而已矣故令禁於已然之後而化
===
漸於未然之前令之所禁由之而可知而
化之所漸用之而不可見聖人之為天下
常使之可用而不使之必知故聖人之功
常始於不可見而終於不可及無他道也
以身先之而已矣樹寛仁之風則無敢以
苛應也躬儉朴之化則無敢以侈應也敷
簡靜之理則無敢以靡應也遵平正之軌
則無敢以譎應也此所謂聖人之權也嗟
乎聖人之權用而終始循環之運在人而

translation_en: … [subjected to] the law, then the customs of those below will [no longer?][?] be slipshod and the empire will have ample wealth [?]. That deliberations and discussions are prolix is because governance is not trusted; the way to remedy this lies in decisiveness and uniformity. When a single word hits the mark, why bother with presentations filling stacked tablets? When a brief statement can settle the matter, there is no need for debates that fill the court; then discussions will be concise and administration streamlined and unified. That literary writing takes flowery novelty as skill is because learning is not illuminated; the way to remedy this lies in honoring the Classics and restoring antiquity. When scholarly learning is rectified, flighty and wavering expressions will be kept at a distance; when pure elegance is restored, thorny and convoluted tunes will cease; then writing will be upright and not biased. Even so, this is not something that legal prohibitions alone can stop. Confucius said: "In shifting winds and changing customs, how could one go from house to house to do it? One simply leads them in person, and that is all." Therefore, ordinances prohibit after something has already happened, whereas moral transformation imbues before it has yet happened. What ordinances prohibit can be known as one follows them, whereas what transformation imbues is put to use without being seen. In governing the empire, the sage always makes it so that the people can put his way to use, without making it necessary that they understand it; therefore the achievements of the sage always begin in what cannot be seen and end in what cannot be equaled. There is no other way: one simply leads them in person, and that is all. Establish an ethos of寬lenience and benevolence, and none will dare respond with harshness; personally embody the transformation of frugality and simplicity, and none will dare respond with extravagance; spread principles of conciseness and tranquility, and none will dare respond with ostentation; follow a path of fairness and uprightness, and none will dare respond with deceit. translation_en:
… and does not rest with Heaven. Therefore, those who claim that the downward flow of rivers and streams cannot be turned back are mistaken.

Third Question
By Sun Kuang 孫鑛

Comment by Associate Examiner Vice Director Chen 陳: The argumentation is balanced and upright, revealing an integrity that neither goes to extremes nor merely follows the crowd. It ought to be recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Examining Editor Xi 習: Nobility, emoluments, and reputation are not mere devices for snaring scholars, yet how could a scholar act solely for himself and flee from them? This is an orthodox argument. How pertinent are the concluding remarks on the righteous duty between ruler and minister!

Comment by Associate Examiner Examining Editor Shen 沈: Ever since doctrines of utilitarianism and profit arose, people have treated nobility, emoluments, and reputation as a marketplace—something even worthies have not been able to avoid. Your discourse upholds what is upright and can serve to lead the scholars. Strive on! I shall hold to this essay in holding you to account.

Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Xu 徐: You are listed on the register of tribute scholars, having come here for emolument and reputation, yet you state that in a ruler employing a minister and a minister serving a ruler, righteous duty transcends both of these things. Because of this, scholars ought to gain in honor and rise in esteem.

Comment by Examiner Hanlin Reader-in-Waiting Academician Wang 王: The diction is antique and elegant, and the argumentation is lofty and pure; from it one may observe a man who has long cultivated high aspirations.

Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Lü 吕: The insight is surpassing and the argumentation upright and grand. Reading this policy essay is enough to know the depth of his self-cultivation.

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
聖人所以為治者二爵祿也名譽也置爵
祿所以為賤榮也而簡節廉取者世謂之
貞重名譽所以為衆使也而晦德不耀者
世謂之高然則政之所貴俗之所賤而上
下恒相持也此可挾勢用術而詭士以必
得哉惟聖王知其然故設禮義忠信以懷
之而交泰之象成一體之義合故曰聖人
有金城者此物此志也論者曰昔在先王
建方畧御倫類因人之欲而立之制民欲
===
富而制之以祿民欲尊而制之以爵民欲
勝而制之以名假之以虚至之物而攝之
以必從之勢今夫臣出身以事主析圭儋
爵懷符剖祿則無令而不從士有說之不
入脅之不下而一旦激於單辭片言奔命
仁義捐靡而不悔者為名高也王者握其
幾可以祿者祿繫之祿之而不足者設名
高以下之蓋制馭人羣之術耳是言也所
謂似之而非者也士為人主用也為爵祿
