punctuated: 聖人所以為治者二：爵祿也，名譽也。置爵祿所以為賤榮也，而簡節廉取者，世謂之貞；重名譽所以為衆使也，而晦德不耀者，世謂之高。然則政之所貴，俗之所賤，而上下恒相持也。此可挾勢用術，而詭士以必得哉？惟聖王知其然，故設禮義忠信以懷之，而交泰之象成，一體之義合。故曰：「聖人有金城者，此物此志也。」論者曰：「昔在先王，建方畧，御倫類，因人之欲而立之制。民欲富而制之以祿，民欲尊而制之以爵，民欲勝而制之以名。假之以虚至之物，而攝之以必從之勢。今夫臣出身以事主，析圭儋爵，懷符剖祿，則無令而不從；士有說之不入、脅之不下，而一旦激於單辭片言，奔命仁義，捐靡而不悔者，為名高也。王者握其幾，可以祿者祿繫之，祿之而不足者設名高以下之，蓋制馭人羣之術耳。」是言也，所謂似之而非者也。士為人主用也，為爵祿
translation_en:
The means by which the sages govern are two: noble rank and emolument, and reputation and praise. Instituting rank and emolument is the means to bring honor to the lowly, yet those who simplify their conduct and take sparingly are called pure by the world; giving weight to reputation and praise is the means to employ the multitude, yet those who conceal their virtue and do not shine forth are called lofty by the world. If that is so, what governance prizes is what custom disdains, and superior and inferior are constantly deadlocked against one another. Can one then rely on power and employ statecraft to trick scholars into being surely won over? Only the sage kings knew it to be so; therefore they established ritual propriety, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness to cherish them,whereby the image of mutual communion and peace was completed, and the principle of forming a single body was united. Hence it is said: "That the sages possess a rampart of metal—it is this very thing, this very intent."

Some disputants say: "In ancient times, the former kings established grand strategies and governed human kind, instituting regulations in accordance with human desires. The people desired wealth, and so they regulated them with emolument; the people desired honor, and so they regulated them with rank; the people desired superiority, and so they regulated them with reputation. They lent them things that arrive as empty tokens, and controlled them through circumstances that compelled obedience. Now, when a subject comes forth in person to serve his ruler, splitting the jade tally and bearing noble rank, clasping the credential and dividing the emolument, there is no command he will not obey. And when there are scholars whom persuasion cannot penetrate and threats cannot subdue, yet who, once stirred by a single phrase or half a word, rush to do the bidding of benevolence and righteousness, sacrificing themselves to destruction without regret—it is for the sake of lofty reputation. The true king grasps this subtle trigger: those who can be won by emolument he binds with emolument, and for those whom emolument does not suffice, he sets up lofty reputation to bring them into submission. This is nothing more than the art of controlling and driving the human herd."

These words are what is called resembling the truth while being false. When a scholar allows himself to be employed by a ruler, is it for the sake of noble rank and emolument…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
乎爵祿者上所貴以酬士而非士之所貴
凡為爵祿来者非士也為名譽乎名譽士
所自有奚藉人主藉人主以就其聲非士
也夫士固有志耳耕草茹木鶉居鷇食其
視鼎珍法膳曾弗腴於此矣師友造化旦
暮古今其視熈鴻鑠景曾弗永於此矣不
察其志而猥以兩者勝士是以驅之之道
縻之也奚可哉惟彼功利之說倡而論者
每下管仲曰祿肥則士不死幣輕則士簡
===
賞萬物輕則士偷幸此何異操贏竒而乗
人之急者君臣之際有市心矣魯仲連耻
之陳埴曰三代而上士惟恐其好名三代
而下士惟恐其不好名彼以三代而下非
其人邪胡不引先民之事責之也彼其意
豈不以負氣矜節之夫非名無以攝之而
不知回遹者將冥力焉徒見飯牛扣角之
朋非祿不足以役之而不知貪冒者争奔
走之漢巳事可徵已漢興高祖詔天下賢

…? Rank and emolument are what the ruler values as a means to reward scholars, not what scholars themselves value; anyone who comes for the sake of rank and emolument is no true scholar. Is it for the sake of reputation and praise? Reputation and praise are things a scholar possesses in himself—why should he depend on a ruler for them? Anyone who depends on a ruler to establish his fame is no true scholar. Indeed, a scholar inherently has his own high aspirations. Plowing among weeds and eating from trees, dwelling like a quail and feeding like a fledgling—in his eyes, tripods of delicacies and courtly feasts are no richer than this. Taking Nature as his teacher and friend, conversing with antiquity and the present as if from morning to evening—in his eyes, resplendent grandeur and glorious renown are no more enduring than this. To fail to examine his aspirations and instead crudely try to win scholars over with these two things is to tether them by the very means that drives them away—how could that be acceptable!

It was only after doctrines of utilitarian expediency were championed that the arguments of commentators grew ever more base. Guan Zhong 管仲 said: "If emoluments are overly rich, scholars will not die for their ruler; if currency is light, scholars will slight rewards; if the myriad goods are cheap, scholars will seek to get by on luck." How does this differ from a merchant hoarding rare goods to profit from people's emergencies? Between ruler and minister there had arisen the mentality of the marketplace—something Lu Zhonglian 魯仲連 would be ashamed of. Chen Zhi 陳埴 said: "From the Three Dynasties on up, the only fear regarding a scholar was that he might be fond of fame; from the Three Dynasties on down, the only fear regarding a scholar was that he might not be fond of fame." Did he consider that from the Three Dynasties on down men were no longer of the same caliber? Why did he not hold them to account by citing the deeds of the ancients? Was his idea not surely that men who pride themselves on spirit and integrity cannot be controlled without fame—while failing to realize that crooked and devious men would blindly scheme after it? And seeing only the likes of those who fed cattle and drummed on their horns, he thought that without emolument there would be no way to employ them—while failing to realize that greedy and unscrupulous men would scramble after it in droves.

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
士大夫能從吾游者吾能尊顯之故士驚
於尊顯蕭曹起刀筆吏碌碌無竒節叔孫
與時變化道固委蛇公孫弘卜式倪寬其
初遠迹羊豕之間張湯陰陽人主與俱上
下所謂得人之盛者大都似此矣自斯以
來官事寝廢九卿救過不贍不暇論於繩
墨之外而貢薛韋匡如波斯靡於是有含
羞蒙垢羽翼猰㺄符命偽作功德競陳如
劉歆之流者此亦重祿之過也建武初首
===
以卓茂為太傅封褒德侯及周黨嚴光陛
見不屈親詘萬乘以高之蓋天下始驚名
也然王良之來東海友人譏其無忠信竒
謀而取大位矣樊英就聘而應對無深策
則壼山蒙其耻聲廣漢楊厚江夏黃瓊微
李固之戒盛名之下亦難副矣鄧彪劉愷
激詭為讓使丁鴻而微悟曷以異茲斯時
也士爭依倚道藝以就其聲價後進希之
以成名世主禮之以得衆而俊厨顧及標

translation_en:
…worthy gentlemen and grandees: "Whoever is able to follow and associate with me, I can make honored and illustrious." Thus scholars were startled into pursuing honor and prominence. Xiao He 蕭何 and Cao Shen 曹參 rose from being petty clerks of knife and brush, ordinary and without extraordinary integrity; Shusun Tong 叔孫通 changed along with the times, his Way inherently accommodating and compliant; Gongsun Hong 公孫弘, Bu Shi 卜式, and Ni Kuan 倪寬 at first kept their tracks far away among sheep and swine; Zhang Tang 張湯 manipulated the ruler with subtlety, rising and falling in concert with him. What has been called a flourishing era of obtaining capable men was for the most part like this. From that time onward, official duties gradually fell into neglect; the Nine Ministers (Jiuqing 九卿) could barely save themselves from fault and had no leisure to discuss matters beyond the strict letter of the rules, while Gong Yu 貢禹, Xue Guangde 薛廣德, Wei Xuancheng 韋玄成, and Kuang Heng 匡衡 drifted along like ripples on water. Thereupon there appeared men who swallowed shame and bore disgrace, acted as wings to rapacious beasts, forged auspicious portents and mandates, and vied in proclaiming merits and virtues—men of the ilk of Liu Xin 劉歆. This too was the fault of placing excessive weight on emoluments.

At the beginning of the Jianwu 建武 era (25–56 CE), the emperor first appointed Zhuo Mao 卓茂 as Grand Mentor (Taifu 太傅) and enfeoffed him as Marquis who Exalts Virtue (Baode hou 褒德侯); and when Zhou Dang 周黨 and Yan Guang 嚴光 were granted an imperial audience and refused to bow, the sovereign of ten thousand chariots personally humbled himself to exalt them. Thus the empire first began to be startled into pursuing reputation. Yet when Wang Liang 王良 came from Donghai 東海, his friend ridiculed him for taking high office without loyalty, good faith, or extraordinary counsel. When Fan Ying 樊英 accepted an imperial summons to office yet offered no profound policies in his replies, Mount Hu 壼山 bore the disgrace of his reputation. As for Yang Hou 楊厚 of Guanghan 廣漢 and Huang Qiong 黃瓊 of Jiangxia 江夏, had it not been for the admonition of Li Gu 李固, it would likewise have been difficult for them to live up to their great reputations. Deng Biao 鄧彪 and Liu Kai 劉愷 engaged in extreme and contrived acts of yielding their titles; had Ding Hong 丁鴻 not come to his senses, how would he have differed from them? At that time, scholars vied to lean upon the Way and the arts in order to build up their reputation and value; juniors emulated them in order to establish a name, reigning sovereigns treated them with ritual courtesy in order to win the multitude, and the categories of the Eminent (Jun 俊), the Kitchens (Chu 厨), the Guides (Gu 顧), and the Exemplars (Ji 及) labeled…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
移成風於是有父盜子名兄竊弟譽骨肉
相詒朋友相詐如徐幹所詬者此亦重名
之過也由此觀之始未甞不匡世振俗而
後稍陵夷也然則握竒蘊珍之士柰何不
視名姓為嚆矢比印佩於鉗鐵歌紫芝而
不來逃吳市而長往耻知名於女子而羞
屈志於功曹哉夫然後知祿與名之不足
恃也先王之治曷甞不用兹二者顧所以
用之有異焉盖物莫貴於難得而賤於妄
===
授衣文繡於倡優則貴人不服矣飲和羮
於廝賤則上客不啜矣澗毛可以薦王公
壺飡可以結死士豈謂物耶亦有所將耳
先王建諸侯而錫爵祿也必於清廟之中
備金石之樂宴賜之禮宗人擯相內史作
策故有賚之頌其官民材也必先論之論
辨而後使之任事而後爵之位定而後祿
之故祿所以祿有德也德有大小而祿随
之如大材為棟小材為桷見其任不問而

… [comparing and] shifting into a prevailing wind. Consequently, there were fathers who stole their sons' fame and elder brothers who pilfered their younger brothers' praise, flesh and blood deceiving one another, and friends defrauding each other, just as Xu Gan 徐幹 denounced—this, too, was the fault of overvaluing reputation. Viewed in this light, in the beginning such practices never failed to rectify the age and rouse popular customs, yet later they gradually declined and decayed. That being so, how could gentlemen who clutch rare talents and harbor precious virtues not regard their own names and surnames as mere whistling arrows, compare official seals and pendants to iron collars and fetters, sing of the purple agaric and refuse to come forth, flee to the marketplace of Wu 吳 and depart forever, feel ashamed to have their names known even by a woman, and blush to bend their ambitions before a Merit Evaluator (gongcao 功曹)? Only then does one realize that emolument and reputation are not enough to rely upon.

In the governance of the former kings, when did they ever fail to employ these two things? Yet the way they employed them was different. For nothing makes things more prized than being hard to obtain, or more cheapened than being recklessly bestowed. If patterned embroideries are clothed upon actors and entertainers, then noblemen will not wear them; if seasoned broth is given to menial servants to drink, then honored guests will not sip it. That stream-side herbs may be presented to princes and dukes, and a gourd of food may bind warriors to the death—is this speaking of the material things themselves? It is simply a matter of the spirit in which they are offered.

When the former kings established the feudal lords and bestowed ranks and emoluments upon them, they invariably did so within the Pure Temple, preparing the music of metal and stone and the rites of banqueting and bestowal; the Master of Ceremonies (zongren 宗人) served as protocol usher, and the Royal Scribe (neishi 內史) composed the patent of investiture—hence there is the sacrificial ode "Bestowal" (Lai 賚). And in appointing talented men from among the people to office, they invariably evaluated them first; only after evaluating and distinguishing them did they employ them, only after they had shouldered responsibilities did they grant them rank, and only after their positions were settled did they grant them emoluments. Thus, emolument was the means of rewarding those who possessed virtue. Virtue was great or small, and emolument followed accordingly—just as large timber is made into ridgepoles and small timber into rafters, where upon seeing the burden it bears, one knows without asking…

text:

者銘書於王之太常祭於大烝其紀績也
王功曰勳國功曰功民功曰庸事功曰勞
治功曰力戰功曰多故名所以名有德也
德有大小而名隨之如長形名長短形名
短非長短之名先立而形隨之故其名足
重也方是時也庸人遯跡而賢士畢來山

…knows its quality; therefore, their emoluments were worthy of esteem. In the age of the former kings, all who had [merit?] had their inscriptions written upon the king's Great Standard (taichang) and received sacrifices at the Great Winter Sacrifice (dazheng). In recording achievements: royal merit was called "distinction" (xun), state merit was called "achievement" (gong), merit toward the people was called "service" (yong), merit in affairs was called "toil" (lao), merit in governance was called "effort" (li), and merit in warfare was called "preeminence" (duo). Thus, reputation was the means of naming those with virtue; virtue was great or small, and reputation followed it—just as a long form is named "long" and a short form is named "short," rather than the names "long" and "short" being established first and the forms following them. Therefore, their reputation was worthy of esteem.

At that time, mediocre men hid their tracks while worthy gentlemen all came forward. The mountains and marshes did not lack treasures, yet men gloried in the bestowal of heng and huang jade pendants to wear at their girdles; the fields and acres were not short of grain, yet men prized the stipends from the Grand Granary to fill their kitchens. Whether it was five liang of silk cord, a half-commission bronze seal, a humble attendant's ration, or a single tablet of writing, there was no one who did not regard the object as a favor of virtue and none who dared take it lightly. Was this because the former kings possessed some extraordinary art surpassing the two founders of the Han? Rather, the Han valued emoluments in themselves, whereas the former kings valued bestowing emoluments upon virtue; the Han valued reputation in itself, whereas the former kings valued matching reputation to reality. Techniques of haltering and tethering had no place to be used, and therefore their acquisition of gentlemen was flourishing.

Yet this is still speaking only within the bounds of ranks, emoluments, and reputation. As for the mind of the former kings, they did not even rely on these two things. In the ruler's song, he put the limbs and trunk [his ministers] first; in the ministers' song, they put the head [the ruler] first. The ruler sang "Cry of the Deer" (Luming) to reward his ministers' toil, and the ministers sang "Heaven Protects" (Tianbao) to answer their ruler. Honest simplicity was not dissipated by carved artifice, and their unity as one body was not compromised by duplicity; they simply trusted mind with mind and cherished virtue with virtue, nothing more. Therefore, they never…

之羣臣之上不為過舉也父三老兄五更
心膂大臣手足羣臣此誠任也然而八法
辨治六敘正吏不為厚防也內諸侯祿外
諸侯嗣盛德入輔者兩其食圭田采地世

translation_en: … never failed to bestow renown and institute emoluments, yet sincere hearts and trustworthy intentions pervaded and circulated thoroughly among them. The inspections by subprefectures, villages, clans, and neighborhoods, and the recommendations based on moral conduct, the Way, and the arts, were indeed selections based on reputation; yet finding a chief minister through a dream or a preceptor through divination, and placing them above all the officials without consulting one's elder kinsmen, was not considered an excessive promotion. Treating the Three Elders as fathers and the Five Experienced Men as elder brothers, regarding the great ministers as heart and backbone and the body of officials as hands and feet—this was sincere trust; yet using the Eight Regulations to distinguish governance and the Six Orders to rectify officials was not considered an overly suspicious precaution. The feudal lords within the royal domain received emoluments, while the feudal lords outside inherited their fiefs; those of abundant virtue who entered the court to assist received double their stipends, and their sacrificial fields and appanages were not cut off for generations—their emoluments were by no means meager; yet keeping Yingqiu and Fuyi within a modest hundred li was not out of stinginess either. Chanting in vocal poems and broadcasting on pipes and strings, with eulogies of "a hundred blessings and a hundred emoluments" and praises of "eternal fame and everlasting words"—their renown was by no means unexalted; yet prizing achievements that are neither heard nor seen, so that names are not inscribed on charts and registers and the annals of the years remain blank—what praise is there in that? Indeed, it was only because the former kings made use of these two things without relying upon them that the wise and discerning attached themselves to their sincerity like arrows hitting the target: the deep pools could not keep them coiled away, nor did the mountains afford them leisure to roost; at a bow with folded hands or a wave of the hand, there was none who did not wish to exhaust his strength. This is what is meant by taking the whole world as a cage from which there is no escape. Why, then, must one ostentatiously hold up the two like the sun and moon in order to compel men to follow? Only when this principle became obscured did the world have rulers who laid heavy store by rank, emolument, and reputation; and only after there were rulers who laid heavy store by rank, emolument, and reputation did the world have subjects who fled from rank, emolument, and reputation. They did not understand that…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
上重之上過也下逃之亦下過也楚子發
獲蔡侯而辭其賞荀卿以爲固金城之役
浩星賜以讓功説趙充國充國不可夫辭
賞弗高於逃禄讓功非亢於逃名然二子
以爲持小廉守末節廢賞功之典而忽謀
國之實棄不取也又况甚焉者乎夫士如
自爲計則巳矣不能自爲計而欲逃之此
逃雨也無之而非是矣嗟夫君臣之義光
於穹宇昞於重離而蝕之者常自賢君賢
===
士始宜廑執事之問也
第四問
王應選
同考試官都給事中朱　批學博見超而諸史異同辨
析允當盖邃心於考古者宜錄以式多士
同考試官編修于　批二史卓絶古今子能晰厥
異同粲然可觀翺翔班馬之林矣而又折衷仲尼以
爲準式是二氏所不及也取之
同考試官編修張　批二子並稱良史所不足者

於穹宇昞於重離而蝕之者常自賢君賢
士始宜塵執事之問也
===
第四問
王應選
同考試官都給事中朱　批〔學博見超而諸史異同辨析允當蓋邃心於考古者宜錄以式多士〕
同考試官編修于　批〔二史卓絕古今子能晰厥異同較然可觀翺翔班馬之林矣而又折衷仲尼以爲準式是二氏所不及也取之〕
同考試官編修張　批〔二子並稱良史所不足者〕
punctuated:
上重之，上過也；下逃之，亦下過也。楚子發獲蔡侯而辭其賞，荀卿以爲固；金城之役，浩星賜以讓功説趙充國，充國不可。夫辭賞弗高於逃禄，讓功非亢於逃名，然二子以爲持小廉、守末節，廢賞功之典，而忽謀國之實，棄不取也，又况甚焉者乎？夫士如自爲計，則巳矣；不能自爲計，而欲逃之，此逃雨也，無之而非是矣。嗟夫！君臣之義，光於穹宇，昞於重離，而蝕之者常自賢君、賢士始，宜廑執事之問也。

第四問
王應選
同考試官都給事中朱　批：學博見超，而諸史異同辨析允當，盖邃心於考古者，宜錄以式多士。
同考試官編修于　批：二史卓絶古今，子能晰厥異同，粲然可觀，翺翔班、馬之林矣。而又折衷仲尼以爲準式，是二氏所不及也。取之。
同考試官編修張　批：二子並稱良史，所不足者，
translation_en:
… When the superior attaches too much weight to them, it is the fault of the superior; when the subordinate flees from them, it is likewise the fault of the subordinate. When Zifa 子發 of Chu captured the Marquis of Cai and declined his reward, Xun Qing 荀卿 considered him obstinate. During the campaign at Jincheng 金城, Haoxing Ci 浩星賜 advised Zhao Chongguo 趙充國 to yield credit for the achievement, yet Chongguo refused. Now, declining a reward is no loftier than fleeing from emolument, and yielding credit is no more high-minded than fleeing from fame; yet those two men regarded such acts as clinging to petty scruples and guarding trivial points of honor, undermining the statutes for rewarding merit and neglecting the substance of statecraft—so they rejected and would not adopt them. How much more so in cases even more extreme! If a scholar takes counsel only for himself, then so be it; if he cannot take counsel only for himself and yet wishes to flee from these things, this is like fleeing the rain—there is nowhere he can go where it is not falling. Alas! The moral bond between ruler and minister shines across the vaulted heavens and blazes like the double brightness of sun and moon, yet its eclipse constantly begins with worthy rulers and worthy scholars. Fitting indeed that this should trouble Your Excellency to ask!

Fourth Policy Question
Wang Yingxuan 王應選
Associate Examiner and Chief Supervising Secretary Zhu 朱 comments: His learning is broad and his insight transcendent, and his analysis of the agreements and divergences among the various histories is judicious and apt. Clearly one who has devoted deep thought to the investigation of antiquity, his essay should be published as a model for the many scholars.
Associate Examiner and Historiographer Yu 于 comments: The two histories stand unsurpassed through ancient and modern times. You are able to clarify their similarities and differences with brilliant lucidity, soaring through the grove of Ban Gu 班固 and Sima Qian 司馬遷. Moreover, you take Confucius (Zhongni 仲尼) as the final arbiter and standard—something that those two masters themselves did not attain. Selected.
Associate Examiner and Historiographer Zhang 張 comments: The two masters are together acclaimed as fine historians; where they fall short …

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
非辭也子能剖析異同而歸之於義信為有見其錄
之以俟載筆者採焉
同考試官編修韓批考訂二史精詳折衷允當
具見二長宜錄以式
同考試官編修田批考據精詳文辭爾雅子其
讀二史而有得者乎錄之
考試官侍讀學士王批博綜精覈而詞足以發之盖
究心於史學者
考試官大學士吕批班馬異同評品允當非有卓
見者不能
===
君子所以載鴻筆而擅著作者二徵文比
事辨分當名若繪山川而肖草木者辭也
品今隲古彰善癉惡若執紀律而嚴步伐
者義也故辭以匠意鳥能若頓轡詞林則
氣貌失真而形似無覩義以作經為鵠必
游精理道斯獨斷以寓而宏識攸彰不朽
之規千載無爽矣執策者既抽此而綜紛
議古者亦鏡斯而定品苟略其先務而評

〔非辭也子能剖析異同而歸之於義信爲有見其錄〕

〔究心於史學者〕
考試官大學士呂　批〔班馬異同評品允當非有卓〕
〔見者不能〕
===
君子所以載鴻筆而擅著作者二徵文比
事辨分當名若繪山川而肖草本者辭也
品令隲古彰善癉惡若執紀律而嚴步伐
者義也故辭以匠意爲能若頓轡詞林則
氣貌失真而形似無覩義以作經爲鵠必
游精理道斯獨斷以寓而宷識攸彰不朽
之規千載無爽矣執策者既抽此而綜紛
議古者亦鏡斯而定品茍略其先務而評
punctuated:
非辭也。子能剖析異同，而歸之於義，信為有見。其錄之以俟載筆者採焉。
同考試官編修韓批：考訂二史，精詳折衷，允當，具見二長，宜錄以式。
同考試官編修田批：考據精詳，文辭爾雅，子其讀二史而有得者乎？錄之。
考試官侍讀學士王批：博綜精覈，而詞足以發之，盖究心於史學者。
考試官大學士吕批：班、馬異同，評品允當，非有卓見者不能。
君子所以載鴻筆而擅著作者二：徵文比事，辨分當名，若繪山川而肖草木者，辭也；品今隲古，彰善癉惡，若執紀律而嚴步伐者，義也。故辭以匠意鳥能，若頓轡詞林，則氣貌失真而形似無覩；義以作經為鵠，必游精理道，斯獨斷以寓而宏識攸彰，不朽之規，千載無爽矣。執策者既抽此而綜紛，議古者亦鏡斯而定品。苟略其先務而評
translation_en:
…is not literary diction. You are able to dissect their differences and similarities and bring them back to moral principle (yi)—truly showing real insight. Let this be recorded to await selection by those who wield the historian's brush.

Associate Examiner Han, Historiographer, comments: Your critical examination of the two histories is precise and detailed, and your balanced judgment is fair and fitting, fully demonstrating the two strengths of a historian. It should be recorded as a model.

Associate Examiner Tian, Historiographer, comments: Your evidential research is precise and detailed, and your literary expression is refined and elegant. Are you not one who has read the two histories and gained true understanding? Record it.

Examiner Wang, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: Broadly synthesized and precisely verified, with diction sufficient to bring it forth—surely one who has devoted his mind to the study of history.

Examiner Lü, Grand Secretary, comments: The evaluation of the similarities and differences between Ban Gu 班固 and Sima Qian 司馬遷 is fair and fitting; none without extraordinary insight could achieve this.

There are two things by which the gentleman wields a grand brush and excels at authorship: verifying documents and arranging events, distinguishing statuses and matching names, like painting mountains and rivers or depicting plants and trees—this is diction (ci); evaluating the present and judging the past, displaying the good and condemning the evil, like upholding military discipline and strictly regulating the ranks and paces—this is moral principle (yi). Therefore, diction takes crafting meaning as its capability [?]; if one merely halts one's reins in the forest of rhetoric, the vital spirit and appearance lose their truth, and even formal resemblance cannot be seen. Moral principle takes the creation of canonical classics as its target; one must immerse one's spirit in principle and the Way, so that independent judgment is lodged within and broad insight is made manifest—an imperishable standard that does not err across a thousand years. Those who hold the bamboo tablets draw upon this to synthesize tangled affairs, and those who discuss antiquity also mirror themselves in this to determine their evaluations. If one neglects what is of primary importance and evaluates…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
□□業昔人還珠之譏其謂是乎請以此
復班馬異同之問粤稽鴻濛世遠丘墳繇
邈蒼頡操簡於黄軒瑣言標迹於汲冢至
周而史職大備珥筆左右各有其人蓋墨
子言吾觀百國春秋則知當時國不乏史
而湮逸無聞已乃若世所傳說者則有國
語左傳所謂聖經之羽翼也由今攷其書
事辭複出體裁不倫陸淳謂其非一人所
作信矣夫惟不出於一人則其同異迥然
===
又何足深辨哉嗣是稱良史者莫如馬遷
班固遷著史記五十萬言劉向諸人服其
辨而不華質而不俚不虚美不隱惡固著
漢書八十萬言范曄稱其贍而不穢詳而
有體比良遷董兼麗卿雲蓋皆纂述漢事
者也固書雖踵遷史而作然務趣簡嚴多
所刪改淵流遂往詳畧異聞王充著書既
甲班而乙馬張輔持論復劣固而優遷軒
輊淄澠代無定評譬之一鬨之市不勝異

punctuated: □□業，昔人還珠之譏，其謂是乎？請以此復班、馬異同之問。粤稽鴻濛世遠，丘、墳繇邈，蒼頡操簡於黄軒，《瑣言》標迹於汲冢。至周而史職大備，珥筆左右，各有其人。蓋墨子言：「吾觀百國《春秋》。」則知當時國不乏史，而湮逸無聞已。乃若世所傳說者，則有《國語》、《左傳》，所謂聖經之羽翼也。由今攷其書，事辭複出，體裁不倫，陸淳謂其非一人所作，信矣。夫惟不出於一人，則其同異迥然，又何足深辨哉？嗣是稱良史者，莫如馬遷、班固。遷著《史記》五十萬言，劉向諸人服其辨而不華，質而不俚，不虚美，不隱惡；固著《漢書》八十萬言，范曄稱其贍而不穢，詳而有體，比良遷、董，兼麗卿、雲。蓋皆纂述漢事者也。固書雖踵遷史而作，然務趣簡嚴，多所刪改，淵流遂往，詳畧異聞。王充著書，既甲班而乙馬；張輔持論，復劣固而優遷。軒輊、淄澠，代無定評，譬之一鬨之市，不勝異
translation_en:
… [□□] work [?]; is this not what the ancients meant by the ridicule of returning the pearl [and keeping the box]? Please allow me to use this to reply to the question regarding the similarities and differences between Ban Gu 班固 and Sima Qian 司馬遷.

Examining remote antiquity when the world was in primordial chaos, the Three Mounds (Sanqiu 三丘) and Five Canons (Wufen 五墳) are distant and obscure; Cangjie 蒼頡 held the bamboo slips under the Yellow Emperor (Huangxuan 黄軒), and the Trivial Words (Suoyan 瑣言) left its traces in the Ji Tomb (Jizhong 汲冢). By the Zhou dynasty, the offices of historians were fully established, with scribes wearing brushes in their caps in attendance on the left and right, each having their designated personnel. Indeed, Mozi 墨子 said: "I have observed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu 春秋) of a hundred states." Thus we know that at that time states did not lack histories, though they have since been lost and remain unheard of. As for what has been transmitted and discussed in the world, there are the Discourses of the States (Guoyu 國語) and the Zuo Commentary (Zuozhuan 左傳), which are called the wings to the Sacred Classic. Examining these books today, their events and wording appear repeatedly and their stylistic formats do not match; Lu Chun 陸淳 said that they were not written by a single person, which is truly so. Now, precisely because they did not come from a single hand, their similarities and differences are vast—how then are they worth arguing over deeply?

After this, none were more praised as good historians than Sima Qian (Ma Qian 馬遷) and Ban Gu. Sima Qian wrote the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji 史記) in five hundred thousand words; Liu Xiang 劉向 and others admired that it was articulate yet not華 (flamboyant), plain yet not vulgar, neither falsely praising nor concealing evil. Ban Gu wrote the Book of Han (Hanshu 漢書) in eight hundred thousand words; Fan Ye 范曄 praised it as rich yet not cluttered, detailed yet structured, matching the excellence of Sima Qian and Dong Hu 董狐 while combining the elegance of Sima Xiangru 司馬相如 (Qing 卿) and Yang Xiong 揚雄 (Yun 雲). Indeed, both compiled and recounted the affairs of the Han dynasty. Although Ban Gu's book was written by following in the footsteps of Sima Qian's history, it strove for conciseness and rigor, making many deletions and alterations; as the source and its stream diverged, their details, omissions, and accounts differed. Wang Chong 王充, in his writings, ranked Ban first and Sima second; Zhang Fu 張輔, in holding forth his argument, conversely judged Ban Gu inferior and Sima Qian superior. Weighing them up and down, distinguishing them like the waters of the Zi and Sheng rivers, generations have had no settled evaluation—like a noisy marketplace, there is no end to differing …

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
意矣于是宋倪思博綜其趣而懼覽者之
弗察也爰合爲一書證厥同異或刪而遺
其事實如季布傳見滕公語酈生傳對齊
王語是也則爲之糾其缺或改而失其本
意如高帝紀以蛟龍爲交龍曹參傳以顜
若爲講若是也則爲之正其訛探玄珠於
崑崙檢良玉於縣圃亦已勤矣然古史之
作非爲摛辭掞藻所以徵往詔来示憲誡
也必總之表志而朝家之規制備必散之
===
紀傳而上下之行事詳猶夫人之身百體
畢具君子考於此故全也思之所撰遺年
表書志而獨專於紀傳世家且决雌黃於
片辭定妍媸於隻字窺文豹而得一斑據
大鼎而竊寸臠盖擷英咀華之具非鉤玄
提要之書可爲欸啓寡聞者資而難爲崇
論欲議者道也豈足以發二子之同異哉
乃其同異則更僕未詳愚請舉其畧言之
遷之年表十固則省而爲八遷之書八固

… opinions. Thereupon, in the Song dynasty, Ni Si 倪思 broadly synthesized their import, and fearing that readers might fail to discern it, combined them into a single book to verify their similarities and differences. Where passages were abridged so that factual details were left out—such as the words spoken when meeting Lord Teng in the "Biography of Ji Bu" (Ji Bu zhuan) or the words spoken in reply to the King of Qi in the "Biography of Master Li" (Li Sheng zhuan)—he pointed out the omissions. Where passages were altered so that the original meaning was lost—such as changing "flood-dragon" (jiaolong 蛟龍) to "intertwined dragon" (jiaolong 交龍) in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Gao" (Gaodi ji), or changing "clear and uniform" (jiangruo 顜若) to "harmonious and uniform" (jiangruo 講若) in the "Biography of Cao Can" (Cao Can zhuan)—he corrected the errors. Like seeking the dark pearl on Mount Kunlun or inspecting fine jade in the Hanging Gardens (Xuanpu), his effort was diligent indeed.

Yet the writing of ancient history was not for the sake of displaying rhetoric and flourishing diction; rather, it was the means to verify the past in order to instruct the future, and to set forth models and warnings. Only when summarized in chronological tables and treatises are the regulations and institutions of the dynasty made complete; only when distributed across basic annals and biographies are the deeds of those above and below recounted in detail. It is just like the human body having all its hundred parts fully present: when the gentleman examines history in this way, it is therefore whole. What Ni Si compiled leaves out the chronological tables, treatises (shu), and monographs (zhi), focusing exclusively on the basic annals, biographies, and hereditary houses. Moreover, he applies his critical revisions to mere fragments of phrasing and judges beauty or ugliness in single characters—peering at a patterned leopard to catch sight of a single spot, orleaning over a great cauldron to snatch a one-inch slice of meat. His work is merely an instrument for plucking blossoms and savoring literary flowers, not a book that probes the abstruse and extracts the essential. It can serve as an aid for those of narrow understanding and scant learning, but is hardly worth discussing with those who engage in lofty discourse and grand deliberation [reading 閎議 for 欲議, ?]. How could it suffice to bring to light the similarities and differences between the two masters?

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
則廣而為志者十遷之諸侯年表年經而
國緯觀其韓信王楚子肥王齊張耳王趙
所以寓天下之形勢也固分為同姓異姓
殊乖親疎相錯之體遷之功臣年表國經
而年緯觀其高祖功臣侯惠景間侯建元
以来侯所以著時政之失得也固乃綜而
為二殊昧因時考政之義律書歷書合為
律歷志禮書樂書合為禮樂志逨矣而不
能正元封冬至日星之謬叙長樂朝儀之
===
詳識者非之易封禪為郊祀易平準為食
貨似矣而遺原廟薦新之事宗廟迭毁之
文以弘羊罔民之術擬成周泉府之法達
觀者有遺論焉且固之譏遷曰先黄老而
後六經退處士而進姦雄踈略抵捂是非
頗謬於聖人而自為書則列儒術於諸家
其後六經孰甚褒郭解以謙愛其進姦雄
孰甚志五行而引書失宜者四叙事乖理
者五其踈略抵捂又孰甚儻聖人復起不

translation_en: … broadened them into ten treatises (Zhi). In Sima Qian's "Chronological Table of the Feudal Lords" (Zhuhou nianbiao), years form the warp and states form the woof; observing how Han Xin was enfeoffed as King of Chu, the Emperor's son Liu Fei as King of Qi, and Zhang Er as King of Zhao, one sees how he conveyed the strategic configuration of the empire. Ban Gu divided them into lords of the imperial surname and those of different surnames, which seriously violated the principle of interlocking close kin and distant allies. In Sima Qian's "Chronological Table of Meritorious Ministers" (Gongchen nianbiao), states form the warp and years form the woof; observing his divisions into Marquises who were Meritorious Ministers under Gaozu, Marquises of the Hui and Jing reigns, and Marquises since the Jianyuan era, one sees how he revealed the successes and failures of contemporary governance. Ban Gu, however, combined them into two tables, quite blind to the meaning of examining governance according to the times. Combining the "Treatise on Pitch-Pipes" (Lüshu) and the "Treatise on the Calendar" (Lishu) into the "Treatise on Pitch-Pipes and the Calendar" (Lüli zhi), and combining the "Treatise on Rites" (Lishu) and the "Treatise on Music" (Yueshu) into the "Treatise on Rites and Music" (Liyue zhi), was commendable [? 逨矣, for 韙矣]; yet he failed to correct the errors regarding the sun and stars at the winter solstice in the Yuanfeng era, or to recount in detail the court ceremonial at the Changle Palace, for which men of discernment have criticized him. Changing "Feng and Shan Sacrifices" (Fengshan) to "Suburban Sacrifices" (Jiaosi), and changing "Balanced Standard" (Pingzhun) to "Food and Money" (Shihuo), seemed appropriate; yet he omitted the matter of offering seasonal firstfruits at the Duplicate Temple (Yuanmiao) and the documents on the successive dismantling of ancestral temples, and he compared Sang Hongyang's schemes for entrapping the people to the Treasury (Quanfu) system of the flourishing Zhou, leaving men of broad vision with lingering criticisms. Moreover, Ban Gu criticized Sima Qian by saying: "He puts Huang-Lao first and the Six Classics after, demotes recluse scholars and promotes treacherous heroes; he is sketchy and self-contradictory, and his judgments of right and wrong err considerably from those of the Sages." Yet in writing his own book, he ranked Confucian learning alongside the various schools—what could put the Six Classics further behind than that? He praised Guo Jie for his modesty and benevolence—what could promote treacherous heroes further than that? In his "Treatise on the Five Phases" (Wuxing zhi), there are four instances where he cites the Book of Documents (Shu) inappropriately and five instances where his narration of events violates reason—what could be more sketchy and self-contradictory than that? title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
謬謂何而班生有知懲此月旦矣愚甞反
復二史而究其同異之辨黜項羽於列傳
以懼僭竊尊孝惠於本紀以崇正統附四
夷於末簡以嚴中國此遷之失固宜異而
異者也張湯當列於酷吏而并恕杜周侯
王當別於世家而雜於列傳大宛當采於
四夷而沒於張騫此遷之得固宜同而不
同者也子贛仲尼之徒而溷於貨殖范蠡
春秋之士而綴於漢書兵說略見於刑法
===
而使漢家經武之制無考此遷與固之所
共失宜異而不異不宜同而同者也大抵
遷承坑焚煨燼之後前無師承獨起義例
其成書也難固當文獻足徵之時多因商
雄歆向之舊而潤色之其成書也易遷之
書并論往古且欲藏之名山故其文質直
而事覈固之書專紀當代且奉詔而作故
其文微婉而事詳遷之才優於固故其得
也什九固之才不如遷故其得也什一此

translation_en: … [if not calling it] erroneous, what would He call it? And if Master Ban [Ban Gu 班固] had consciousness in the afterlife, he would take warning from this critical appraisal! I have repeatedly examined the two histories and investigated the distinctions in their similarities and differences: demoting Xiang Yu 項羽 to the arrayed biographies in order to strike fear into usurpers, elevating Emperor Xiaohui 孝惠 to the basic annals in order to honor the legitimate succession, and appending the four barbarian peoples at the end of the work in order to maintain the strict dignity of the Central States—these were Sima Qian's 司馬遷 failings, where Ban Gu ought to have differed and did indeed differ. That Zhang Tang 張湯 should have been placed among the harsh officials rather than excusing both him and Du Zhou 杜周, that the marquises and kings should have been distinguished in the hereditary houses rather than mixed into the arrayed biographies, and that Dayuan 大宛 should have been gathered under the four barbarian peoples rather than subsumed under the biography of Zhang Qian 張騫—these were Sima Qian's successes, where Ban Gu ought to have agreed and yet did not agree. That Zigong 子贛, a disciple of Zhongni 仲尼 [Confucius], was muddled among the money-makers; that Fan Li 范蠡, a man of the Spring and Autumn period, was appended to the Book of Han (Hanshu 漢書); and that the discussion of military affairs was only briefly shown within the treatise on penal law, leaving the Han dynasty's institutions for military governance with nowhere to be investigated—these were failings shared by both Sima Qian and Ban Gu, where they ought to have differed yet did not differ, and ought not to have agreed yet agreed. On the whole, Sima Qian wrote in the aftermath of the burning of the books and burying of the scholars, when all was reduced to ashes; having no predecessors' models to inherit, he alone originated the principles and conventions, so completing his book was difficult. Ban Gu lived at a time when textual and documentary evidence was sufficient for verification, and he largely relied on the earlier works of Chu Shaosun 褚少孫 [? written 商, likely馮商 Feng Shang], Yang Xiong 揚雄, Liu Xin 劉歆, and Liu Xiang 劉向, embellishing them, so completing his book was easy. Sima Qian's book encompassed discussions of antiquity and was intended to be hidden away in a famous mountain, so its style is plain and direct and its facts are verified. Ban Gu's book exclusively recorded the reigning dynasty and was composed by imperial command, so its style is subtle and tactful and its facts are detailed. Sima Qian's talent was superior to Ban Gu's, so his successes were nine out of ten; Ban Gu's talent did not match Sima Qian's, so his successes were one out of ten. This…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
其同異之大凡也噫史之難也久矣臆度
則艱於通方互證則苦於相左年世遠則
瑕瑜易淆汗簡繁則亥豕莫辨假令事緣
目擊猶懼傳訛矧智者千慮豈無一失而
觀者乃兼極索瘢癡窮洗垢詆訶言辭掎
摭利病炫已識之奇博彰前修之骫骳遂
至單辭取訕細事蒙嘲是猶睹豫章之材
而以維籜蔽其美執夜光之璧而以微纇
揜其珍此古人所以致論於目睫也率是
===
而談遷固何可以厚非耶遷固而後荀悅
漢紀史稱辭約事詳論辨多美矣然混淆
倒置君子謂之舛范曄後漢書自謂體大
思精不減過秦論矣然詭譎佻巧君子謂
之詖他如後漢紀作於袁宏時號精密漢
晉春秋作於習鑿齒世稱公論然或略而
不精或逸而不存又皆君子所不道也是
諸人者皆殫力窮年勒成漢事豈不自謂
彎龍虎之文握隨和之寶哉第工於乘人

則艱於通方互證則苦於相左年世遠則
瑕瑜易淆汗簡繁則亥豕莫辨假令事緣
目擊猶懼傳訛矧智者千慮豈無一失而
觀者乃魚極深淵獺窮洗垢試詞言辭摘
摭利病然巳識之尚博彰前修之釁戮遂
至單辭取訕細事蒙譏是猶睹豫章之材
而以維葦蔽其美執夜光之璧而以微纇
揜其珍此古人所以致論於自睫也率是
===
而談遷固何可以厚非耶遷固而後荀悅
漢紀史稱辭約事詳論辯多美矣然混淆
倒置君子謂之舛范曄後漢書自謂體大
思精不減過秦論矣然詭譎佻巧君子謂
之詖袁宏後漢紀作於東晉時號精密漢
晉春秋作於習鑿齒世稱公論然或略而
不精或逸而不存又皆君子所不道也是
諸人者皆殫力窮年勒成漢事豈不自謂
轡龍虎之文握隨和之寶哉第工於乘人
punctuated: 其同異之大凡也。噫！史之難也久矣。臆度則艱於通方，互證則苦於相左，年世遠則瑕瑜易淆，汗簡繁則亥豕莫辨。假令事緣目擊，猶懼傳訛；矧智者千慮，豈無一失？而觀者乃兼極索瘢，癡窮洗垢，詆訶言辭，掎摭利病，炫已識之奇博，彰前修之骫骳，遂至單辭取訕，細事蒙嘲。是猶睹豫章之材，而以維籜蔽其美；執夜光之璧，而以微纇揜其珍。此古人所以致論於目睫也。率是而談，遷、固何可以厚非耶？遷、固而後，荀悅《漢紀》，史稱辭約事詳，論辨多美矣；然混淆倒置，君子謂之舛。范曄《後漢書》，自謂體大思精，不減《過秦論》矣；然詭譎佻巧，君子謂之詖。他如《後漢紀》作於袁宏，時號精密；《漢晉春秋》作於習鑿齒，世稱公論；然或略而不精，或逸而不存，又皆君子所不道也。是諸人者，皆殫力窮年，勒成漢事，豈不自謂彎龍虎之文，握隨和之寶哉？第工於乘人，
translation_en:
…is the general outline of their similarities and differences. Alas! Writing history has long been difficult. If one relies on conjecture, it is hard to achieve comprehensive understanding; if one cross-verifies sources, one suffers from their contradictions; when eras are distant, flaws and merits are easily confused; when bamboo slips are numerous, scribal errors like mistaking hai for shi cannot be distinguished. Even when events are witnessed firsthand, one still fears transmitting errors; how much more so when even a wise man, in a thousand considerations, cannot avoid a single slip? Yet readers go to extremes in searching for scars and foolishly exhaust themselves washing away dirt to find defects—carping at the phrasing, picking out faults and flaws, showing off the novelty and breadth of their own knowledge, and exposing the crookedness and shortcomings of former worthies, until a single word invites ridicule and a trivial matter suffers mockery. This is like looking at camphor and楠 timber yet letting clinging bamboo sheaths obscure its beauty, or holding a night-shining jade disk yet letting a tiny blemish conceal its preciousness. This is why the ancients directed their discourse to the inability of the eye to see its own eyelashes. Judging by this principle, how can Sima Qian 司馬遷 and Ban Gu 班固 be severely faulted?

After Sima Qian and Ban Gu, Xun Yue's 荀悅 Annals of the Han (Han ji 漢紀) was praised by historians for its concise language, detailed facts, and many admirable critical discussions; yet because of its confusions and inversions, gentlemen call it erroneous. Fan Ye 范曄, in his Book of the Later Han (Hou Han shu 後漢書), boasted that its grand structure and refined thought were no less than those of the "Discourse on the Faults of Qin" (Guo Qin lun 過秦論); yet because it is deceitful, frivolous, and overly clever, gentlemen call it biased. As for others, such as the Annals of the Later Han (Hou Han ji 後漢紀) written by Yuan Hong 袁宏, which was acclaimed in its time for precision, and the Spring and Autumn of Han and Jin (Han Jin chunqiu 漢晉春秋) written by Xi Zaochi 習鑿齒, which the world praised for its impartial judgments—some are sketchy and imprecise, while others have been lost and no longer survive, so gentlemen do not speak of them either. All these men exhausted their strength and spent their years compiling the affairs of the Han; did they not consider themselves to be drawing thepatterned bow of dragon and tiger, and grasping the treasures of the Marquis of Sui and Bian He? Yet they were skillful at taking advantage of others…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
拙於用已匪無弋獲終愧通才究所造詣
曾未能升司馬之堂入班生之室而欲盡
掩前秀參軌作者之塗難以冀矣語曰視
日月而知衆星之蔑也仰聖人而知衆說
之小也古今之言史者宜折衷於孔子矣
孔子之作春秋也觀舊法於周禮遵遺文
於魯策據行事闡人道就敗以明罰因興
以立功假日月而定曆數藉朝聘而正禮
樂微言奧旨褒貶攸寓雖游夏文學莫贊
===
一辭猶歆然不自居曰其義則竊取之而
知我罪我惟斯編也以故能折衷百王而
並稱六籍非作者謂聖其孰能與於此乎
噫專辭而略義遷固之所以不古若也顧
後之載筆者吾惑焉覃精二史見謂爾雅
極力追摹曰班曰馬遂使唐襲秦官宋仍
漢制寶玉大弓終非已有矧未得國能而
又失其故步哉以是求同于班馬此正倪
思之所謂同異吾無取也楊雄有言人有

translation_en: … yet clumsy at drawing upon their own resources. Though not without occasional hits, in the end they fall short of comprehensive mastery. If we examine their actual attainments, they have not even ascended the hall of Sima Qian or entered the inner chamber of Master Ban [Ban Gu]; yet to wish to completely overshadow earlier talents and join the tracks of true creators—that is hard to hope for indeed. As the saying goes: "Look at the sun and moon, and you know the insignificance of the myriad stars; look up to the Sage, and you know the pettiness of the myriad doctrines." Those past and present who speak of history ought to take Confucius as their final arbiter. When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), he observed the old regulations in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) and followed the surviving records in the tablets of Lu. Basing himself on actual deeds, he elucidated the Way of humanity: seizing upon failures to clarify punishments, building upon successes to establish merit, making use of days and months to fix the calendrical sequence, and relying on court visits and diplomatic missions to rectify rites and music. Subtle words and profound purport are wherein praise and blame reside; even with the literary accomplishments of Ziyou [Yan Yan] and Zixia [Bu Shang], they could not add a single word. Yet he remained modestly unassuming [reading 歆 as 欿] and did not claim the credit for himself, saying, "Its meaning I have ventured to deduce," and that "those who understand me and those who condemn me" would do so solely because of this compilation. For this reason it was able to serve as the standard for a hundred kings and be ranked alongside the Six Classics. Were it not that a true creator is called a sage, who could partake in this? Alas! Focusing exclusively on diction while neglecting moral principle is why Sima Qian and Ban Gu do not match antiquity. Yet as for later wielders of the brush, I am perplexed by them. Devoting their deepest energies to those two histories, they consider this to be refined elegance, exerting all their strength in imitation while speaking ever of Ban and Sima. Consequently, they make the Tang inherit Qin offices and the Song retain Han institutions; the precious jade and great bow are, in the end, not their own possession—how much worse when they have not even acquired the national skill of Handan and have already lost their own original gait! title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
稱仲尼者可謂仲尼乎其文是也其質非
也故懷鉛握槧之士能因仲尼之文而求
其質則庶幾哉可與言史矣
第五問
陳與郊
同考試官都給事中劉批用人理財時政之最大者
場中類能言之此篇獨得救時之切要處蓋不可以
經生目之也
同考試官右諭德王批此
===
國家二大政言者紛紛未有必然之畫是作揚搉古今持論有體蓋經生
知時務者錄之
考試官侍讀學士王批儒生搦管談時務鑿鑿中肯
綮庶幾俊傑者錄之
考試官大學士呂批究論時務一一確當經生而
有經世之志者取之
明主所以均一海内垂衣而萬事理者無
他故焉以天下才治天下事使各得其職
焉耳矣以天下財制天下用使各得其宜

…is called Zhongni [Confucius], can he truly be called Zhongni? His outward refinement is the same, yet his essential substance is not." 人有餘是以愈不足也從其有餘者而慎
用之才何不足之有天下之大亦非乏財
也經費濫而用有餘是以愈不足也從其
有餘者而慎節之財何不足之有斯兩者
明主察之所以庶官無曠六府咸修不越
階序而運天下也執事策士以用人理財

Now, in a realm as vast as All-under-Heaven, there is no shortage of talent; rather, when name and reality are confused and personnel are in surplus, there is all the more a shortage. If, starting from that surplus, one employs men with care, what shortage of talent could there be? In a realm as vast as All-under-Heaven, there is likewise no shortage of wealth; rather, when regular expenditures are extravagant and spending is in excess, there is all the more a shortage. If, starting from that excess, one economizes with care, what shortage of wealth could there be? When an enlightened ruler examines into these two matters, the various offices are left without neglect, the Six Treasuries of nature are all well maintained, and without stepping beyond the courtyard steps he revolves the empire in his hands. Your Honor has posed a policy question to the candidates on employing men and managing finances—is this not the great Way of governing the state? Allow me to set forth the essentials suited to the times. I humbly observe that in the empire today, moral transformation spreads far and wide, and the sound of stringed instruments and chanting of texts is heard for ten thousand li—who among them is not awaiting orders to serve? Scholars waiting upon selection by the Ministry of Personnel gather like fish scales at the imperial capital: what an abundance of talent! In the empire today, the central lands are girdled like a bowl, and tribute baskets arrive from ten thousand states—which of these is not delivered to the keepers of the state treasuries? Officials transporting the annual revenues follow carriage-to-carriage along the roads: what an abundance of wealth! Yet when selections must be made in an emergency, there is the sighing and slapping of the thigh for want of capable men; and when unscheduled provisions must be supplied, there is the anxiety of draining the marshes dry. Why is this so? I have humbly pondered this: the affairs of the empire are just like those of a household. When the members of a household manage their livelihood, in the beginning when they establish their estate amid hardship, a few servants suffice to be put to work, and a few pieces of gold suffice to bring about affluence. By the time later generations arrive, the household accumulates a thousand mouths, yet they are not even enough to match the usefulness of a single man; the grain baskets and coffers take in income daily, yet it is not even enough to meet the needs of a single morning. 置一歲漕粟數十萬石耳其後增置官七

用之愈匱有餘不足所以相反此其故歟

祖宗朝墾田征稅歲供有常額京朝外服位置
有常員載在職掌為萬世規當斯之時樞
機綜于上法守信于下懸不次以待儁英

punctuated:
異此？請借近事為喻：漢初併官，□□□中置一，歲漕粟數十萬石耳；其後增置官七千員矣，利析秋毫矣。唐初省官七百餘員，歲入二十萬耳；其後萬八千員矣，進奉無萬萬矣。宋初設官近萬員，内府出貸有司者且三百萬焉；其後三萬餘員矣，歲供至六千萬矣。始乎簡實，卒乎冗；始乎儉實，卒乎奢。人浮於虛名，財浮於虛費，取之愈多，用之愈匱，有餘不足所以相反，此其故歟？
惟我祖宗朝，墾田征稅，歲供有常額；京朝外服，位置有常員，載在職掌，為萬世規。當斯之時，樞機綜于上，法守信于下，懸不次以待儁英，朝詣公車，暮登鼎鉉，士無所芬華，而上重之，誰敢倖進其間者？浣濯在御，素絲在列，軍國之需，寬然有餘，屬有舉事，程盈縮而燭照之，又誰敢漁穴其間者？天下之士靡有伏遺，而官常不必備；天下事一切經營…
translation_en:
…differ from this? Allow me to draw analogies from more recent history. At the beginning of the Han dynasty, offices were consolidated, with one established among [?] [□□□], and the annual grain tribute transported by water was only a few hundred thousand piculs; later, officials were increased to seven thousand personnel, and profits were analyzed down to an autumn hair. At the beginning of the Tang dynasty, officials were reduced to just over seven hundred personnel, and annual revenue was only two hundred thousand; later, there were eighteen thousand personnel, and tribute presentations reached tens of millions without limit. At the beginning of the Song dynasty, nearly ten thousand officials were established, and the Inner Treasury even loaned three million to the authorities; later, there were over thirty thousand personnel, and the annual supply reached sixty million. What begins in simplicity and substance ends in superfluity; what begins in frugality and substance ends in extravagance. Men exceed need through empty titles, and wealth is wasted on empty expenditures; the more is exacted, the more scarce it becomes in use. Is this not the reason why surplus and deficiency are thus reversed?

In the reigns of our Imperial Ancestors, land reclamation, taxation, and annual supplies had fixed quotas; positions in the capital court and provincial administration had fixed numbers of personnel, recorded in the statutory duties as a standard for ten thousand generations. At that time, the pivotal administration was synthesized from above, and adherence to the law was trusted below. Extraordinary promotions were held ready to await outstanding talents: in the morning they reported to the Office of Public Carriages, and by evening they ascended to the high ministerial posts. Scholars had no ostentation, yet the ruler valued them—who dared seek advancement among them by mere luck? Washed garments were worn by the sovereign, and plain silk stood in the ranks of officials. The needs of the military and the state were amply met with surplus; whenever an undertaking arose, surpluses and deficits were measured and illuminated as if by torchlight—who then dared to prey and burrow for illicit gain among them? Among the scholars of the realm, none were left hidden or overlooked, yet offices did not always need to be fully staffed; in all affairs of the realm, everything was being planned and…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
創始而有無多寡常不必言豈不至足哉
歷禩二百時易事殊解額倍盈冗列洊置
輸鬻途岐遷敘太驟士競於趨進而當事
嘆才難矣鹽筴改折餉邊浩大內帑難程
更需外府權宜補濟靡弗竟盡而持籌詘
策矣積漸之弊已至若斯苟非作新而振
起之亦何異於前代之季世哉仰惟
皇上睿明天錫恭儉夙成
即位之初沛然發
===
勑勵之詔與廷臣更始頃又大計肆覲之吏
召問其廉能異等而治其尤不才者內外諸臣
有不洗心易慮而共職業者乎
內廷之供難裁也竊聞
留神裁省矣邊費工料存留逋積當覈也竊見
詔旨每下罔弗嚴稽之矣海內有不嚮風敦素
而登殷阜者乎執事謂持銓主計之臣何
以仰承萬一則愚竊計之矣盖天下有不
足之弊有有餘之弊今之用人者豈獨患

而登殷阜者乎執事謂持銓主計之臣何
以仰承萬一則愚竊計之矣盖天下有不
足之弊有有餘之弊今之用人者豈獨患
punctuated: 創始，而有無多寡常不必言，豈不至足哉！歷禩二百，時易事殊。解額倍盈，冗列洊置；輸鬻途岐，遷敘太驟；士競於趨進，而當事嘆才難矣。鹽筴改折，餉邊浩大；內帑難程，更需外府；權宜補濟，靡弗竟盡，而持籌詘策矣。積漸之弊，已至若斯，苟非作新而振起之，亦何異於前代之季世哉？仰惟皇上睿明天錫，恭儉夙成。即位之初，沛然發勑勵之詔，與廷臣更始；頃又大計肆覲之吏，召問其廉能異等，而治其尤不才者。內外諸臣，有不洗心易慮而共職業者乎？內廷之供難裁也，竊聞留神裁省矣；邊費、工料、存留、逋積當覈也，竊見詔旨每下，罔弗嚴稽之矣。海內有不嚮風敦素而登殷阜者乎？執事謂「持銓主計之臣，何以仰承萬一」，則愚竊計之矣。盖天下有不足之弊，有有餘之弊。今之用人者，豈獨患
translation_en:
… initiated from the beginning, yet whether there was something or nothing, much or little, never needed to be spoken of—was that not supreme sufficiency?

Through two hundred years, times have changed and affairs have grown different. The quotas of candidates forwarded from the provinces have multiplied, and superfluous posts have been repeatedly established; the paths of advancement through grain contributions and office purchase have branched out, and promotions in rank have become far too rapid; scholars vie with one another in rushing forward for advancement, while those in charge of affairs sigh over the difficulty of finding talent. Since the salt monopoly was converted to silver payments, the provisioning of the frontiers has grown vast; the Inner Treasury is hard to regulate and instead draws further upon the outer treasuries; every expedient measure to patch and relieve the shortfall has been exhausted, and those who hold the tallies are at their wits' end for a policy. The abuses accumulated gradually have already reached such a pass as this; if we do not renew and rouse things up, how will it differ from the declining ages of former dynasties?

Looking up, I reflect that His Majesty is endowed by Heaven with sagely intelligence and was early accomplished in reverence and frugality. At the very beginning of his accession to the throne, he abundantly issued edicts of admonition and encouragement to make a fresh start with his court officials; recently, at the Great Reckoning, he received the officials who came for audience, summoned and questioned those of exceptional integrity and ability, and punished the most incompetent among them. Among all the officials within the court and in the provinces, is there anyone who does not cleanse his heart, change his thoughts, and reverently attend to his duties? The supplies for the Inner Court are difficult to curtail, yet I have privately heard that he has given his attention to curtailing and economizing them; frontier expenditures, construction materials, revenues retained locally, and accumulated tax arrears ought to be audited, and I have privately observed that whenever an imperial edict is handed down, none fails to strictly investigate them. Within the four seas, is there anyone who does not turn toward this moral influence, esteem simplicity, and ascend to abundance and prosperity?

Your Excellency asks how the ministers who hold the scales of personnel evaluation and preside over fiscal calculation are to look up and fulfill even one ten-thousandth of His Majesty's intentions; I have privately given thought to this. In general, the empire suffers from the abuse of insufficiency and also from the abuse of surplus. Those who employ men today—do they merely worry about…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
乏人哉亦患賢不肖雜進飾其有餘者以
罔上之求而上不盡察此所以投之緩急
而不足也今欲治之其唯重士行乎理財
者豈獨患乏用哉亦患屑越於晏閒無益
之用恃其有餘莫肯顧惜此所以需之倉
卒而不足也今欲治之其唯重國計乎誠
使持銓者於用人之中而寓重士之意使
士皆有以自重而不炫飾于功名然後真
才可得而用也其說有三夫士惟質直不
===
阿而後能勿欺以事君若人者其執義常
固其持法常嚴則有所不諧于俗而士之
巧宦者或乃脂韋宛轉以求便於時用於
是擔荷之力弱而執諍之義微矣法紀之
壞未必不由於此愚以為用人莫若重質
直也名節士之藩墻未有寡廉鮮耻其中
能植者故林樾有弓旌之賁疎逖有夢卜
之求凡以抑浮鎮競而從雅化耳或乃謂
廉節為拘曲即清談玄論之士且如夜蛾

之求凡以抑浮鎮競而從雅化耳或乃謂
廉節為拘曲即清談玄論之士且如夜蛾
punctuated: 乏人哉？亦患賢不肖雜進，飾其有餘者以罔上之求，而上不盡察，此所以投之緩急而不足也。今欲治之，其唯重士行乎！理財者豈獨患乏用哉？亦患屑越於晏閒無益之用，恃其有餘，莫肯顧惜，此所以需之倉卒而不足也。今欲治之，其唯重國計乎！誠使持銓者於用人之中而寓重士之意，使士皆有以自重，而不炫飾于功名，然後真才可得而用也。其說有三：夫士惟質直不阿，而後能勿欺以事君。若人者，其執義常固，其持法常嚴，則有所不諧于俗；而士之巧宦者，或乃脂韋宛轉，以求便於時用，於是擔荷之力弱，而執諍之義微矣。法紀之壞，未必不由於此。愚以為用人莫若重質直也。名節，士之藩墻，未有寡廉鮮耻，其中能植者。故林樾有弓旌之賁，疎逖有夢卜之求，凡以抑浮鎮競，而從雅化耳。或乃謂廉節為拘曲，即清談玄論之士，且如夜蛾
translation_en:
…a shortage of men? They also suffer from the worthy and the unworthy advancing together, embellishing their superfluities to deceive the sovereign in his search for talent while the sovereign does not fully discern it—this is why, when cast into moments of crisis, they prove insufficient. If we wish to remedy this today, must it not be by prizing the moral conduct of scholars? For those who manage finances, do they merely suffer from a shortage of funds? They also suffer from squandering resources on useless expenditures in times of peace and leisure, relying on their surplus without anyone willing to cherish or spare it—this is why, when funds are needed in an emergency, they prove insufficient. If we wish to remedy this today, must it not be by prizing the fiscal plans of the state?

If those in charge of personnel selection truly embed the intention of prizing scholars within the process of employing men, causing scholars to all have the means to respect themselves and not show off or embellish themselves for the sake of merit and fame, only then can true talent be obtained and used. There are three arguments for this:

First, only when a scholar is upright, straightforward, and unbending can he serve his ruler without deception. Men of this sort are always firm in upholding righteousness and always strict in maintaining the law, and thus they are somewhat out of harmony with vulgar custom. Meanwhile, scholars who are clever at official careers may instead be as pliable as greased leather and accommodating, seeking convenience for current employment; consequently, the strength to shoulder heavy responsibilities weakens, and the principle of firm remonstrance fades. The deterioration of laws and discipline does not necessarily fail to stem from this. I humbly consider that in employing men, nothing is better than prizing straightforwardness.

Second, reputation and integrity are a scholar's protective wall; there has never been one lacking in modesty and a sense of shame who could stand firm within. Therefore, in the forest shades there were the honors of bows and banners used to summon recluse worthies, and among the distant and estranged there were searches conducted through dreams and divination—all in order to suppress superficiality, calm ambitious competition, and follow refined transformation. Yet some call integrity and modesty narrow-minded and rigid, and even scholars who engage in pure conversation and abstruse discourse are like night moths…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
之赴燭而人滋不敢信矣愚以爲用人莫
若厲廉耻也人之才故不甚相遠其能肩
鉅致遠者類沉涵而不耀乃戔戔者流則
經綸在唇吻耳世或覩其唇吻而任焉功
不可成者倖其成法不當變者輕於變非
是則彼無所售其技而天下滋紛紛矣愚
以爲用人又莫若毋急功名也夫養德望
厲廉隅遵成法此非
上之德意乎誠奉宣斯意以作新今日之才譬
===
若操斧柯而適鄧林之野即勁榦弗勝材
也如此則官安得冗而天下豈真少於才
也哉主計者於惜財之日常存惜民之心
使所節者必有寬於國課而上不藉是以
爲用然後財可得而足也其說亦有三前
代會計有籍必準于初制以知登耗之由
謂宜籍今之出入一稽于舊貫從其所以
約酌其所以浮品式成書宮府一體玩好
營作皆可防於未萌而冗濫亦不勝節矣

也如此則官安得冗而天下豈真少於才
也哉主計者於惜財之日常存惜民之心
使所節者必有寬於國課而上不藉是以

約酌其所以浮品式成書宮府一體玩好
營作皆可防於未萌而冗濫亦不勝節矣
punctuated:
之赴燭，而人滋不敢信矣。愚以爲用人莫若厲廉耻也。人之才故不甚相遠，其能肩鉅致遠者，類沉涵而不耀；乃戔戔者流，則經綸在唇吻耳。世或覩其唇吻而任焉，功不可成者倖其成，法不當變者輕於變，非是則彼無所售其技，而天下滋紛紛矣。愚以爲用人又莫若毋急功名也。夫養德望、厲廉隅、遵成法，此非上之德意乎？誠奉宣斯意以作新今日之才，譬若操斧柯而適鄧林之野，即勁榦弗勝材也。如此則官安得冗，而天下豈真少於才也哉？

主計者於惜財之日，常存惜民之心，使所節者必有寬於國課，而上不藉是以爲用，然後財可得而足也。其說亦有三：前代會計有籍，必準于初制，以知登耗之由。謂宜籍今之出入，一稽于舊貫，從其所以約，酌其所以浮，品式成書，宮府一體，玩好營作，皆可防於未萌，而冗濫亦不勝節矣。
translation_en:
…darting toward a candle flame, so that people become even more afraid to trust them. In my humble opinion, in employing men there is nothing better than sharpening the sense of integrity and shame. Men's talents by nature do not differ greatly from one another. Those capable of shouldering great burdens and reaching distant goals are generally deep, self-contained, and unostentatious, whereas shallow and petty types have all their statecraft on the tips of their tongues. When the world sees their glib talk and entrusts them with office, they gamble on success in undertakings that cannot succeed, and lightly alter laws that ought not to be altered—for otherwise they would have no way to peddle their skills, and the realm is thrown into ever greater confusion. In my humble opinion, in employing men there is also nothing better than not being overeager for quick achievements and fame. Now, nurturing moral prestige, encouraging upright conduct, and abiding by established laws—are these not the benevolent intentions of His Majesty? If we truly uphold and proclaim these intentions so as to invigorate and renew the talents of today, it will be like taking an axe handle and going into the wilderness of the Deng Forest (Denglin): there will be more sturdy trunks than one can ever cut for timber. If this is done, how could offices be superfluous, and how could the realm truly be lacking in talent?

Those in charge of fiscal administration, in a time of economizing on wealth, should always preserve a heart that cherishes the people, ensuring that whatever is saved goes to ease the state's tax quotas and that the court above does not rely on those savings for its own expenditures; only then can wealth be made sufficient. For this, too, there are three proposals. In previous eras there were registers of accounts (kuaiji lu) that were always benchmarked against the original foundational regulations in order to understand the causes of increases and decreases. I submit that we should compile a register of present revenues and expenditures and verify everything against the old precedents—following where they were frugal and weighing why they have become inflated—and codify the standards and formulas into a book by which the inner palace and the outer government abide as one body. In this way, curiosities, luxuries, and construction projects can all be forestalled before they even sprout, and superfluous extravagance will be curbed beyond measure.…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
是故制財之出莫若定經費也凡財之羨
苟無漁蠹積月累日有時而盈方今
主德躬素疆圉晏如內之供應外之調發必有
積餘視嘉隆間寧啻數倍而或乾沒於私
橐蠶食於豪猾有羨餘之名無積貯之實
諸如此類宜令計臣條上其弊而一清之

translation_en:
Therefore, to regulate fiscal expenditures, nothing is better than establishing fixed regular budgets. Whenever there is a surplus of revenue, if there are no predatory embezzlers or parasites, it will accumulate over months and days and in due time reach fullness. At present, our Sovereign in His virtue personally practices frugality, and the frontiers are peaceful; in both internal provisioning for the court and external troop deployments and requisitions, there must be an accumulated surplus—how could it be merely several times greater than during the Jiajing (1522–1566) and Longqing (1567–1572) reigns? Yet some of it is embezzled into private pockets or nibbled away like silkworms by powerful and cunning scoundrels, so that there is the name of a surplus without the reality of stored reserves. In all matters of this sort, the fiscal ministers should be ordered to itemize the abuses in memorials and thoroughly clear them away; then perhaps the annual tax quotas can be supplemented and the material strength of the people can be given relief. Therefore, to audit the accumulation of wealth, nothing is better than clearing out the sources of abuse. From antiquity, the source of wealth has come from the cultivated fields—even Guan Zhong and Yan Ying were able to speak of this. At present, north and south of the Yangtze and Huai rivers, places everywhere are desolate and bleak. Good local administrators should be selected to grant the people complete rest and recuperation in all things. When firewood-gathering is strictly prohibited, curved shoots and sprouts all grow to maturity; when the well-rope does not enter, the dredged well naturally becomes clear. Therefore, to nurture the source of wealth, nothing is better than not treating the strength of the people lightly. Personally practicing frugality, valuing the livelihood of the people, and clearing up arrears and accumulations—are these not the benevolent intentions of His Majesty? If we truly uphold and propagate these intentions in order to economize and nurture the wealth of the empire, it is like gathering a hundred rivers and pouring them into the vast expanse of the ocean: even the smallest trickle becomes moisturizing grace. If this is done, how could expenditures become superfluous, and how could the empire truly be lacking in wealth!

Even so, in the employment of men today, the laws have not been ruined, so one can discuss it as easily as pointing to one's palm; managing finances, however, is the most difficult of difficulties. Moreover, …

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
宗藩歲禄可九百萬盡天下不足以供足自
益乎各邊歲餉可三百五十餘萬歲入止
什之四况日重乎議者謂事窮宜變請開
四業之途而常患親親之情有未通又謂
安邊足食宜復屯鹽之舊入粟塞下而常
患歲額之需有難處今者上下泰交奚情
弗通節約裕人何事難處誠及此時思亢
極之勢圖長永之策毅然集議斷以必行
豈特省天下財力之大半已乎夫會簿書
===
慎出納者有司之守也酌經權圖久大者
經國之慮也今
天子方虛心慎好以臨天下而或因循旦暮無
以定萬世之長策雖杞藿之徒安敢謂非
公卿大臣之責也

公卿大臣之責也
punctuated: 宗藩歲禄可九百萬，盡天下不足以供，足自益乎？各邊歲餉可三百五十餘萬，歲入止什之四，况日重乎？議者謂事窮宜變，請開四業之途，而常患親親之情有未通；又謂安邊足食，宜復屯鹽之舊，入粟塞下，而常患歲額之需有難處。今者上下泰交，奚情弗通？節約裕人，何事難處？誠及此時思亢極之勢，圖長永之策，毅然集議，斷以必行，豈特省天下財力之大半已乎？夫會簿書、慎出納者，有司之守也；酌經權、圖久大者，經國之慮也。今天子方虛心慎好以臨天下，而或因循旦暮，無以定萬世之長策，雖杞藿之徒，安敢謂非公卿大臣之責也！
translation_en: …the annual stipends for the imperial clansmen amount to some nine million, which the resources of the entire empire are insufficient to supply—can that suffice to benefit them themselves? The annual military provisions for the various frontier garrisons amount to more than three million five hundred thousand, while annual revenues cover only four-tenths of that—how much more so when the burden grows heavier by the day? Those who deliberate on state affairs say that when matters reach an impasse there ought to be change, and they ask to open the path of the four occupations to the imperial clan, yet they constantly worry that the sentiment of affection for kin may not be fully accommodated; they also say that to pacify the frontiers and provide sufficient food, we ought to restore the old system of military state farms and the salt monopoly, having grain delivered directly to the frontier posts, yet they constantly worry that the required annual quotas in silver will be difficult to manage. Now, when ruler and ministers are in harmonious communion, what sentiment cannot be communicated? When frugality is practiced to enrich the people, what matter is difficult to manage? If we truly take advantage of this moment to ponder the trend that has reached an unsustainable extreme, plan permanent and far-reaching policies, resolutely gather for deliberation, and decide with a determination to carry them out, would this merely save more than half the financial resources of the empire and nothing more? Now, keeping account books and exercising caution over receipts and disbursements is the duty of the functioning officials; weighing standard principles against expedient measures and planning for what is enduring and great is the concern of statecraft. Today the Son of Heaven is justamente governing the empire with an open mind and prudent desires; if anyone should merely follow routine from day to day without establishing a long-term policy for ten thousand generations, even humble folk who eat wild greens and bean leaves—how could they dare say this is not the responsibility of the high ministers and great officials!

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the spring of the second year of the Wanli reign (1574), scholars from throughout the realm accompanied the tribute-bearing officials up to the Ministry of Rites. His Majesty commanded Grand Secretary, your servant [Lü] Tiaoyang (呂調陽), to oversee the evaluation of their literary compositions, and assigned your servant [Wang] Xilie (王希烈) to assist him as vice examiner. Having reverently discharged our duties and brought the affair to completion, the examination record has been compiled for presentation to the throne. By virtue of my official duties, your servant Xilie ought to append a few words on the final slips by way of further admonition to the many scholars.

Your servant reflects that in the well-governed ages of antiquity, people esteemed uncarved simplicity and purity, looking to those above to see what to love and what to hate. Those above practiced fasting and purification before speaking to them, and used drumming and song to inspire and animate them. The essential aim lay in establishing the Supreme Standard (Huangji), enabling all under Heaven to attain fulfillment in their innate nature and emotions, while dissolving their selfish tendencies toward factionalism and perverse partiality. Thus, whenever they were tried and employed, they unfailingly yielded substantial results, and customs and achievements were glorious and admirable; this too was the effect of how those above swayed them. In later ages, moral teaching declined, and scholars steeped their minds in belles-lettres and utilitarian gain. Then, even though those above established examination regulations and instituted selection guidelines in the hope of obtaining worthy men, none who were genuinely benevolent in substance and steadfast in righteousness were found fit to fill the offices. Indeed, human minds and the Moral Way of the world have weighed upon one another for a long time.

Now the Son of Heaven embodies sagely virtue in His own person, treads upon a flourishing destiny, reflects upon the wellsprings of moral transformation, and answers above to the beginnings of antiquity. translation_en: …the prescribed format of the authorities. Given my own foolishness and narrowness, to have me seek out scholars through their literary craft and gauge whether the inclinations of their hearts and minds are upright or not—like guessing what lies beneath an overturned bowl—can this not be called difficult? Moreover, this difficulty does not apply to me alone. Indeed, as the ancient saying goes: "To be a subject and official is not easy." Now, when serving an enlightened and sagely ruler, it is difficult to measure up to his expectations; when encountering an era of order and peace, it is difficult to distinguish oneself. I humbly observe that His Majesty is endowed by Heaven with sagely qualities; having succeeded to the throne at a flourishing young age, he daily grants audience to the assembled officials and personally decides affairs of state. Even the one or two veteran statesmen well-versed in precedent wait upon his inquiries with reverent trepidation, fearing only that they might fail to match His Majesty's intentions. Furthermore, this coincides with a time when the realm, both within and without, is free from alarm, moving with awe-inspiring momentum toward the flourishing state in which every household is worthy of enfeoffment and even the most distant barren lands belong to a single family. Even if a scholar has some service he wishes to render, how could it be hastily achieved between morning and evening…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
援契而取者故曰難也抑臣
又聞天下無不可任之事亦
無不能任事之人精祲之變
也金石之堅也而意有所注
則鬼神助之此事易任之效
也才有細鉅可量而受智有
淺深可諗而圖力有強弱可
===
併而趨抱關之守其神凝而

punctuated: 援契而取者？故曰難也。抑臣又聞：天下無不可任之事，亦無不能任事之人。精祲之變也，金石之堅也，而意有所注，則鬼神助之，此事易任之效也；才有細鉅，可量而受，智有淺深，可諗而圖，力有強弱，可併而趨，抱關之守，其神凝而無外慕，則其上無不可為者，此人能任事之效也。故任事非難，正心術為難。平好惡則心正，審趣舍則心正，先公家後私家則心正，先人後已則心正，先事後功則心正，心正
translation_en: …be grasped as if holding a tally and claiming one's due? That is why I say it is difficult. Yet your servant has also heard that in the world there is no affair that cannot be shouldered, nor any person incapable of shouldering affairs. Subtle and ominous are the transformations of atmospheric vapors, and hard are metal and stone; yet when one's intent is focused upon them, even ghosts and spirits lend their aid—this is the proof that affairs can easily be shouldered. Talents may be small or great, yet one can measure them and accept a fitting charge; wisdom may be shallow or deep, yet one can deliberate and lay plans; strength may be vigorous or weak, yet one can pool it and press forward. If a humble gatekeeper keeps his spirit concentrated and harbors no extraneous ambitions, then for those above him there is nothing that cannot be accomplished—this is the proof that men are capable of shouldering affairs. Therefore, shouldering affairs is not what is difficult; rectifying the disposition of the mind is what is difficult. When likes and dislikes are balanced, the mind is rectified; when what one pursues and what one eschews are carefully examined, the mind is rectified; when the public interest is put before private family interest, the mind is rectified; when others are put before oneself, the mind is rectified; when the task is put before the reward, the mind is rectified. Once the mind is rectified…

title: 萬曆二年會試錄
text:
而行業從之矣且
主上信至神聖豈嘗令禹司稼夷
典樂重課人以不及之事而
士即以時平無所表見至如
砥節奉公於日用猶水火可
不勉哉臣誠自度駑下不敢
望孟氏知言之萬一顧今日
===
所圖報
上者惟此心所期信于多士者亦
惟此心多士且謂何矣昔洪
範敘休徵之應曰乂用明俊
民用章士當斯時稟仰
皇極正心術以應

punctuated: 而行業從之矣。且主上信至神聖，豈嘗令禹司稼、夷典樂，重課人以不及之事？而士即以時平無所表見，至如砥節奉公，於日用猶水火，可不勉哉？臣誠自度駑下，不敢望孟氏知言之萬一，顧今日所圖報上者惟此心，所期信于多士者亦惟此心，多士且謂何矣？昔《洪範》敘休徵之應，曰：「乂用明，俊民用章。」士當斯時，稟仰皇極，正心術以應上求，亦
translation_en: …and their conduct and accomplishments will follow. Moreover, our Sovereign Lord is truly most divine and sage; would He ever order Yu 禹 to manage agriculture or Yi 夷 [Kui 夔?] to direct music, heavily tasking men with matters beyond their reach? And even if scholars have no way to distinguish themselves because the times are peaceful, when it comes to honing their integrity and devoting themselves to the public good—which in daily life are as essential as water and fire—how could they not exert themselves? Your servant truly measures himself as dull and inferior, not daring to hope for even one ten-thousandth of Mencius's (Mengshi 孟氏) understanding of words. Yet today, that by which I seek to repay the Sovereign is solely this mind, and that by which I hope to be trusted by the many scholars is likewise solely this mind; what, then, will the many scholars say? In antiquity, when the "Great Plan" (Hongfan 洪範) set forth the responses of auspicious signs, it said: "When order is achieved through enlightenment, men of eminence are thereby made manifest." For scholars at this time to revere and look up to the August Ultimate, rectifying the art of their minds in order to respond to the Sovereign's search, is likewise…

translation_en:
… an auspicious sign for the Dynasty. Your servant shall divine this from the very beginning of their becoming distinguished. With this, I conclude my words.
Respectfully prefaced by Wang Xilie 王希烈, Grandee for Aid in Governance, Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently Academician Reader-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy, in charge of the affairs of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent.
